## Filing the first source that is not an arXiv paper, and moving to luria 0.8

*2026-09-05 16:31:47 · curation · tooling*

**The Falcon-H1-Tiny blogpost ([LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md)) and what filing it required
([ADR-009](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-009.md)).** The request was to add one
technical blogpost to the corpus. It turned into three pieces of work, and
the order they arrived in is the useful part.

**Getting the text.** The sandbox's egress policy blocks `huggingface.co`,
the Space's `hf.space` subdomain, the Wayback Machine and the authors' own
sites, so the article could not be fetched. The Space's page on
huggingface.co is only a wrapper: it embeds the article in an iframe and
carries none of its text, so pasting that page's HTML yields metadata
(created 2026-01-15, last modified 2026-01-16) and nothing else. A PDF
export of the article, supplied by hand, did work — after two false starts.
`pypdf` and `pdfminer.six` both import the system `cryptography` wheel,
which is broken in this image (`_cffi_backend` missing, a pyo3 panic on
import); `pymupdf` bundles its own renderer and extracted all 71 pages
cleanly. Worth knowing before the next PDF.

**Filing it.** `luria new lit` scaffolds `arxiv: '0000.00000'`, and the
scheme required the field. The blogpost has no arXiv posting — its own
BibTeX is `@misc{falcon_h1_tiny}` with no identifier — and the two ids it
could borrow (the Falcon-H1 report, the learnable-multipliers preprint)
name other documents. The wrong theory, briefly held: that the `arxiv:`
field is what the ARXIV remote resolves, so a wrong id would at least be
caught. It is not; the field is a plain required field, and the remote only
resolves `ARXIV-` codes in prose. A borrowed id would have passed silently.
Luria 0.7 ships `field_groups` with `require = "at-least-one"`, in exactly
this shape in its `knowledge-base` example, so the fix was configuration
plus a decision record rather than code.

**Upgrading.** The workflow pinned luria 0.4.2 in three places (two action
tags and a `pip install`); 0.8.0 and then 0.8.1 were published the same
day as this entry, the second carrying the two fixes below.
The upgrade's one visible effect on the record: `luria lint` now reports a
`status:` that carries a note, and `luria repair` moves the note to
`status_note:` and the successor to `superseded_by:`. It did so for eleven
documents, writing the successor as a one-item list under `superseded_by:`.
A `grep` for the key showed the key alone, I read that as "empty", and the
scalar I filled in by hand sat above the list item — invalid YAML that took
the next `luria index` down. The repair had been right; look at the file,
not the grep. Two other repaired notes ([LIT-031](../../record/literature.d/LIT-031.md), [LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md)) named their
successor only in prose, which the repair cannot read; 0.8's lint asks for
the code in `superseded_by:`, and they now carry it. Two luria gaps came out of
[LIT-031](../../record/literature.d/LIT-031.md): an arXiv code in `superseded_by:` was truncated to `ARXIV-2110`
before the check saw it, and a `# inactive-ok:` comment in the frontmatter
was not read, so the only acknowledgement that reached the field was
file-scoped. Both are fixed upstream in 0.8.1 (dmarx/luria#163); the note
now names both successors and excuses the rejected one at the field.

**Tracing the references.** The blogpost cites 56 works. Ten of them are
invoked to justify a decision rather than to name a benchmark, a baseline,
a data source or a serving tool, and none of the ten was in the corpus:
the Falcon-H1 report the architecture and µP recipe come from, the
learnable-multipliers preprint, the Muon scaling report, the looping paper
that explains the chain-of-thought filtering, the three FIM papers, GRPO,
Falcon-H1R for the reasoning data, and a tiny-model DPO write-up that is
itself a blog post — the second `url:`-only note, filed a day after the
rule that allows one. Left out at first: Olmo 3, cited only to describe the
pipeline the authors depart from — and that was the wrong cut. An anthology
that keeps what it stopped believing ([DP-003](../design-principles.md#dp-3)) needs the predecessor filed,
not only the successor, or the departure has nothing to be traced back to.
Olmo 3 is now [LIT-130](../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md), the three-stage recipe it states is [SOTA-129](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-129.md), its
<!-- inactive-ok: SOTA-130 — a Proposed practice, named as part of the chain -->
RL-Zero variation is [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md), and the anti-curriculum names both. Left out
still: SmolLM2, MobileLLM-R1, Gemma 3 and
Qwen3 as comparison points; FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu as sources; and every
benchmark paper. The abstracts had to come from search snippets — arxiv.org,
its export API and Semantic Scholar are all blocked from the sandbox — so
each note records what the paper establishes at abstract depth, and no
practice is drawn from any of them yet.

**Kimi K3, and the chain it closes.** Added on request, and it turned out
to be the far end of a chain the blogpost had opened. [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) adopts Muon
with weight decay and RMS matching from the Moonshot scaling report; Kimi
K2 found that recipe lets attention logits run past 1000 at a trillion
parameters and added QK-Clip; K3 keeps the result at 2.8T. So K3 came in
with K2, and the Muon practice from the blogpost now names its successor
rather than standing as the last word. K3's architecture is likewise three
published papers assembled — Kimi Linear's interleaved delta-rule attention,
Attention Residuals, and its own LatentMoE — and the record files the two
papers rather than sourcing practices to the report, whose ablations I
could not read. The K3 report is on arXiv, so nothing here needed the
`url:` field; the abstracts again came through search, since arxiv.org is
unreachable from the sandbox.

**Qwen3.8-27B, and the correction it forced.** Added on request. It has no
report — the citation block on its GitHub page points at a blog post whose
title is about a different model — so it is the record's third `url:`-only
note, sourced to the model card. Two things came out of tracing it. First,
the predecessor is Qwen3.6-27B, not 3.5: the 3.8 configuration is
byte-for-byte the 3.6 architecture, and the generation's gains are
post-training. Second, the architecture is the Qwen3-Next design of
September 2025, which shipped the 3:1 Gated DeltaNet to gated-attention
hybrid a month *before* Kimi Linear's controlled comparison — so the
hybrid-attention practice I had sourced to Kimi Linear and described as
lacking independent replication had, in fact, been preceded in production
by the other group. The practice keeps Kimi Linear as its source (it is
the paper with the fair comparison) and now carries the sequence from the
Gated DeltaNet paper's own hybrids through Qwen3-Next to the two current
lines. The two layer types got their own papers filed and a practice each.
qwen.ai, alibabacloud.com and the model card are all unreachable from the
sandbox; the numbers come from search snippets of the card and the post.

**DeepSeek-V4, and the first practice filed already retired.** Added on
request. V4 sits at the end of three lines the record now carries: Muon (a
third laboratory, reportedly without QK-Clip because QK-norm does the same
job — marked as reported, since the report itself is unreachable), sparse
attention (NSA → DSA → CSA/HCA, each DeepSeek's own), and the residual.
The residual line is the instructive one. ByteDance's Hyper-Connections
widened the stream with free mixing and reported gains; DeepSeek's mHC
paper says the free mixing broke identity mapping and could not scale,
and constrains it. That is a supersession in the plain sense, so the
<!-- inactive-ok: SOTA-137 — a Superseded practice, named as the predecessor in the chain -->
record files both: [LIT-141](../../record/literature.d/LIT-141.md) and [SOTA-137](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-137.md) arrive `Superseded` by [LIT-140](../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) and
<!-- inactive-ok: SOTA-136 — a Proposed practice, named as part of the residual chain -->
[SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md), with the reason in the status note — the first documents in this
anthology filed retired on arrival, because a reader who meets mHC needs to
know what it fixed, and [DP-003](../design-principles.md#dp-3) says the contrast is the content. mHC's
sibling, Attention Residuals, stays a separate Proposed practice; the two
replacements for the residual have not been compared by anyone, and the
record says so from both sides.

**What the blogpost is worth.** Single-run ablations at one size, on
benchmarks the authors call noisy at 90M. Every practice from it is scoped
to tiny models, and two are `Proposed` rather than `Active` — the
learnable multipliers because the larger-scale evidence lives in a preprint
not in the record, and the memorization window because the source itself
says the study is future work. Filing a hedge as a hedge is what the status
field is for.

## Filing the schedule and parameterization the 2025 recipes assume, and retiring the cosine practice

*2026-09-05 18:38:20 · curation*

**Seven papers the record was already leaning on.** After the Falcon-H1-Tiny
work merged, a pass over the corpus showed that every 2025–2026 report it
holds trains with a stable-then-decay schedule and several with µP, while
the corpus's own schedule practice was still GPT-3's single cosine cycle and
µP appeared only as a word inside other notes. The recommendation was to
file this group first, and this entry does: WSD as MiniCPM shipped it, the
Hägele et al. study that measured it against cosine, the Power scheduler
that sets its peak, Straight to Zero on how far the decay should go, and
the µP → u-µP → CompleteP line for hyperparameter transfer.

<!-- inactive-ok: SOTA-039 — the retired cosine practice, named as the predecessor in the chain -->
**The first retirement on later evidence.** [SOTA-039](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-039.md), "single cycle of cosine
decay is sufficient", was one of the 119 migrated practices. It is now
`Superseded` by the WSD practice, with the reason in its status note and a
short section in its body saying what it got right — one cycle over
several — and what moved — the cycle's shape. That makes the schedule chain
<!-- inactive-ok: LIT-042 — the retired warm-restarts paper, named as the start of the schedule chain -->
readable from warm restarts ([LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md), retired at migration) through cosine
to WSD, and it is the first time a practice this record inherited has been
retired by a practice it added. [DP-003](../design-principles.md#dp-3) in action rather than in prose.

**Statuses, and why two are Proposed.** Linear decay to zero is one group's
study, and the production recipes already in the record still decay to a
floor, so the record does not yet assert it. CompleteP is one group and no
production run. Both say what would promote them. The Power scheduler is
Active on the strength of Falcon-H1-Tiny adopting it independently, which
is the kind of evidence the earlier entries kept asking for.

**Method note.** Abstracts again came through search snippets, arxiv.org
being unreachable from the sandbox; each note claims that depth. The
scaffolding fix from earlier today held: no HTML comments in frontmatter,
checked strictly before pushing.

<a id="20260905191918"></a>

## Checking twenty-five notes filed without a network, and what that says about which claims to distrust

*2026-09-05 19:19:18*

[LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) through [LIT-143](../../record/literature.d/LIT-143.md) were filed in a session with no outbound network.
This entry is what came back when every one of them was checked against
its source.

## The headline is that the notes held up

All twenty-five arXiv identifiers resolve, and every resolved title matches
the recorded title exactly. That is worth stating plainly because the prior
was the opposite: the batch includes five works published after the filing
model's training cutoff, and identifiers are the easiest thing in the world
to confabulate. They were not confabulated. Neither were the hard numbers.
[LIT-134](../../record/literature.d/LIT-134.md)'s Attention Residuals note gives GPQA-Diamond +7.5, Minerva Math
+3.6, HumanEval +3.1, a 1.25x compute advantage and sub-2% latency
overhead; all five are in the paper, verbatim. [LIT-135](../../record/literature.d/LIT-135.md) claims Qwen3.8-27B
carries the same configuration as Qwen3.6-27B — every field of the two
`config.json` files is identical, which is a stronger claim than the note
makes. [LIT-142](../../record/literature.d/LIT-142.md)'s indexer warm-up (1,000 steps, 16 sequences x 128K tokens,
2.1B tokens) is exact. [LIT-139](../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md)'s whole DeepSeek-V4 paragraph — 33T and 32T
tokens, the 4K/16K/64K/1M ladder, dense warm-up for 1T tokens, sparse
attention introduced at 64K — is exact.

## Where it broke is more interesting than that it broke

Five errors, and four of them share a shape: **the note is precise where
its source is vague.**

- [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) said Tulu3 was repeated "on the order of 400 times". The blogpost
  says ">=100 repetitions". The direction of the error is invention of
  precision, not a misreading.
- [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) said learnable multipliers give "up to a 20% relative gain on
  MMLU, BBH and GSM8K" at 200 GT. The blogpost quantifies nothing here — it
  shows a plot and says "considerable and consistent". The preprint has the
  numbers, and they do not support the sentence: the average moves +1.10
  points, BBH +3.39 and GSM8K +2.61 carry it, and **MMLU is flat**, 47.98
  against 47.96. A benchmark named as improving was the one benchmark that
  did not move.
- [LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) gave Kimi K3's context window as "1,048,576 tokens". The report
  says one million. 2^20 is the kind of number that is *right-looking*
  rather than sourced.
- [LIT-140](../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) read a single 6.7% overhead figure, stated once at expansion rate
  n = 4, as "6-7% at 3B, 9B and 27B" — the three sizes of a different
  experiment in the same paper, welded onto the one number.

The fifth is a naming error in the same family: [LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) attributed
"MuonClip" to the K3 report, which never uses the word. It says "the
weight-clipping mechanism introduced in Kimi K2". The substance was right
and the citation was not.

The lesson for the next offline batch is narrow and usable: **prose about
mechanisms survived without a network; digits did not.** Where a note is
vaguer than you expect, that is usually the source being vague, and
sharpening it is where the error enters.

## A hedge that was right, and worth keeping the habit

[LIT-139](../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) said DeepSeek-V4 drops QK-Clip and added "the report's own wording
has not been read". The report's wording is "Consequently, we do not employ
the QK-Clip technique in our Muon optimizer", and the reason is an RMSNorm
on queries and compressed KV entries. The guess was correct, and the hedge
still earned its place — it is what made the claim cheap to resolve rather
than something to re-derive. That is the pattern to keep.

## What the network turned up that no amount of care would have

Two papers, both from after the batch was written:

- **oHC** ([LIT-151](../../record/literature.d/LIT-151.md)) argues against [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) on its own terms. mHC's doubly
  stochastic constraint bounds the mixing factor at one from above and
  nothing from below, and the paper proves the slack is spent shrinking the
  differences between streams — so the widened residual homogenizes with
  depth, which is the thing widening it was for.
- **The Qwen3.8-Next design report** ([LIT-152](../../record/literature.d/LIT-152.md)) runs mHC, Attention
  Residuals and its own Gated Residual in one harness. They come out level.
  [LIT-134](../../record/literature.d/LIT-134.md) and [LIT-140](../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) both said, correctly at the time, that no such
  comparison existed.

Neither retires anything. oHC is one model size from one group and says so;
mHC ships in a 1.6T-parameter model. But [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md)'s *reason* is weaker than
it was this morning, and a reader meeting it should meet both papers.

## A finding outside this batch

The check was run over all 139 arXiv identifiers in the record, not just
the new ones, and 53 of the pre-existing 118 fail. Some are truncations —
[LIT-100](../../record/literature.d/LIT-100.md)'s title is the real paper's title with the subtitle dropped. Many
are not: [LIT-099](../../record/literature.d/LIT-099.md) is filed as the PaLM 2 technical report against an
identifier belonging to a paper on quantum secret sharing. These came in
with the migration and are recorded here rather than fixed, because the
right repair is per-entry and wants its own contribution.

<a id="20260905200044"></a>

## A quarter of the practice registry rested on papers that do not exist

*2026-09-05 20:00:44*

Checking the newly filed notes against arXiv meant checking all of them, and
the result was worse than the batch that prompted it: **53 of 139 arXiv
identifiers did not resolve to the paper the note named.** This entry is
about the 31 that were not cosmetic, and particularly about the 16 that
turned out not to be citation errors at all.

## Two different failures wearing the same shape

The cosmetic 22 are unremarkable — a dropped subtitle, or a nickname the
record had prepended, `AdamW:` in front of *Decoupled Weight Decay
Regularization*. Worth fixing because a title is a claim about what was
published, and one of them was materially wrong: [LIT-031](../../record/literature.d/LIT-031.md) read "Neural
Networks are Surprisingly Modular" when the paper is "***Pruned*** Neural
Networks are Surprisingly Modular", which is a different and much weaker
statement.

The other 31 pointed at real papers on unrelated subjects. [LIT-099](../../record/literature.d/LIT-099.md) cited
measurement-device-independent quantum secret sharing as the PaLM 2
technical report. [LIT-059](../../record/literature.d/LIT-059.md) cited electron losses in hypersonic flows for
checkpointing advice. [LIT-063](../../record/literature.d/LIT-063.md) cited chromatic number and Hamiltonicity of
graphs for compiler optimization. The identifiers were syntactically
plausible and in the right year range, which is exactly why nothing caught
them: `2111.09432` looks like a checkpointing paper from late 2021 if you
don't fetch it.

## The part that mattered

Splitting the 31 by whether the recorded title named a findable work gave 15
that did and 16 that did not. The 16 share a signature:

- a generic title of the form *A Systematic Approach to X* or *X for
  Large-Scale Models*, naming no specific contribution;
- exactly four takeaway bullets, each a noun phrase, none a claim — "Pipeline
  optimization strategies", "Memory management techniques", "Bottleneck
  analysis";
- an author surname that is plausible for the field and unconnected to any
  such work. WebDataset was attributed to *Amodei et al.*

These were never citation errors. They are synthetic entries that entered
with the pre-migration YAML, and **39 practices — a little over a quarter of
the 139 in the registry — were sourced to them.** [SOTA-042](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-042.md) through [SOTA-045](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-045.md)
on data loading, [SOTA-054](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-054.md) through [SOTA-057](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-057.md) on checkpointing, [SOTA-081](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-081.md)
through [SOTA-084](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-084.md) on compilers: real, sensible advice, resting on nothing.

## Why we did not just retire them

The obvious move — mark the 16 `Rejected`, let the lint light up 39
practices — is what [DP-1](../design-principles.md#dp-1) seems to demand, and it is wrong. It converts a
quiet problem into a loud one without fixing anything: the advice in those
practices is not bad, it is *unattributed*, and deleting its attribution
leaves the reader worse off than a wrong citation did. A registry with a
quarter of its entries flagged is a registry nobody reads.

So each of the 16 was re-sourced in place to the work its practices actually
rest on, with `history:` recording what the entry used to claim. The
mappings were not hard to find once the question was asked properly — not
"what paper has this title" but "what published work is this practice an
instance of":

- checkpointing frequency, async writes, multi-level strategy → **CheckFreq**
- operator fusion, memory layout, hardware mapping → **TVM**
- fuse ops, align dimensions, memory access patterns → **Data Movement Is
  All You Need**
- tar archives, sharded streaming → the **actual WebDataset paper**, which
  exists, and whose real title is *High Performance I/O For Large Scale Deep
  Learning*
- loss spikes, gradient-norm ratios, NaN detection → **GLM-130B**, which is
  in the record precisely because it published its failures

Nine more practices did not need a new note at all: the right paper was
already in the corpus and nobody had connected them. [SOTA-050](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-050.md) says "scale
attention weights by 1/sqrt(head_dim)" and is now sourced to *Attention Is
All You Need*, which is where that comes from, and which the record has held
as [LIT-008](../../record/literature.d/LIT-008.md) the whole time.

## Two things found on the way

**A repair can create a duplicate.** Correcting [LIT-105](../../record/literature.d/LIT-105.md)'s identifier landed
it on 2302.06675, which [LIT-090](../../record/literature.d/LIT-090.md) already held — the migration had filed one
paper twice, once under its title and once under the name of the optimizer
it discovers. Nothing in `luria lint` looks at whether two documents name
one source, so the corpus held a contradiction (one note `Rejected`, one
`Proposed`, same paper) with a green build. Filed as luria#165.

Worse, [LIT-090](../../record/literature.d/LIT-090.md)'s retirement reason — "a research direction without
demonstrated practical impact" — had been written against the synthetic
four-bullet summary rather than against the paper, which is the Lion
optimizer with cross-domain results and a named production deployment. The
status is left as found, because reversing it is a curation call and not a
citation repair, but it is now labelled as inherited and unreviewed.

**Retirement is sometimes the lazy answer.** [LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md) was `Superseded` with
the note "single-cycle cosine decay proved better at scale" — a correct
judgement, recorded against "SGDR++", which does not exist. Retiring the
note would have broken the schedule chain that PR [#16](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/16) builds on. Re-sourcing
it to the real SGDR keeps the chain and keeps the judgement, which now
applies to the paper that actually made the claim.

## What is left

Three places where a practice and its new source disagree are marked rather
than smoothed over. [SOTA-055](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-055.md) gives an epoch-based rule for saving optimizer
state; CheckFreq's whole argument is that iteration granularity is available
and epochs are the wrong unit. [SOTA-078](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-078.md) and [SOTA-080](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-080.md) give a buffer size and
a worker count that are operational folklore, not results in the WebDataset
paper. [SOTA-100](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-100.md) asks for warmup proportional to model size; its new source
shows the need for warmup is a property of Post-LN and largely disappears
under Pre-LN.

Those are re-readings for someone with the practices in front of them, not
citation work. The point of leaving them visible is that they are now
*answerable*: the practice names a paper you can go and read.

<a id="20260905202452"></a>

## The schema could not represent the problem it had, which is why nobody saw it

*2026-09-05 20:24:52*

Two days of citation repair ended with a question worth more than the
repair: why did a record built specifically to make evidence structural sit
for two years with a quarter of its practices resting on papers that do not
exist?

The answer is not that nobody looked. It is that **the schema had no way to
express the difference between a well-supported practice and an unsupported
one**, so looking would not have helped.

## The cardinality was the camouflage

`source:` held exactly one code. That made every practice look identical in
the only dimension that matters for judging evidence: each had one source,
so each was maximally sourced.

The 39 practices that turned out to rest on synthetic notes were therefore
*indistinguishable from the best-supported practices in the registry*.
[SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md) (use Muon) has scaling-law evidence, a 1T-parameter production run
and independent adoption at 90M. [SOTA-044](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-044.md) ("pin memory for CPU-GPU
transfers") had a fabricated citation. Both had one source. Both passed the
lint. Nothing could ask the question that separates them.

Meanwhile the practices with the *most* evidence were the ones the field
served worst. [SOTA-132](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-132.md)'s body names seven notes; its `source:` named one. So
the structured field was not merely uninformative for the strongest entries
— it was actively misleading, reporting one paper where seven exist. That is
[DP-002](../design-principles.md#dp-2)'s failure mode with a twist: not a field that says nothing, but a
field that says something false with confidence.

[ADR-010](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-010.md) makes it a list. The immediate payoff is a query that could not be
written before:

    Proposed practices, by source count:
      [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md)  1   [SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md)  1   [SOTA-125](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-125.md)  1   [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md)  1
      [SOTA-133](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-133.md)  1   [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md)  1   [SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md)  1   [SOTA-144](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-144.md)  1

All eight sit at exactly one. That is the record obeying a rule it had
written down in prose and could not enforce — [LIT-121](../../record/literature.d/LIT-121.md) and [LIT-134](../../record/literature.d/LIT-134.md) each say a
practice "stays Proposed until a result from outside the authors' group is
in the record". It was true, and until now, unverifiable.

## The guard was fired before it was trusted

Following luria's rule that a new check runs once on a real case first,
three deliberate breakages, all caught:

- `source: LIT-999` → *resolves to no LIT document*
- `source: ADR-001` → *is not a LIT code — a SOTA document's `source` names
  a LIT document*
- a valid first element with a broken second → *LIT-998 resolves to no
  document*

The third is the one that matters, and is the reason `many = true` is not
cosmetic. Without it luria stringifies a list and checks only its first
element, so a practice could name one real note and three imaginary ones and
pass. That is the exact failure this record just spent two days repairing,
and it would have been reintroduced by a plural `source:` declared carelessly.

## What was rejected, and why it was tempting

`source:` plus a separate `corroborated_by:` reads better and keeps the
primary unambiguous. It was rejected because it asks the filer to grade
evidence at the moment they are least able to: whether a second paper
corroborates a practice or merely touches it usually becomes clear only when
a third arrives. A flat list with a meaningful first element records the one
thing reliably known at filing time — which paper this came from — and defers
the grading. The graded version can be layered on; ungrading would mean
re-litigating every entry.

## The collision, and the thing luria already had

Two branches opened ninety minutes apart both minted [LIT-144](../../record/literature.d/LIT-144.md) and [LIT-145](../../record/literature.d/LIT-145.md) for
different papers. Nothing would have caught it: each branch was internally
consistent, `luria lint` had no reason to look, and git merges two files with
different names and no conflict. It was caught because one session read the
other's pull request.

luria has had `allocate = "merge"` and temporary codes for exactly this the
whole time, and this record had never turned it on — the default is
filing-time allocation, and the default had been fine while there was one
contributor. [ADR-013](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-013.md) turns it on for all four schemes.

The lesson generalizes past numbering: **the record adopted a tool and then
used the parts of it that resembled what it did before.** Field groups,
reference typing with `many`, merge allocation, content pins — all of it was
sitting in the configuration surface unused, and two of the four failures
this week were things luria could already prevent. The next review should
probably read `luria --help` against the record rather than the other way
round.

## Left open

[ADR-011](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-011.md) (lineage as a field) and [ADR-012](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-012.md) (practice altitude) are filed as
Proposed rather than adopted, because both need something before they are
safe: [ADR-011](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-011.md) needs a chain view upstream, since a relation that is declared
but never rendered looks maintained while rotting, and [ADR-012](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-012.md) needs its
three-value vocabulary tried on the practices whose filers are still
reachable before it is imposed on the inherited 119.

<a id="20260905215138"></a>

## The first backlog group corrected the practice it was filed to support

*2026-09-05 21:51:38*

Group 2 of [#17](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/17) was catalogued as "extends the Muon chain". It does, and it
also does something the catalogue only hinted at: it takes a number out of a
live practice.

## The 2× was not wrong, it was unaccompanied

[SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md) recommends Muon, sourced to the Falcon-H1-Tiny blogpost and
resting on [LIT-122](../../record/literature.d/LIT-122.md)'s scaling-law claim of "roughly 2× the computational
efficiency of AdamW". Wen et al. tune ten optimizers *separately* — the
baseline included — across 0.1B–1.2B and 1–8× Chinchilla, and measure at the
end of training. They get **1.4× at 0.1B, falling to 1.1× at 1.2B**.

Two of their methodological findings explain how a larger figure is reached
honestly:

1. **Optimal hyperparameters do not transfer between optimizers.** Handing
   the challenger the baseline's schedule, or vice versa, is the ordinary way
   a comparison tilts, and it tilts toward whichever one the schedule was
   tuned for.
2. **Rankings flip mid-run.** Two optimizers compared before the target
   budget can swap places by the end, because learning-rate decay has not
   finished. Any number read off an intermediate checkpoint is provisional.

Neither is an accusation against [LIT-122](../../record/literature.d/LIT-122.md) — different scales, budgets and
baselines, and Moonshot's runs are at a scale Wen et al. never reach. But the
record was quoting one number as though it were the answer, and it is the
high end of a range whose low end is 1.1×.

**The practice did not move; the number did.** 1.1× at 1.2B is still free
once the recipe is in place; the optimizer-state saving and the
hyperparameter transferability are not what that study measures; and every
frontier adopter the record holds — Kimi K2, K3, DeepSeek-V4 — trains orders
of magnitude above the largest model tested. What changed is that [SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md)
now carries a "How much it buys" section with the range in it, and says
plainly which figure to stop repeating.

This is the first time a backlog item has revised a practice rather than
adding to one, and it is an argument for working the backlog rather than
only extending the frontier: the papers that check earlier claims are less
exciting to file and are where the corrections live.

## A convergence worth the filing

The Hyperball follow-up and Learnable Multipliers ([LIT-121](../../record/literature.d/LIT-121.md)) turn out to be
about the *same phenomenon*, from groups citing different literatures.

Both start from the observation that under weight decay a matrix settles at
an equilibrium norm determined by the hyperparameters rather than by the
data. LRM concludes the scale should be **learned** and gives it its own
parameter. Hyperball concludes the scale should be **removed** as a degree of
freedom and pins the Frobenius norms to constants. Both report gains over the
same baseline; Hyperball adds the claim that this equilibrium is *why*
matrix optimizers' advantage shrinks with scale, which — if it holds — makes
the shrinkage an artefact of a tuning convention rather than a property of
the optimizer.

Nothing here promotes [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md). Its stated condition is a result from outside
the authors' group, and this is the same group with a different remedy. But
the two notes now sit next to each other, which is the point of filing the
predecessors.

## Filing notes

Seven notes, all written from the papers. All six with arXiv identifiers pass
`source-mismatch` against what the API serves, which is the first time that
check has run on notes as they were written rather than on a corpus being
repaired.

The Muon blog post is the third `url:`-only source after Falcon-H1-Tiny and
BytePS, and the clearest case for [ADR-009](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-009.md) yet: three laboratories pretrain
frontier models with this optimizer and there is no paper to cite. [LIT-122](../../record/literature.d/LIT-122.md),
[SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md) and [SOTA-131](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-131.md) each described it as "not in the corpus"; three
sentences deleted.

[SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md) is also the first practice to use [ADR-010](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-010.md)'s plural `source:` for what
it was designed for — an entry whose body already leaned on four notes while
the field named one.

## What is left

Groups 3, 4 and 5 of [#17](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/17): architecture (MoE, MLA, Mamba, MTP — about fifteen
papers), data (five), post-training (seven). All 33 identifiers in the issue
were verified against the API before any of this was written, and all 33
resolve. Two of the issue's own titles were slightly off — 2501.00656 is
titled "2 OLMo 2 Furious", and the "seen by title only" guess for 2606.16899
was exactly right.

<a id="20260905222121"></a>

## Filing the predecessors turns a list of models into a set of arguments

*2026-09-05 22:21:21*

Groups 3, 4 and 5 of [#17](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/17) — 27 notes. The catalogue described them as gaps,
and filling them mostly did what filling gaps does. Three things it did that
a catalogue could not predict.

## The record now holds a disagreement it was only half of

[SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md) says high-quality data can be repeated freely when its epoch
size exceeds the model's memorization window, which is how Falcon-H1-Tiny
repeated Tulu3 a hundred times. It was filed *Proposed* with a note that this
"compares with the standing guidance that repetition past about four epochs
stops paying" — guidance the record did not contain.

It does now, and there are three positions rather than two:

- **Four epochs** ([LIT-166](../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md)) — up to four epochs of repeated data
  changes loss negligibly against unique data; past that the value of added
  compute decays to zero. 400 runs, up to 900B tokens and 9B parameters.
- **Epoch size, not epoch count** ([SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md)) — one figure and an argument
  its own authors call early.
- **Augmentation** ([LIT-175](../../record/literature.d/LIT-175.md)) — autoregressive pretraining overfits
  severely under repetition, but the overfitting belongs to the *objective*
  and is removable, so hundreds of epochs become productive.

The third is the useful one because it makes the other two falsifiable in
shared terms: if augmentation is what buys productive multi-epoch training,
a recipe repeating a source a hundred times is either augmenting implicitly
or paying an unmeasured cost. And the first two may not conflict at all — one
repeats a whole corpus at fixed compute, the other one source inside a
mixture where a small share means a long delay between repeats. Nobody has
run the experiment that separates them, which is now written down where the
practice is.

## Two model reports explained a design the record had only observed

Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 and DeepSeek-V4 all ship a multi-token-prediction head that
is later fine-tuned into an EAGLE-3-style draft model. Each report states it
as settled fact. The record had recorded the arrangement three times without
holding either paper.

Filed together, they explain it, and the explanation is a coincidence rather
than a design: [LIT-163](../../record/literature.d/LIT-163.md) proposes multi-token prediction as a *training*
objective that improves sample efficiency at no training cost, mentioning
faster inference as a side-effect. [LIT-185](../../record/literature.d/LIT-185.md) designs a draft model whose
structure happens to match what that objective leaves behind. Neither
proposes the combination. The model reports discovered it, and which of the
two motives is doing the work at frontier scale is not isolated by any of
them.

## The residual constraint is now the least defended part of its own practice

[SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) recommends mHC — widen the residual into several streams, mix them
with doubly stochastic matrices. Within one month two groups disputed the
*constraint*, from opposite directions:

- **oHC** ([LIT-151](../../record/literature.d/LIT-151.md)): the doubly stochastic set is bounded above but not
  below, so mixing can only shrink what distinguishes the streams, and the
  streams homogenize with depth.
- **sHC** ([LIT-181](../../record/literature.d/LIT-181.md)): the same set is degenerate near the identity, and
  its non-negativity forbids subtractive feature disentanglement entirely.

Different arguments, same verdict, opposite remedies — a rotation group
versus a spectral sphere. Meanwhile Qwen's Gated Residual ([LIT-152](../../record/literature.d/LIT-152.md)) drops the
mixing matrix altogether and matches.

What all five papers agree on is untouched: widening the stream helps, and
the mixing needs *some* constraint. That agreement is probably the practice
the record should carry, and [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) currently carries something narrower
and more contested. Left as a note rather than acted on — rewriting a
practice to be about what its literature agrees on is a bigger move than a
backlog pass.

## My own check caught my own bug

Running `luria lint` over the finished 186-note corpus produced one
`source-mismatch`:

    `arxiv: 2404.19737` resolves to "Better &amp; Faster Large Language
    Models via Multi-token Prediction", not "Better & Faster Large Language
    Models via Multi-token Prediction"

arXiv's Atom feed serves escaped XML and the resolver never unescaped it. A
false positive, and the kind that gets a category switched off — fixed
upstream at the fetch rather than at the comparison, so the lockfile records
a title rather than markup.

Worth recording as a pattern rather than a bug: **every fixture had an ASCII
title.** The check was tested against invented data that shared an
unexamined assumption with the code, and only a real corpus of 186 notes
had an ampersand in it. This is the third time in two days that running
something on the actual record found what the tests could not.

## Costs

The lint now takes about a minute on a contribution that adds 16 notes,
because `network = "auto"` fetches each unknown identifier with a courtesy
delay. That is the design working — the alternative is a freshly typed wrong
citation passing silently — but "bounded by how many citations a
contribution adds" reads differently at 1 than at 27, and a batch this size
is better served by running `luria remotes --resolve` once up front.

<a id="20260905231501"></a>

## Two promotion conditions were met on the same day; only one of them should have been applied

*2026-09-05 23:15:01*

[#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) asks for three things: deepen the notes written from abstracts, verify
the claims marked as reported, and re-examine the `Proposed` practices whose
promotion condition was "the larger-scale evidence lives in the preprint".
The third turned out to be the interesting one, and not for the reason the
issue anticipated.

## Two conditions met, one applied

[SOTA-133](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-133.md) (Attention Residuals) and [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) (mHC) were filed a day apart
with nearly identical conditions — one group, one paper, one production
model; *promote on an independent result*. The Qwen3.8-Next design study
([LIT-152](../../record/literature.d/LIT-152.md)) is an independent result for **both**: a different laboratory
ran both designs in its own harness against its own competing one, and found
all three level.

By the letter, both promote. Only one did.

**[SOTA-133](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-133.md) is now Active.** An outside group with a rival design implemented
AttnRes, measured it, and it worked — 1.762 against 1.789 for the pre-norm
baseline. That is the strongest form the condition could have asked for, and
there is nothing pulling the other way.

**[SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) stays Proposed**, and the practice now says why in those terms
rather than leaving the status as a silent non-decision. Two *other*
independent results arrived in the same window and both attack the specific
thing it recommends — the doubly-stochastic constraint. [LIT-151](../../record/literature.d/LIT-151.md) proves the
Birkhoff polytope is bounded above but not below; [LIT-181](../../record/literature.d/LIT-181.md) names identity
degeneration, an expressivity bottleneck from non-negativity, and unstable
Sinkhorn projection. Opposite remedies, same verdict on the constraint.

So the practice's **claim** has independent support and its **mechanism**
has independent opposition, and "an independent result" cannot tell those
apart. The condition was the wrong condition — it counted papers when it
should have asked what they were papers about.

That is the transferable lesson: a promotion condition phrased as a
*quantity of evidence* will eventually be satisfied by evidence pointing the
wrong way. The conditions in this record should say what a result has to
**show**, not how many there have to be.

## The same failure, caught earlier, in [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md)

[SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md) asked for "an independent reproduction **or** a result above 1B".
[LIT-153](../../record/literature.d/LIT-153.md) is an independent group at 1.2B working on precisely the
phenomenon the practice rests on — the weight-decay equilibrium that fixes a
matrix's norm by hyperparameters rather than data — who confirm the
diagnosis and adopt the **opposite** remedy: pin the norms to constants
rather than give the scale a learned parameter.

Confirming the mechanism while declining the fix satisfies the `or` and
means nothing. The condition now asks for gains from learned per-row and
per-column multipliers specifically. [SOTA-144](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-144.md) gets the same treatment for
the same paper's depth-transfer result: two routes to one property is
evidence the property is reachable, not that this route works.

## The reported claims

Both outstanding items from [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18)'s checklist resolve against the primary
sources, and both were slightly wrong in ways worth having caught:

- DeepSeek-V4's FP4 quantization-aware training does cover "MoE expert
  weights and the indexer QK path" — but the report places it in
  **post-training**. [LIT-139](../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) had it in a pretraining-infrastructure bullet.
  The distinction matters: [LIT-186](../../record/literature.d/LIT-186.md) shows quantization damage grows with
  how much data a model was trained on, so *where in the pipeline* the low
  precision sits is the decision, not an implementation detail.
- Kimi K3's gated MLA is **not** quite [SOTA-134](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-134.md)'s gate. The report says "an
  input-dependent, channel-wise full-rank output gate"; the practice's source
  ablates a *head-specific* sigmoid. Same position in the block, same
  justification, finer granularity — so the practice covers it, and the
  granularity is a free parameter nobody has swept. [LIT-138](../../record/literature.d/LIT-138.md)'s "appears to be
  the same idea" is replaced with what the report actually says.

## What reading the report rather than the abstract bought

[LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) was the last note still declaring itself filed at abstract depth.
Reading it turned up something no abstract would carry and that bears on a
practice: **Kimi K3 applies no positional encoding at all to its MLA
layers**, letting the interleaved KDA layers supply position sensitivity and
recency instead.

The consequence the report names is the useful part — extending the context
no longer means retuning a RoPE frequency base or applying YaRN, because
there is no positional parameter in the global layers to retune. That is a
*second* argument for the hybrid layout, independent of cost per token, and
[SOTA-132](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-132.md) was filed without it. It also makes [SOTA-139](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-139.md)'s staged context
extension a smaller operation for anyone using the layout.

Which is the case for [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) in one paragraph: the abstract tells you what a
paper claims, and the report tells you which of the record's other claims it
touches.

<a id="20260906003150"></a>

## Nine promotion conditions, written honestly, and what writing them exposed

*2026-09-06 00:31:50 · record*

The rule [ADR-014](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-014.md) adopted is that a `promote_when:` names a *kind* of
result, not a quantity of them, and the test is: could this be satisfied by a
paper that would not actually change my confidence? Writing nine of them was
supposed to be the real test of the rule. It was, and the interesting part is
how often the honest answer was narrower than the practice's own body
suggested.

Three of the nine had to be written as **exclusions**, because the evidence
that does not count had already arrived:

- [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md) (learnable multipliers) waits on a group *training with them*.
  [LIT-153](../../record/literature.d/LIT-153.md) confirmed the weight-decay equilibrium the practice diagnoses, at
  1.2B, from an independent group — and adopted a different remedy. Confirming
  a diagnosis is not adopting a treatment.
- [SOTA-144](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-144.md) (CompleteP) waits on a group training *under CompleteP*. [LIT-153](../../record/literature.d/LIT-153.md)
  again: depth transfer reached by pinning weight-matrix norms instead. Two
  routes to one property is evidence the property is reachable.
- [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) (mHC) waits on an answer to the Birkhoff-polytope objection, not
  on a further independent evaluation — one of those arrived and is the
  reason this practice's condition had to be rewritten at all.

Two turned out to be waiting on something the field may never produce in the
form the practice asked for:

- [SOTA-120](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-120.md) is `Deferred` because the *claim* is settled and its adoption
  is not, so its condition asks for a report that states the choice rather
  than leaving it implicit in a config. Most reports do not.
- [SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md) (decay to zero) had to exclude a comparison that shares one peak
  learning rate across schedules, because that compares peaks, not schedules
  — which is the whole methodological point of the source paper.

And one — [SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md), the memorization window — turned out to be waiting on a
*second measurement of the same quantity*, which nobody has published. The
practice rests on one data point plus an assumed linear scaling in
parameters. Writing that down as a condition is the first time the record has
said so plainly.

The count that matters: before today, four of 144 practices stated a
condition anywhere, all in prose. Now every practice that is not in force
states one, in a field, and the lint will not accept a new provisional
practice without it.

<a id="20260906171657"></a>

## Ten consensus readings, and the 134 the record admits it has not made

*2026-09-06 17:16:57 · record*

The new axis is only worth having if the values are defensible, so the
editorial rule was: assign where the record already carries the grounds, and
leave everything else `unassessed`. That produced ten, and the shape of the
ten is itself informative.

**Four `unreplicated`** — [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md), [SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md), [SOTA-125](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-125.md), [SOTA-144](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-144.md). All four are
one group, one result, and in every case the record already said so in the
body; what it could not say is that nobody has *disagreed* either. That is the
distinction `Proposed` was hiding, and it is the difference between "waiting
for someone to look" and "people looked and differ".

**Two `contested`** — [SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) and [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md). Both have credible published
opposition: two independent critiques of mHC's constraint within a month, and
[LIT-167](../../record/literature.d/LIT-167.md) undercutting the attribution RLVR-Zero rests on. Neither is a doubt
this record invented; both are arguments happening in public.

**Two `emerging`** — [SOTA-133](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-133.md) and [SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md). Moving, not arrived. [SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md) is
the more interesting: nobody argues decay-to-zero is *wrong*, the frontier
recipes in this record simply still decay to a floor. "Not adopted" and
"disputed" are different states and now say so.

**Two at the top** — [SOTA-001](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-001.md) `universal` and [SOTA-120](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-120.md) `converged`.

[SOTA-120](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-120.md) is the one that justifies the whole change. It is `Deferred` — the
record declines to assert it — and `converged`, because AdamW is the default
optimizer and decoupled decay is what nearly everyone runs whether or not
they chose it. **High consensus, low editorial confidence.** One axis cannot
hold that, and the practice has been sitting in an uncomfortable status for
weeks because of it.

What I deliberately did not do: file the trunk practice. [LIT-181](../../record/literature.d/LIT-181.md) says the
record should *probably* carry "widen the residual stream, constrain the
mixing somehow" *eventually*, and turning that hedge into an assertion is a
judgement someone should make on purpose rather than a side effect of
building the mechanism to hold it. The fork renders without it.

The number to watch is 134. Most of this corpus has no consensus reading, and
the default makes that visible rather than papered over — but it also means
the axis is one person's ten judgements until somebody does the rest.

<a id="20260907033446"></a>

## GRPO enters the practice registry, in two pieces

*2026-09-07 03:34:46 · practices*

Two notes had already asked this question and left it open on purpose.
[LIT-168](../../record/literature.d/LIT-168.md): *"whether GRPO's successors warrant a practice of their own depends
on whether the anthology wants to carry RL algorithm choice as practice, and
nothing does yet."* [LIT-180](../../record/literature.d/LIT-180.md): *"the RL-algorithm question stays out of the
practice registry until the record decides it wants to carry it."*

The record has decided. The gap those notes were describing is precise:
[SOTA-129](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-129.md) and [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md) argue about *when* to run RL with verifiable rewards —
three stages, or skip the SFT one — and neither names an algorithm, while
GRPO is cited by five notes and is what all of them actually run.

## Why two documents and not one

Filing "use GRPO" would have asserted something this record's own evidence
contradicts. [LIT-168](../../record/literature.d/LIT-168.md)'s standing section says it outright: *"'we ran GRPO' is
under-determined: three papers within a year each found a different defect in
it worth naming."*

So the evidence was split where it actually splits.

**Agreed:** drop the critic, take the baseline from a group of samples for the
same prompt. [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) runs it at 0.6B, and [LIT-167](../../record/literature.d/LIT-167.md), [LIT-168](../../record/literature.d/LIT-168.md) and [LIT-180](../../record/literature.d/LIT-180.md) each
examined this objective closely enough to publish a correction — and not one
of them proposed bringing the critic back. That is what `converged` records:
not that nobody looked, but that people looked hard and changed something
else.

**Unsettled:** the rest of the objective. Dr. GRPO's length bias, DAPO's
decoupled clip and dynamic sampling, GSPO's sequence-level importance ratio.
Three defects, three fixes, no two the same, and no comparison.

## The word that did not fit

The fork looked like `contested` — an agreed trunk with disputed branches is
the phrase in `consensus.yaml` itself. It is not.

`contested` means credible groups publicly disagree, and these three are not
arguing with each other; each found a real defect, published a real fix, and
left the others alone. [ADR-016](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-016.md) is what made the difference legible: it
requires a `contested` practice to name what contests it, and there was
nothing honest to put in the field. Three sources agreeing that a thing is
broken are not evidence against the practice that says so.

`emerging` — several independent groups, moving toward a default without
being there — is the accurate reading, and the guard is what forced looking
for it.

## What would move it

The `promote_when:` asks for a comparison of the three corrections on one base
and one dataset, or a frontier recipe naming which it runs and why —
explicitly not a fourth paper naming a fourth defect. Three already exist, and
that is the problem rather than the evidence.

<a id="20260907034818"></a>

## Two Active practices that disagreed, and the paper neither of them knew about

*2026-09-07 03:48:18 · practices · corrections*

Looking for practices hidden from the graph the way GRPO was turned up
something worse than an absence.

## The record was arguing with itself

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| [SOTA-023](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-023.md) | `Active` | "Use multi-query attention for decoder-only models" |
| [SOTA-024](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-024.md) | `Active` | "Keep key/value projections shared across heads" — the same paper, the same claim |
| [SOTA-109](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-109.md) | `Active` | "Prefer GQA to MQA or MHA" |

All three in force at once. Two of them recommend the thing the third
recommends against.

None of this was visible to any check. Each document is individually valid —
a real source, a resolvable code, a status from the vocabulary — and nothing
in the record compares two practices' *claims*. The lint cannot know that
"use MQA" and "prefer GQA to MQA" are the same question answered twice.

All three were migration stubs: a title, a source line, no body. That is what
made it survivable for so long. A practice with no body has nothing to
contradict.

## And the successor was sitting in the corpus

[LIT-174](../../record/literature.d/LIT-174.md) is DeepSeek-V2, the MLA
paper. Its own standing section says filing it "closes the largest single hole
the architecture half of the record had" — and then no practice was drawn from
it. Meanwhile [SOTA-132](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-132.md) already
recommends a layer layout **defined in terms of MLA layers**, so the record
was recommending a ratio of a thing it had never defined.

MLA is filed `Active`, `emerging`. `Active` because four models across two
labs from 236B to 1.6T is unusually strong evidence for an architecture
choice. `emerging` because two labs is not the field: Llama, Qwen and Mistral
still ship GQA, and the record is out slightly ahead of consensus here, which
is the corner [ADR-015](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-015.md) added the second
axis to be able to say.

It does **not** supersede GQA. They are `compared_against`: two answers to the
KV cache that give up different things, and GQA stays the default for a model
not paying MLA's implementation cost.

## Two attributions that were simply wrong

`first_author: 'Dao'` on Shazeer's "Fast Transformer Decoding". `'Yang'` on
Ainslie's GQA. Both propagated into three practice summaries.

Checked against the arXiv API rather than corrected from memory, which is the
same standard the id repair held itself to. Worth noting what the existing
guard does and does not cover: `luria lint` compares recorded **titles**
against arXiv, so both notes passed every run. Nothing checks authors.

## What the temp code hid

[SOTA-145](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-145.md) cites [SOTA-146](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-146.md) in prose without an acknowledgement, and that
finding could not appear until after the merge that concretized the codes.

This entry first said that was because "there was no document for it to have
a status", which is wrong: the file existed throughout and carried
`status: Proposed` in its own frontmatter. The real reason is two independent
blind spots, and both had to be true for the finding to stay hidden.

**The document was not loaded.** `Scheme.documents()` keyed by number and
skipped any file it could not get one from, so a temp-coded document never
reached `load_docs()`. The status checker held no record of it at all.

**The citation was not scanned.** `ref_status.CODE_RE` required digits —
`[A-Za-z]{2,10}-\d{1,4}` — so a temp-tailed code was not read as a citation
site either.

So a merge-allocated document was invisible to the status checker from both
ends, and the asymmetry was the interesting part: the *link* checker handled
temp codes fine, which is how `luria link --fix` wrote these references in
the first place. Reference resolution and reference *standing* disagreed about
whether a temporary code is a code, and only one of them said so.

Filed upstream as [dmarx/luria#203](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/203)
and fixed in luria 0.10.4, which loads merge-allocated documents alongside the
numbered ones and admits the temp tail to the citation pattern. This record has
pinned that version since [#53](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/pull/53).

<a id="20260907040501"></a>

## The premise a dozen recommendations rested on

*2026-09-07 04:05:01 · practices*

[LIT-170](../../record/literature.d/LIT-170.md) left this open with an
argument, not a shrug: whether the anthology should carry MoE routing as
practice "is not obvious… since the choice is upstream of almost everything it
does recommend."

That argument is worth answering rather than dismissing, because it is half
right. Being upstream is exactly why the record should say it — once, plainly
— rather than leave it as the unexamined premise of everything downstream.
[SOTA-146](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-146.md) is what made the cost visible:
it carries a caveat that the RL objective is unstable on mixture-of-experts
specifically, qualifying an architecture the registry had never recommended.
A caveat with nothing behind it.

## What the corpus actually supports

The claim is filed `Active`, `converged`, on four labs and every frontier model
the record holds from 2024 on — DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba, NVIDIA. The one
dense frontier recipe in the corpus is Llama 3, from 2024.

The evidence is ratios rather than scores, which is how an efficiency claim
should be read: DeepSeekMoE 16B matching LLaMA2 7B at ~40% of the compute,
145B approaching the same team's dense 67B at 28.5%.

The design half is separate and weaker — `emerging`, not `converged`. Fine
segmentation plus a shared expert is DeepSeek's shape, taken further by Kimi
K3's 16-of-896, and the record does not know whether Qwen or NVIDIA segment
this finely. You can accept sparsity and reject fine segmentation, so the two
are filed apart.

## The part that was wrong, and then was not

[LIT-170](../../record/literature.d/LIT-170.md) did not introduce
mixture-of-experts. It diagnoses "conventional top-K-of-N routing, as in
GShard" and improves on it — and the corpus held no GShard, no Switch
Transformer, no Shazeer 2017. The trunk practice was drafted sourced against
[#17](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/17)'s own rule
that a practice names the paper that introduced the change, naming the paper
that measured it instead.

That gap is closed in the same contribution rather than deferred. All three
are filed, the practice is sourced to Shazeer et al. (2017), and the record
holds the line end to end:

    the sparsely-gated layer      2017   capacity without compute, and the
                                         auxiliary balancing loss
      GShard                      2020   into the transformer, sharded; top-2
        Switch Transformers       2021   top-1, float32 router, a trillion
        DeepSeekMoE               2024   many small plus one shared

Reading it as a line is what makes it worth holding. GShard says route to two
experts, Switch says one, DeepSeekMoE says many small ones and take more of
them — three answers to how finely the router should choose, and the record
recommends the third.

The same span covers load balancing, which is the nicer find. Shazeer's paper
introduces an auxiliary loss for balance because the gate self-reinforces;
[SOTA-148](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-148.md) recommends taking that loss
back out seven years later. The record now holds both ends of one argument
that ran for the whole history of the technique.

## Three documents, one family

[SOTA-148](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-148.md) gains an `extends:` so the
chain page shows what [LIT-171](../../record/literature.d/LIT-171.md)
predicted — "three practices' worth of material with nowhere to sit" — now
sitting somewhere:

    make the layer sparse            (Active, converged)
      keep the experts balanced      (Proposed, unreplicated)
      cut the experts up finely      (Active, emerging)

Three claims a reader can accept or reject independently, which is why they
are three documents.

<a id="20260907055403"></a>

## Reading the primary sources for the five claims #18 flagged

*2026-09-07 05:54:03*

The session that filed those notes could not reach arxiv.org, huggingface.co
or the model cards — every request returned an egress 403 — so five claims
were written from secondary coverage and labelled as such. This session can
reach all of them. Full HTML for all three arXiv reports, and the Hub for the
Qwen configs.

**All five hold.** That is worth saying plainly, because the interesting
outcome of a verification pass is usually a correction and this one has
almost none. The record was accurate about what it had, and honest about
where it got it.

What changed is the standing of the claims, and in two places their
precision:

- The Qwen3.8-vs-3.6 configuration claim was the weakest of the five, resting
  on somebody else's comparison of two files. Fetching both and diffing them
  makes it the strongest: they differ in exactly one key,
  `transformers_version`, which records the library that serialised the file.
  Every architectural field — `model_type`, all 64 entries of `layer_types`,
  the head counts on both attention paths, `attn_output_gate`, the vision
  block — is identical. "Same configuration" understated it.
- DeepSeek-V4's refusal of QK-Clip was the claim most likely to have been
  garbled in transmission, because it inverts a practice this record holds.
  It is not garbled: the report has a heading for it and one sentence that
  says exactly what the note said it did.

## The one thing that was wrong was a guess about what a paper contains

[LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md)'s *Standing* said the K3 report's "ablation tables are still
unmined". Nobody had looked. The report has five tables — an architectural
comparison with K2, two benchmark tables, an in-house web-development
comparison, and third-party evaluations — and **not one component ablation**.

That matters more than the sentence did. The headline claim is roughly 2.5×
the scaling efficiency of K2, read off fitted scaling-law curves on held-out
out-of-distribution data, and the report credits it to the architectural,
data and training changes *collectively*. There is no number in it that
apportions the gain to Attention Residuals, or the KDA/MLA hybrid, or the
LatentMoE. A future reader tempted to cite K3 as evidence for any one of
those components has to know that, and now the note says it.

The general lesson: "the ablations are unmined" and "there are no ablations"
look identical from outside a paper, and only one of them is a promise the
record can keep.

## A finding that is not this issue's

Reading K3 §3.2 turned up a controlled comparison the record needs to answer
for. The team argues that comparing warmup-stable-decay against cosine under
one hyperparameter set is unfair — the two schedules' optimal peak learning
rates and batch sizes differ substantially even at matched size and budget,
so a shared setting silently favours whichever it suits. They run an
independent scaling-law search per schedule, and under each schedule's own
optimum cosine decay consistently reaches the lower final loss. K3 adopts
cosine.

[SOTA-140](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-140.md) says to use WSD, is Active, and its summary claims WSD is "the
schedule of every 2025–2026 report in the record". A July 2026 frontier
report that ran the fairer comparison and went the other way is exactly what
[ADR-016](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-016.md)'s `contested_by` was added for. The finding is in [LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) here,
where it belongs; what it costs the practice is a judgement about the state
of the field rather than a fact about a paper, so it is filed on its own.

## The transcribed Falcon numbers hold, and no Proposed practice moves

*2026-09-07 06:05:02*

Two items off [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18), both of which could have gone either way and both of
which came back mostly negative. Negative results are the ones that go
unrecorded, so they are recorded here.

## The spot-check found no misalignment

[#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) flagged that the benchmark figures in [SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md) – [SOTA-128](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-128.md) came from a
PyMuPDF extraction of the Falcon-H1-Tiny blogpost's PDF export, and that
table extraction can silently misalign columns. The rendered post is
reachable now, so every figure the record attributes to it was checked
against the HTML tables.

They all hold, and the column assignments in particular hold:

- [SOTA-123](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-123.md)'s IFEval pair, `50.1 vs 40.8` before DPO and `66.1 vs 53.5`
  after, maps onto the post's four columns — SFT 40.77, SFT-DPO 53.47,
  SFT-pretrain 50.11, SFT-pretrain-DPO 66.08 — in the right order, which is
  exactly what a misaligned extraction would have got wrong.
- [SOTA-123](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-123.md)'s reasoning row (AIME24 6/30 vs 3/30, AIME25 9/30 vs 2/30,
  MATH500 0.4 vs 0.2), [SOTA-126](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-126.md)'s `40.8 to 53.5`, [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md)'s post-GRPO
  AIME24 75.0 and MATH500 94.0: all exact.
- The prose numbers too: [SOTA-125](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-125.md)'s 27-layer/512-hidden mid config against
  the 50-layer deep one, the "roughly a 2x decrease for training
  throughput", the reduction from 27 layers to 24 to land on 90M — all
  verbatim from the post's own config listings.

One thing did not survive. [SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md) quoted "up to a 20% relative gain on
MMLU, BBH and GSM8K" and dropped the four words that follow it in the
source: **from random values**. At 90M those three benchmarks sit near
chance, so a fifth of the distance above chance is a much smaller claim than
a fifth of the score. That is not a transcription error of the kind [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18)
worried about — the table was fine — it is a summarisation error, which is
the failure mode reading a rendered table would never have caught.

## None of the Proposed practices moves

[#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) asked for the practices whose promotion condition was "the larger-scale
evidence lives in the preprint" to be re-examined now that the preprints are
readable. [SOTA-133](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-133.md) turns out to have been promoted to Active already. Of the
rest:

**[SOTA-136](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-136.md) (mHC)** was the interesting one. Half its condition asks for "a
production report at depth whose streams stay distinct", and DeepSeek-V4 is
the production report at depth — 1.6T, shipping mHC. Read in full, it does
not answer the objection. Its argument for the doubly-stochastic constraint
is that projecting onto the manifold bounds the spectral norm at 1, so the
residual transformation is non-expansive and both passes are numerically
more stable. That is the property [LIT-151](../../record/literature.d/LIT-151.md) grants and then turns around: a
mapping that can only contract can only erode what distinguishes the
streams. V4 reports no stream statistic, and *homogenize*, *diversity* and
*distinct* appear nowhere in it. So the condition is unmet by the report
most likely to have met it, and the practice now says so — because a reader
who knows mHC ships at 1.6T will otherwise assume shipping settled it.

**[SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md) (decay to zero)** gained a sharper version of its own
consensus_note. DeepSeek-V4 decays to exactly 10% of peak, which is the
customary floor [LIT-147](../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md) names in its first sentence and argues against. Not
a team that weighed decaying to zero and declined — a team that used the
default, at 33T tokens.

It also gained a trap worth naming. K3's schedule study *looks* like the
second half of [SOTA-141](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-141.md)'s promotion condition, which asks for "a second
group's schedule comparison with the peak retuned per schedule". K3 is
exactly that. But it runs the comparison "under a fixed minimum learning
rate", and the minimum is this practice's variable. A study can satisfy the
methodology a practice demands and still not be about it, and a promotion
condition written in terms of method rather than question is how you fail to
notice.

**[SOTA-122](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-122.md) (learnable multipliers)** and **[SOTA-144](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-144.md) (CompleteP)** both need
an independent group adopting the technique. Nothing in the four reports
read this session does. Searched, not found, and that is the whole result.

<a id="20260907130811"></a>

## The reference pass, and what it found the record leaning on

*2026-09-07 13:08:11*

The last item on [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18): run mechanically, for the other model reports, the
"which works does this paper lean on to justify its decisions" pass that was
done by hand for [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md). Result filed as [#40](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/40). This entry is the method and
the two things worth remembering about it.

## Semantic Scholar was not the way in

[#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) named `api.semanticscholar.org`, and it is reachable but rate-limits an
unauthenticated caller hard — roughly one request in three succeeded, with
no key available. That turned out not to matter, because the better source
was already local: every one of these reports has an arXiv HTML build, and
the build carries the bibliography as markup. Parsing `li#bib.bibN` out of
it gives titles, arXiv identifiers and — this is the part a citation API
does not have — **the sections each reference is cited from**.

152 entries for K3, 257 for Olmo 3, 125 for Falcon-H1, 103 for DeepSeek-V4.
Subtract the corpus by arXiv id and by normalised title, drop
benchmarks and datasets, and what remains is the gap list.

## The back-references are the whole filter, and two builds do not have them

K3's and V4's builds carry "Cited by: §2.1.1" on each entry, so a reference
can be scored by *where* it is used: a work cited from §2 (Architecture) is
a design justification, and one cited only from §6 (Evaluations) is a
baseline. That is exactly the distinction [#18](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/18) asked for, and it is free.

Falcon-H1's and Olmo 3's builds have none — 0 of 125 and 0 of 257 entries
carry them. The first run reported "0 design-cited references missing" for
both, which read like a clean result and was an artefact of a filter with
nothing to match. Caught by asking why two large bibliographies would have
*exactly* zero, which is the shape a broken filter makes and a real answer
almost never does. Those two were re-run on titles alone and [#40](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/40) says so.

## What the pass is actually good at

Not "find every missing paper" — a title filter cannot tell a method from a
benchmark reliably, and judgement is still required per row. What it is good
at is the **multiply-cited absence**: a work that two independent labs both
reached for, and the record does not have. Six of those, and they are the
top of [#40](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/40)'s list.

The other thing it surfaced is sharper than any single paper. **[SOTA-134](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-134.md)'s
headline benefit is that the gate removes the attention-sink pattern, and
the phrase "attention sink" appears in exactly one file in this record —
[LIT-138](../../record/literature.d/LIT-138.md)'s own summary.** The record recommends removing a phenomenon it has
never described. A reference pass looking for what the corpus leans on found
a hole in what the corpus explains, which is not what it was pointed at.
