<a id="20260907170207"></a>

## Mining the lineages out of the prose

*2026-09-07 17:02:07*

The record documented two lines of work and four lines of practice. The
question was whether more were hiding in the topology. They were, but not
where I first looked.

## What the graph does not tell you

The obvious move is connected components. It does not work, for a reason
worth writing down.

Components over `source:` find **bundles, not chains**: [LIT-051](../../record/literature.d/LIT-051.md) is cited by
seven practices, [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md) by six. That is one paper fanning out into several
recommendations — co-derivation. Nothing succeeds anything.

Components over prose citations find one blob. The practice corpus has a
single connected component of 25 documents and two small ones; the literature
corpus has one of 94. Recent documents cite recent documents, and "cites" is
not "descends from". Mutual prose citation — both documents naming each other
— narrows it to 212 pairs in the literature, which is still an order of
magnitude more than the real lineages.

Topology alone cannot distinguish succession from adjacency, because the
record does not encode the difference anywhere the graph can see it.

## Where it actually was

`## Sequence`. Seven practices carry a section by that name, and it does
exactly what the relation was declared for — spells out an order, step by
step, in a paragraph:

> Muon → weight decay and RMS matching so AdamW's hyperparameters transfer
> ([SOTA-121](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-121.md)) → QK-Clip so the attention logits stay bounded at scale (this
> practice) … **Each step keeps the one before.**

One of those seven declared \`extends:\`. Six did not. The structure was in
the record the whole time, written by hand, in the one form nothing can
traverse — which is the exact failure [ADR-011](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-011.md) was filed to prevent, reopened
by accretion.

So the mineable signal was not the graph. It was **prose that describes an
edge the frontmatter does not declare**, and a grep for one section heading
found more than any component analysis did.

## What declaring costs, and what it buys

Two things fell out that prose had been able to avoid.

**It caught an error I shipped a week ago.** [LIT-194](../../record/literature.d/LIT-194.md) said GLA was one of
Gated DeltaNet's two parents. Writing \`extends:\` forces the question "which
document, exactly" — and the answer is that Gated DeltaNet's own abstract
names Mamba2's gate and DeltaNet's rule, and its title is *Improving Mamba2
with Delta Rule*. GLA is not in that line. Prose could gesture at "the
data-dependent gate"; a code cannot.

**It broke the renderer, correctly.** Declaring Gated DeltaNet's two parents
made the first real DAG in any luria record, and the chain page — which
carries nesting as indentation and ordered steps by \`(depth, code)\` —
started asserting that Kimi Linear descends from Mamba-3. Fixed upstream
before landing this, because the alternative was to drop a true edge to keep
a view honest. [LU-#206](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/206).

## What I did not declare

**[SOTA-129](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-129.md) and [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md).** Its summary says it was filed "so its variations
([SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md)) and its tiny-scale successor ([SOTA-123](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-123.md)) have something to be
traced back to" — an explicit invitation. But \`compared_against\` means *a
comparison was run*, and [SOTA-130](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-130.md)'s own \`promote_when\` asks for exactly the
head-to-head that does not exist. Declaring it would assert the evidence the
practice says is missing.

That is a gap in the vocabulary rather than in the record: there is no way to
say "rival answers to one question, nobody has compared them". Worth a
decision before it gets invented ad hoc.

**Model-report genealogies.** V3.2 → V4, K2 → K3, Qwen3-Next → 3.8. The
mechanisms descend; whether the *reports* do is a different question, and
answering it by hand in a mining pass would commit the record to a whole
dimension it has not decided on.

<a id="20260907175621"></a>

## The positional line was two lines and a missing paper

*2026-09-07 17:56:21 · lineage · literature*

Asked to find a lineage containing RoPE and NoPE. The record held five of the
six documents it needed and none of the edges.

## What was already there, unconnected

`LIT-045` (RoFormer), `LIT-048` (ALiBi), `LIT-192` (Position Interpolation),
`LIT-193` (YaRN), and two practices — `SOTA-063` "use RoPE" and `SOTA-151`
"rescale it". The chain page rooted the rescaling line at Position
Interpolation, because nobody had declared the edge to the thing it
interpolates. Position Interpolation's own first sentence says it extends the
context window of "RoPE-based pretrained LLMs"; the method is a rescaling of
RoPE's position indices and is meaningless without them. One line of
frontmatter, and the line roots where it belongs.

`SOTA-151 extends SOTA-063` was missing for the same reason and is the same
shape: rescaling RoPE is what a model that used RoPE does next.

## The paper that was not there

NoPE appeared in four documents — `LIT-131`, `LIT-193`, `SOTA-132`,
`SOTA-151` — plus two changelog fragments, always as *a thing Kimi models do*.
No note, no source, no author. The anthology's own rule is that a practice
names a source; this slipped past because NoPE was never the subject of a
practice, only a paragraph inside two of them.

The document that did *not* mention it is the tell: `LIT-133`, Kimi Linear,
whose paper gives NoPE a design section, an ablation table and the citation
everything else here rests on. The note was written about KDA, so the
positional half of the paper went unrecorded, and every later document then
attributed NoPE to K3 — the model report that adopted it — rather than to the
method paper sitting in the record already. `LIT-133` gains the paragraph.

Kazemnejad et al. (2023) is the source, and Kimi Linear cites it directly
(reference [49]). Filed as `LIT-207`. The thing worth knowing about it,
which the "K3 doesn't need YaRN" framing loses: it is a *controlled* study —
five positional schemes, identical hyperparameters, one model configuration —
and it comes with a theorem saying a decoder-only transformer can represent
absolute and relative position with no encoding at all. NoPE is not a model
told less; it is a model not told which function to use. It is also 107M
parameters on synthetic tasks, which is the honest limit on it.

## What was deliberately not declared

`LIT-133 compared_against LIT-045`. Kimi Linear does run NoPE against RoPE —
Table 5, a Kimi Linear (RoPE) baseline at matched 48B configuration — and it
was tempting to declare, because it is the scale evidence the 2023 paper
lacks.

It is the wrong relation. [ADR-011](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-011.md) defines `compared_against` as "this work
evaluates itself against that one", and what Kimi Linear ran is an ablation of
its own design: itself with the encoding and itself without. That is evidence
*about* the RoPE/NoPE question, not a comparison against RoFormer, and it
belongs in prose — where it now is, in the new note and in `SOTA-132`.

Declaring it anyway was tried, to see. It collapses the page: `compared_against`
joins components, so one edge fused the positional line into the delta-rule
line, six sections became five, and the merged section was titled "From
RoFormer" with eleven members including Mamba. Worth knowing before someone
declares a cross-family sibling for a good reason — the relation is right for
a rival *within* a family and expensive for a rival that already belongs to
another one.

## Left open

There is a practice-shaped hole: *apply NoPE to the global-attention layers of
a linear-attention hybrid*. `SOTA-132` carries it as "a second benefit the
practice was filed without", which is the shape of a recommendation living
inside somebody else's document. The evidence exists — Kimi Linear's ablation,
K3 at 2.8T, Falcon-H1's near-NoPE base frequency, and SwanGPT's RoPE/NoPE
interleave, which is named in Kimi Linear's related work and has not been read
here. Not
filed here, because filing a recommendation is an editorial act with a status
and a consensus level attached, and this contribution was asked for a lineage.

<a id="20260907181553"></a>

## The bibliography of a paper already in the record held two papers the record needed

*2026-09-07 18:15:53 · literature · method*

The NoPE practice was going to be filed on one laboratory's evidence — Kimi
Linear's ablation and K3's deployment — at `Proposed` and `unreplicated`. It
is filed at `Active` and `emerging` instead, on three, and the difference came
from four lines of a related-work paragraph.

## What happened

Deciding the consensus value meant deciding whether anyone outside Kimi had
done this. Kimi Linear's related work says its findings "align with prior
results [110, 7, 19]" and mentions SwanGPT [76] by name. Resolving five
bracketed numbers against the bibliography took one command and produced:

- **[110]** Yang et al., *Rope to Nope and Back Again* (Cohere, January 2025)
  — the paper this practice most wants, whose title is the lineage.
- **[76]** Puvvada et al., *SWAN-GPT* (NVIDIA, April 2025) — the same layout
  again, independently.
- **[7]** Barbero et al., *Round and Round We Go! What makes Rotary Positional
  Encodings useful?* — not filed, but the obvious next candidate.
- **[19]** DeepSeek-V3, whose decoupled RoPE head is the partial-RoPE version
  of the same idea.
- **[126]** Falcon-H1, already in the record as `LIT-120`, cited here for a
  base frequency near 10^11 that pushes it to a near-NoPE state — a fact the
  record's own Falcon-H1 note does not carry.

## Why the earlier passes missed them

The reference pass in [#40](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/40) worked from the *citation graphs* of five model
reports — what cites what — and these three were sitting in a sentence of
prose that says "others found this too". A citation graph cannot distinguish a
paper cited for its result from one cited in passing, and the numbers it
ranks by are the ones a bundled reference list produces. Reading one
related-work paragraph on a paper the record already holds found more, faster,
than the graph pass did.

## And one of them was a correction

SWAN-GPT converts an existing 8B RoPE model pretrained on 15T tokens to a
NoPE-global architecture by continued pretraining, at parity on short
benchmarks. `SOTA-151` had been asserting that a model which already exists
cannot take the NoPE option, and that assertion was doing real work: it was
the stated reason the two practices are not filed as contesting each other.
The reason survives, weakened — conversion costs a continued-pretraining run,
which most readers will not do — but the claim as written was false, and it
was written twice, in two practices, before anything checked it.

The general shape is worth keeping: a claim about what is *impossible* is the
most expensive kind a record can hold, because nothing routine ever tests it.
The lint checks that citations resolve and that statuses are current. It has
no way to notice a confident negative.

<a id="20260907183753"></a>

## A retraction test for whether a citation belongs in `source:`

*2026-09-07 18:37:53 · method · literature*

[#58](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/58) needs a rule sharp enough to apply thirty-two times without drifting.
[ADR-010](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-010.md) says `source:` holds every paper a practice rests on, and `SOTA-132`
supplies the working distinction — *support and corroboration go in `source:`;
contrast and alternatives stay in the body*. That is right and still leaves
the hard cases undecided, because most citations read as vaguely supportive.

The test that worked:

> **If this paper were retracted tomorrow, would the practice need
> rewriting?**

It separates the batch cleanly.

- `SOTA-122` without `LIT-121` has no claim left — the blogpost validated
  something, and the something is in the paper. **Add.**
- `SOTA-124` without `LIT-120` has no memorization window, which is the
  quantity the whole recommendation is stated in terms of. **Add.**
- `SOTA-129` without `LIT-127` says "some other RL algorithm" and carries on.
  **Body.** Without `LIT-119` it loses an arithmetic aside in its conditions.
  **Body.** Without `LIT-172` its third stage has no origin. **Add.**
- `SOTA-124` without `LIT-166` loses the position it argues against, which
  makes the practice *less* interesting and not less supported. **Body** —
  and this is the case the vague version of the rule gets wrong, because a
  paper you spend two paragraphs on feels like a source.

## The one that was already right

`SOTA-128` cites `LIT-124` and `LIT-125` and should not name them. It cites
them for what they do *not* say — whether to mask the loss on a FIM sample's
prefix and suffix is "left unstated in one and only implicit in the other" —
which is the reason the source's own two 90M runs are worth reporting. A
citation can be load-bearing and still not be support.

## What the pass is actually finding

Not sloppiness. Every one of these was filed when `source:` took exactly one
code, and each names the single most defensible one. `SOTA-130`'s body says
it outright — Olmo 3 "remains **the** source" — in the singular, months after
[ADR-010](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-010.md) made the field a list. The schema changed and the documents written
under the old one did not get revisited, which is the ordinary way a record
goes stale: not by being wrong when written, but by being right under rules
that have since moved.

Worth checking after the pass: whether `consensus` values set while the
source list understated the support are still correct. A practice reading
`unreplicated` on a one-entry list that should have held three is not
reporting the field, it is reporting the field it was written next to.

<a id="20260907203215"></a>

## Eleven edges gain a sign, and `tail` hid two findings for a day

*2026-09-07 20:32:15 · lineage · process*

[ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) said succession gains a sign and named the mechanism: a second
relation, once a chain's spine could walk more than one. [LU-#211](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/211) shipped that
in 0.11.0, so this is the decision becoming the record's shape.

## What the sign changed, and what it did not

Not the pages. Six literature lines and eight practice lines, every step
nesting exactly where it did before — because `extends:` and `corrects:` are
one spine and the walk cannot tell them apart. That is the correct outcome and
worth stating plainly: the information gained is structural, not visual.

What it did change is what a document can be asked. `LIT-140` now reads
`corrected_by: [LIT-151, LIT-181]` — two independent groups naming defects in
mHC's constraint, legible from mHC itself without opening either. `SOTA-121`
reads `corrected_by: [SOTA-131]`, so "Muon needs QK-Clip at scale" is a fact
about Muon and not only a fact about QK-Clip. Getting the converse for free is
why this was a second relation rather than an attribute on `extends:`.

## Where the sign is still invisible

The lineage page renders code, title and facets, and says nothing about which
relation a step arrived on. So the record knows the difference and the reader
of the generated page does not. Filed upstream as [LU-#213](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/213) rather than worked
around: it
was an open question in [LU-#211](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/211) and the implementation deliberately left it
out, so the walk could land without a rendering decision attached to it.

## The process failure worth keeping

Two findings shipped in [#64](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/pull/64) and survived a merge because the lint output was
being read through `tail -3`. `luria lint` prints its warning *headline* first
and the individual findings under it, so a tail shows the last classes and
hides the first: a code resolving to nothing and a `Proposed` practice cited
unacknowledged were both above the cut, in the same PR that introduced them.

This is the second instance today of the same shape — the first was
`luria index >/dev/null 2>&1` hiding a config error, recorded upstream. The
general rule is the same and now has two witnesses: **do not truncate the
output of a command you are running in order to decide whether something is
clean.** A summary line is not a substitute for the findings, and the cheap
habit that hides them is the one that feels like tidiness.

Both are fixed here rather than filed, because they are small and they are
ours.

<a id="20260907210155"></a>

## What the source pass found, and what it cost

*2026-09-07 21:01:55 · method · literature*

[#58](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/58) is done: thirty-two practices examined, seventeen changed, fifteen
correct as filed.

## The shape of what was wrong

Not sloppiness, and not one mistake repeated. Three distinct causes, in
roughly equal measure.

**The schema moved and the documents did not.** Most of it. Every practice
corrected here was filed when `source:` took exactly one code, and each named
the single most defensible one. `SOTA-130`'s body still said Olmo 3 "remains
**the** source", singular, months after [ADR-010](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-010.md) made the field a list.

**The prose already knew.** In nearly every case the missing source was
argued for, at length, in the body of the document that failed to name it.
`SOTA-140`'s Source section named Hägele's controlled comparison from the day
it was filed; the frontmatter named only MiniCPM. `SOTA-138`'s Conditions
counted NSA's from-scratch result as evidence in the same sentence that the
field omitted it. `SOTA-145` enumerated four works and put three in the field.
The pass was mostly transcription, not discovery.

**Adoption was doing a job nothing had assigned it.** `SOTA-132` carried four
production lines in `source:` while reading as unassessed on the consensus
axis — the evidence for "the field does this" filed under "this is why it is
true". That one needed a decision before it could be fixed, which is why
[ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) came in the middle of the pass rather than before it.

## What the decision was worth, measured

The first thirteen practices took two batches under a rule invented for the
occasion. The last nineteen took two more under [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md), and the second half
went roughly twice as fast per practice — not because the cases were easier,
but because "did this work run the comparison, or did it ship the design?" is
answerable by reading one paragraph, while "does this feel like support?" is
answerable only by argument.

The decision also made the only *removals* in the pass possible. Every batch
before it could add a source; none could take one out, because nothing said
what did not belong.

## Two the record got right before the rule existed

Worth naming, because they are the argument that the rule was discovered
rather than imposed. `SOTA-151` says of `LIT-210`: it "explains why the
problem exists; it does not evidence that rescaling is the answer, and the
sources of a practice are what its recommendation rests on." `SOTA-152` says
Olmo 3 and DeepSeek-V4 "both cite this work, which is adoption rather than
replication — neither reports what it did for them." Both were written before
[ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) and both state its two halves exactly.

## What is left

The `consensus` values. `SOTA-132` gained one in this pass because the
evidence moved out of `source:` and needed somewhere to go, but the other
sixteen changed practices had their support lists altered without their
consensus readings being re-derived — and several were set while the list
understated the support. That is a smaller pass than this one and it wants
the group count `LU-#209` asks for, since every consensus value in this record
is a hand-count of laboratories that nothing can recompute.

<a id="20260907211428"></a>

## A pass can only find the defect its method is shaped like

*2026-09-07 21:14:28 · method · literature*

The consensus re-derivation was supposed to be a small tidy-up after
[#58](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/58): seventeen practices had their support lists changed without
their consensus readings being re-read. Two of those readings needed work.
The pass found something else on the way, and the something else is the more
useful half.

## What re-reading the notes found

`SOTA-141` was `emerging` while its own note ended "the field has not moved".
`emerging` means "several independent groups, moving toward default"; the
note says the opposite in plain words, three lines below the value. It is now
`unreplicated`, with the note saying precisely what [LIT-145](../../record/literature.d/LIT-145.md) corroborates (the
endpoint) and what it does not (the claim).

`SOTA-125` said "at one scale" while its sources span 90M and 1.5B. The value
survives — two scales from one group is still one group — and the note did
not.

That is two out of twenty-two, which is roughly what a tidy-up should look
like.

## What the method could not see

[#58](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/58)'s candidate list was *codes cited in the body that `source:` does not
name*. Every batch could therefore **add** a source and none could **remove**
one, because a code wrongly present in the field produces no body-only
citation to flag it. `SOTA-132` was caught in the last batch only because it
happened to be missing a source as well.

Asking the opposite question — which `source:` entries are model reports? —
returns nineteen practices, and most are fine: Falcon-H1-Tiny is a blogpost
full of its own ablations, and a report that ran the experiment is a source
whatever else it is. Three were not fine, and one of them says so itself:

> Then four generations of adoption rather than one result:
> — `SOTA-147`, *The evidence*

All four were in its source list. The practice wrote down the distinction
[ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) would later make, and then filed against it.

## The lesson, which is about passes and not about sources

**A pass finds the defect its query is shaped like, and is silent on the
inverse.** Nothing about [#58](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/58) was wrong; it was a search for absence, so it
could not see presence. The check [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) shipped has the same shape —
`source:` ⊆ the body — and the same blind spot, which is worth knowing before
someone treats a clean run as a clean record.

The general form: after a pass over a relation, run it once in the other
direction. It is cheap, it takes minutes, and here it found three practices
whose consensus readings could not be checked against their own evidence
because the evidence and the adoption were in the same list.

<a id="20260907215040"></a>

## Proposed is where a recommendation waits, and declining to file is not the same as filing a doubt

*2026-09-07 21:50:40 · method · record*

**The first batch of [#56](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/56) was filed as four notes and zero practices, and that
was wrong.** The three papers with a recommendation in them are now
[SOTA-156](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-156.md), [SOTA-155](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-155.md) and [SOTA-154](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-154.md), all `Proposed`. Writing down
why the first pass went the other way is worth more than the correction,
because the mistake was not about these papers.

## The rule I applied, and why it is the wrong rule

The reasoning was: *a practice needs the thing to work, and somebody at the
relevant scale to be doing it.* All three papers fail the second half —
Schedule-Free's evidence tops out far below where [LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) and [LIT-145](../../record/literature.d/LIT-145.md)
disagree, DiLoCo is 8 workers on C4, ES is two tasks at 8B and below — so
none of them became a practice.

That sentence is a correct description of the bar for **`Active`**. It was
applied to the question of whether the document should **exist**, and those
are different questions. `statuses.yaml` says so in as many words:

> `Proposed` — *early results are good, validation at scale is missing — the
> old `experimental` flag*

That is a description of all three papers. The vocabulary already had the
slot; the filer used the top of the scale as the entry requirement.

## Why the error is not cosmetic

**A refusal has nowhere to put the thing that would reverse it.** Each of the
three notes ended with a sentence naming what would change the answer, in
prose, in a `LIT` document. [ADR-014](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-014.md) exists because that exact arrangement
failed before: a promotion condition living in prose is invisible when the
evidence arrives, and it was found last time only because somebody happened
to be re-reading two practices the same afternoon. Declining to file the
practice reproduces the failure [ADR-014](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-014.md) fixed, one layer up — the condition is
now not merely prose, it is prose attached to the wrong document.
`promote_when:` is a required field on a `Proposed` practice, and it was
sitting empty because no practice existed to require it.

**Consensus is a per-practice field, so a paper with no practice cannot
accumulate one.** [ADR-015](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-015.md) put `consensus:` on `SOTA` deliberately: it is a
claim about how far the field has moved on *a recommendation*. The second lab
to publish a Schedule-Free run has nowhere to be recorded if there is no node
to move from `unreplicated` to `emerging`. A refusal does not just withhold
an endorsement; it removes the counter that would have earned one.

**And it starves the status vocabulary.** [DP-2](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-2) is that a field every record
shares is not a field. If only practices that already clear the `Active` bar
get filed, `Proposed` fills up with nothing but the cases somebody filed
optimistically and never revisited — which is precisely the distribution the
lint's `inert-status` check exists to catch, arrived at from the other
direction.

## What the notes were right about

The refusals were well-argued as *statements of what is missing*, and that
content survives intact — it moved into `promote_when:` and the "what is not
established" sections, where a machine can point at it. Two things also
stayed literature-only for a reason that holds up:

- The Veo 3 note reports emergent capability and recommends nothing. There is
  no instruction to file.
- The JEPA line is vision self-supervision, and `tags.yaml` gives `SOTA`
  seven primary topics, none of which is a vision category. The practice
  scheme is scoped to language-model training *by construction* — which is a
  much better reason than the one first given, and worth knowing about.

## The rule that replaces it

**File the practice whenever the paper contains an instruction; let `status:`
carry how much you believe it.** The question at filing time is "is there a
recommendation here", not "would I put my name on it today". A `Proposed`
practice with an honest `promote_when:` costs a paragraph and creates the
node that everything later attaches to. A refusal costs nothing now and costs
the node forever.

## Two mechanics of the acknowledgement directive, learned the slow way

Filing three `Proposed` practices meant three new inactive-citation findings
to acknowledge, and it took three lint cycles because the directive is
stricter than it looks:

- **It must name the code it vouches for.** `inactive-ok-block:` followed by
  a prose reason and no code acknowledges nothing — the finding stays, and
  the comment reads to a human as though it had been handled.
- **It must be contiguous with the block.** A blank line between the comment
  and the paragraph ends the block, so the directive covers only itself.
- And a corollary: a code written *inside* the comment is itself a citation
  at that line. Vouching for two codes takes two directives stacked, not one
  comment mentioning both — which is what the existing sites in this record
  already do, and now I know why.

One more, found by deleting the comment to see what happened: **journal
entries are not subject to the check at all.** The directive this entry
originally carried was doing nothing. It is removed rather than left in
place, because a directive that vouches for nothing is the same failure as a
field every record shares — it looks like a handled finding and is not.

<a id="20260907215631"></a>

## Every practice in the registry says "autoregressive transformer" and none of them writes it down

*2026-09-07 21:56:31 · method · literature*

**Filing LLaDA ([#56](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/56), batch B) turned up something about the registry rather
than about diffusion language models.** The paper's argument is that the
capabilities everyone attributes to LLMs are attributed to *autoregressive*
modelling specifically, and that the attribution is unearned: hold the
paradigm fixed, swap only the factorization, and an 8B model is competitive
with LLaMA3 8B. Whether or not that holds up, writing the note required
asking what the record would have to change if it did — and the answer was
not obvious, which is the finding.

## The qualifier nothing needed until now

Every practice here is advice about training an autoregressive transformer.
Not one of them says so, because nothing in the corpus has ever been anything
else. The assumption is not hidden, exactly; it is *ambient*, which is worse,
because an ambient assumption cannot be cited, contested, or scoped.

Sorting the registry against it, the practices fall into two groups that are
easy to name and were not obvious before the sort:

- **Indifferent to the factorization.** AdamW's decoupled decay, µP and
  CompleteP, warmup-stable-decay and the peak-LR power law, MoE routing and
  expert granularity, best-fit packing. These are about optimization and
  capacity. A diffusion language model would want all of them.
- **Load-bearing on it.** Fill-in-the-middle training, multi-token
  prediction, speculative decoding, KV-cache compression, context extension
  by RoPE rescaling. These exist *because* generation is left-to-right and
  cached. Under a masked-diffusion decoder some are unnecessary and some are
  incoherent.

## Where the sort now lives

The sort above is a first pass by one reader, and it has the shape of a
thing that will look obvious and be wrong in places — the boundary runs
through the attention material in particular, where a practice can be about
the cache (load-bearing) or about the attention pattern (not).

It is written into the diffusion practice itself, under the heading "what
adopting this would cost, which nobody has costed", rather than left as a
journal observation. A recommendation whose adoption cost is unknown should
say so at the point of recommending; leaving it here would have implied the
cost was zero, which is the thing the sort exists to deny.

That the practice exists at all is the other half of the same correction. The
first pass filed these four papers as notes and no practices, on a rule —
"somebody at the relevant scale has to be doing it" — that describes the bar
for `Active` and was applied to whether the document should exist. The
companion entry for batch A works through why that is wrong; the short form
is that a paper with no practice has no node, and a node is what accumulates
`consensus:` and carries `promote_when:`.

## The three that stay literature-only, and one good reason

Three of batch B's four notes carry no practice, and only now for reasons
that survive scrutiny.

**The Veo 3 note recommends nothing.** It reports emergent capability in a
closed model and draws an analogy. There is no instruction in it to file, so
there is nothing for a `Proposed` practice to say.

**The JEPA line cannot be filed, structurally.** `tags.yaml` gives `SOTA`
seven primary topics — training, systems, stability, distributed, data,
attention, architecture — and none of them is a vision category. `LIT` has
five more, including `vision-and-graphics`, which is how these notes are
filed at all. So **the practice scheme is scoped to language-model training by
construction**, and a vision self-supervision recommendation has no primary
topic to take. That is a much better reason than "no adoption at scale", and
it is a live question rather than a closed one: if the record ever wants
vision practices, the change is to the primary-topic vocabulary, which
[ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md) made binding.

The temptation with all three is to skip the note: no practice will cite
them, so what is a note for?

What a note is for, here, is the boundary. Each of the three says in its
Standing section what the record does *not* hold and what would move the
paper inside. That turns "the anthology has nothing on video" from a silence
— which reads identically to an oversight — into a filed position. Luria has a
design principle for this shape (an absence reads like success); the
anthology's version of it is that a subject nobody filed and a subject
somebody declined to file look the same from the index, and only the second
one is a decision.

<a id="20260908001616"></a>

## The registry was missing nodes at both ends, and only one end had a story

*2026-09-08 00:16:16 · method · record*

**Auditing the curation log for practices skipped the way batch A's were
found three, and then found two more by the opposite failure.** The first
three are the pattern already named: a recommendation refused because nobody
at frontier scale has adopted it, which is the `Active` bar applied to the
question of whether the document should exist. The other two had no story at
all, and that is the more interesting half.

## The three refused for adoption

- **The hyper-connections trunk.** [ADR-015](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-015.md) says outright: "The trunk
  practice that paragraph describes is deliberately not filed here… converting
  a hedge into an assertion is an editorial act." But `Proposed` *is* the
  hedge, so filing it converts nothing. This one is the worst shape of the
  three, because the record had already filed both **branches** — the
  doubly-stochastic constraint and the free mixing it replaced — and not the
  trunk they fork from. The disputed part had a node and the agreed part did
  not, which is how the record ended up recommending a layer ratio defined in
  terms of a structure it had never stated.
- **Data mixing laws** ([LIT-201](../../record/literature.d/LIT-201.md)): refused because "none of the frontier
  reports in this record says it used a mixing law". The note itself draws
  the parallel to [SOTA-142](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-142.md), which sets the peak learning rate by a fitted
  power law and *is* filed. Same move, one filed and one not.
- **Mamba-3** ([LIT-165](../../record/literature.d/LIT-165.md)): "Nothing in the record ships Mamba-3, so it stays
  a note."

## The two nobody refused, because nobody noticed

**Deduplication** and **multi-token prediction** were not skipped by an
argument. No note says "not filed as a practice" about either. They simply
never came up, because *a step everyone agrees on generates no debate to
notice*.

[LIT-202](../../record/literature.d/LIT-202.md)'s own standing section had said it plainly for weeks — "the
foundation under a step that appears in every pipeline this record describes
and had no source" — and the sentence reads as a compliment to the paper
rather than as a hole in the registry. [LIT-163](../../record/literature.d/LIT-163.md) is the same: five model
reports ship an MTP head and each mentions it as settled, so there was
nothing to argue about and therefore nothing to write.

## The shape, which is the useful part

The two failures are mirror images and they have opposite tells:

|  | refused | unnoticed |
|---|---|---|
| **Trigger** | a paper too new to endorse | a technique too settled to discuss |
| **Tell** | a sentence saying "not filed as a practice" | silence |
| **How found** | grep the record for the refusal | ask which notes no practice sources |

Only the first leaves evidence. Grepping for refusals is a complete method
for one half of the problem and finds nothing at all of the other — which is
the same lesson the earlier entry drew about passes finding the defect their
query is shaped like, arrived at again from a different direction. The
inverse query here is *which notes does no practice source?*, and it returns
115 of 218.

Most of those 115 are correct: the pre-migration vision and generative
corpus, which the practice scheme cannot express because `tags.yaml` has no
vision category, and the model reports, which are adoption rather than
evidence ([ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md)). Narrowing to post-migration notes carrying a
`SOTA`-eligible primary topic leaves 38, of which these five are the ones the
curation log pointed at. The other 33 are a sweep, filed as an issue rather
than done here, because each needs the same judgement — is there an
instruction in this paper — and thirty-three of those in one sitting is how a
taxonomy gets baked in badly.

## One thing the lint got right

`SOTA-132` was cited with an `inactive-ok-block:` written from memory of when
it was `Proposed`. It is `Active` now, and the lint said so: "annotation no
longer applies". That is the acknowledgement mechanism working in the
direction nobody designs for — catching a vouch that has outlived its reason,
rather than a citation that lacks one.

<a id="20260908002300"></a>

## Two trunk practices in one day, found by different routes and missing for the same reason

*2026-09-08 00:23:00 · method · record*

**The first cluster of the [#73](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/73) sweep produced three practices, and the useful
finding is that one of them is the same shape as the one filed an hour
earlier for a completely different subject.**

The hyper-connections trunk was found by grepping [ADR-015](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-015.md) for a refusal.
The matrix-preconditioner trunk was found by asking which optimizer notes no
practice sources. Different subjects, different search methods, identical
defect: **the record had filed the branches and not the thing they fork
from.**

## The shape, stated once

- `SOTA-136` and `SOTA-137` are two answers to *how* to constrain the mixing
  in a widened residual stream. The width itself — which all four papers
  agree on — had no document.
<!-- inactive-ok-block: SOTA-131 — Active; named as the correction riding
     with the Muon branch. Kept short deliberately: see below. -->
- `SOTA-121` is Muon. The class it belongs to — precondition with matrices
  rather than entrywise — had no document, while two separate notes argued
  in prose that the class is where the win lives. [LIT-157](../../record/literature.d/LIT-157.md): "what SOAP
  supplies is the argument that the win belongs to the class rather than to
  the particular algorithm." [LIT-156](../../record/literature.d/LIT-156.md): "every fastest optimizer — Muon and
  SOAP among them — preconditions with *matrices*… That is a real structural
  finding and it survives the fair comparison."

## Why trunks go missing, which is not the same reason branches do

A branch gets filed because somebody published it: a paper arrives, it has a
name, it makes a claim, and the claim becomes a practice. A trunk has no
paper. It is what several papers agree on, and agreement is nobody's
contribution — so there is no arrival event to prompt the filing.

That makes trunks a third category alongside the two the previous entry
named. Refusals leave a sentence to grep for. Too-settled techniques leave
silence. **Trunks leave prose in the notes saying the trunk is the
interesting part**, written by whoever noticed, in a document that cannot
carry a practice's status.

Which suggests the query: *where does a note's Standing section make a claim
about what several papers agree on?* Both of today's trunks would have been
caught by it, and neither was caught by the other two methods.

## A smaller thing, twice

Two directives in this batch were written from memory — `SOTA-131` and
`SOTA-132` acknowledged as `Proposed` when both are `Active` now — and the
lint rejected both with "annotation no longer applies". That is three
instances today of writing a status from recall rather than reading it. The
fix is not to try harder: it is that the acknowledgement is cheap to add and
the lint always checks, so the cost of the mistake is one cycle. Worth
noting only because the same failure would be expensive anywhere the guard
did not exist.

<a id="20260908011915"></a>

## Three of the four papers were already load-bearing, and none of them carried a practice

*2026-09-08 01:19:15 · method · record*

**The precision cluster produced four practices, and the thing worth writing
down is what these four papers were already doing in the record before
today.** Three of them are what the frontier reports cite for decisions the
record already records:

- Kimi K3 keeps the attention output in FP32 and redesigns its kernel to
  absorb the doubled footprint. [LIT-131](../../record/literature.d/LIT-131.md) says so. [LIT-198](../../record/literature.d/LIT-198.md) is the paper it
  is citing, and without it the choice reads as caution rather than as a fix
  for a named failure mode.
- DeepSeek-V4 and Kimi K3 both quantize to "FP4" and "MXFP4". [LIT-197](../../record/literature.d/LIT-197.md) is
  what those words mean — a 4-bit element in a 32-element block with a shared
  power-of-two scale, not a bare 4-bit float.
- [SOTA-034](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-034.md) is `contested` on the strength of [LIT-200](../../record/literature.d/LIT-200.md) and K3's SiTU-GLU.

So the record was already *using* these papers to explain its own contents.
What it could not do was state what a reader should therefore do — because
the statement had nowhere to live except inside a note about a different
paper.

## A fourth category, or the second half of the third

The previous entry named three ways a practice goes missing: refused for
adoption, too settled to discuss, and a trunk nobody publishes. This cluster
adds a variant of the last one, and it is worth distinguishing.

**A paper cited to explain somebody else's decision is not the same as a
paper nobody read.** These four were read closely — the notes are detailed,
they are cross-referenced from the model reports, and they carry the exact
sentences the practices now carry. The failure is one step later: the reading
was filed as *exegesis of a model report* rather than as advice, because the
prompt to write it was "why does K3 do this" rather than "what should I do".

The tell is a note whose Standing section explains another document's
decision. That is a different query again from the previous three, and it
would have found all four of these.

## And the trunk pattern showed up a third time

[LIT-200](../../record/literature.d/LIT-200.md)'s own Standing section had already done the analysis: "Neither
cites a problem with SwiGLU's quality; both object to its **range**." Two
groups, two remedies, no comparison between them — so the record can state
the agreement without picking a function, and could not before, because the
only nodes available were `SOTA-034` (SwiGLU, contested) and nothing.

Three trunks in one day, found by three different methods, in three unrelated
subjects. That is no longer a coincidence about hyper-connections; it is what
this record's filing habit does. A branch has an arrival event and gets
filed. Agreement has no arrival event and does not.

## The acknowledgement mechanic, again, in the other direction

This batch wrote **four** directives vouching for documents that turned out to
be `Active` — no acknowledgement needed — and the lint rejected all four with
"annotation no longer applies". Yesterday's instance was the same mistake;
today's is at four times the rate, because I was writing acknowledgements
defensively rather than from the report.

The fix is mechanical and worth stating: **write the acknowledgement after
running the lint, from the list of findings, not while writing the prose.**
The report says exactly which citations need one. Guessing produces both
kinds of error — a missing vouch and a vouch for nothing — and only the first
is the one anybody worries about.

<a id="20260908014038"></a>

## Four conflict resolutions taught nothing, which is what a misplaced file feels like

*2026-09-08 01:40:38 · method · mechanism*

**The tell was that resolving the conflicts was never interesting.** Four
times today two branches collided on generated pages, and four times the
resolution was the same ritual: `git checkout --theirs docs/`, rerun `luria
index`, re-stage, commit. Nothing was learned. No judgement was exercised.
The correct content was a pure function of sources that were not themselves
in conflict.

That is the signature of a file in the wrong place, and it took four
repetitions to read it as one rather than as friction to be absorbed. Luria's
own principle covers this — a guard that keeps catching you is a bug report
about the workflow — and the same shape applies to a merge conflict that
keeps arriving with no information in it.

## What the cost actually was

Not the resolutions. The resolutions were minutes. The cost was:

- **A recovery from a failed `git stash pop`** earlier in the day, where
  regenerated views blocked the merge and four untracked notes had to be
  verified intact by hand before anything could proceed.
- **A second conflict on the same branch after the first merge**, because the
  bot's regeneration commit on `main` rewrites the same shared files — and
  that time `luria concretize` had also renamed the temp-coded documents the
  first merge numbered, so the second resolution was against files with
  different names.
- **A stack three deep** that had to be collapsed and landed in one merge to
  avoid two more rounds of it.

None of that is inherent to the work. All of it came from regenerating
shared files on branches.

## The fix, and the thing that made it available

`docs.yml` now mirrors the shape luria uses on its own record: generate and
commit views on the push to `main`, and on a pull request run the generate
action with `views: "false"` plus the lint action in the same job, so source
repairs land on the branch and no view is written.

Worth recording how close this came to being blocked. Checking whether the
pinned action supported `views:` at all, the first attempt was `git show
0.11.0:actions/generate/action.yml` in a clone whose tags had never been
fetched — the tag did not resolve, the command failed, the `|| echo "NOT
PRESENT"` fallback fired, and the answer read as a clean negative. It was
wrong. `views:` is in 0.11.0.

**A shell fallback that cannot distinguish "absent" from "the lookup
failed" will report the second as the first**, and it will do so in the
confident voice of a successful command. The same shape as suppressing
stderr, which this journal already records once. The version that would not
have lied: resolve the ref first, then read the file, and let the failure be
a failure.

## What it changes for a contributor

Run `luria index` locally anyway — `docs/reports/reference-status.md` is what
tells you which citations the lint is about to flag, and reading it before
writing acknowledgements is the fix for the *other* recurring mistake this
week. Then throw the views away before committing. A branch carrying views is
not more up to date; it is a conflict with every other branch.

<a id="20260908014807"></a>

## The record was arguing with two papers it had not marked itself as contested by

*2026-09-08 01:48:07 · method · record*

**Filing the repetition cluster turned up a defect in a practice the cluster
was not about.** [SOTA-124](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-124.md) said `consensus: unreplicated`, with a note ending
"Nobody has contradicted it either" — and three paragraphs of its own body
argue in detail with [LIT-166](../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md) and [LIT-175](../../record/literature.d/LIT-175.md), both of which contradict it.

The frontmatter was written when it was true and never re-read when the body
changed. That is the same failure the consensus re-derivation pass found in
`SOTA-141` a day earlier — a value set correctly, then outlived by the prose
below it — and it is worth noticing that the pass which was *designed* to
catch exactly this missed this one, because `SOTA-124`'s support list had not
changed and so it was not on the candidate list.

**A pass keyed to "what changed" cannot see a document whose surroundings
changed instead.** That is a third variant of the shape this journal keeps
recording: a query finds the defect it is shaped like.

## The cluster itself: a fourth trunk, of a different kind

The FIM practice is the fourth case this week of a refinement filed without
the thing it refines. [SOTA-128](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-128.md) — whether to mask the loss on the prefix and
suffix of a FIM sample — has been in the record since the migration. The
practice it is a footnote to, *train with FIM at all*, was filed today.

But the mechanism is not the one the earlier entries named. The
hyper-connections and matrix-preconditioner trunks went missing because
agreement has no arrival event. This one went missing for a different reason:
**the refinement was the part somebody in this project had measured.**
`SOTA-128` is sourced to Falcon-H1-Tiny's two 90M runs. FIM itself was
established in 2022 and simply assumed. The trunk was missing not because
nobody published it but because it was too old to feel like news when the
corpus was being built.

So: agreement has no arrival event, and neither does a four-year-old default.
Both are invisible to a filing habit that runs on arrivals.

## Three positions on one question, and none of them is wrong

The nicest thing in this cluster is that the repetition disagreement is
genuinely unresolved and now legible as such:

- **`SOTA-124`** — repetition is safe when epoch *size* exceeds the
  memorization window. One figure, one scale, authors call it early.
  Falcon-H1-Tiny repeated sources 100×.
- **The four-epoch practice** — four epochs, then the value of added compute
  decays. 400 runs, released models and datasets.
- **The augmentation practice** — repetition overfits severely, and the
  overfitting is a property of the *objective*, removable.

They are not measuring the same quantity: a whole corpus under fixed compute,
against one high-quality source inside a mixture, against the objective
itself. The third makes the first two falsifiable in the same terms, which is
why it is the most useful of the three even though it is the least
established. Filing all three is what lets a reader see that the question is
open rather than picking whichever document they happened to find.

<a id="20260908015313"></a>

## A temporary code is branch-local, and two parallel branches cannot cite each other

*2026-09-08 01:53:13 · method · mechanism*

**The lint caught something the new workflow made possible.** With views no
longer generated on branches, two clusters can be worked in parallel off
`main` instead of stacked — and the first time that happened, one practice
cited `SOTA-171`, a temporary code that exists only on the *other*
branch.

`luria lint` reported it as an unresolved code, which is exactly right and
worth writing down as a rule rather than an incident:

> **A merge-allocated temporary code is branch-local by construction.** It is
> a placeholder for a number that will be assigned when the branch merges,
> and two branches in flight have no way to know each other's assignments —
> so a cross-branch reference is not merely unresolvable now, it would resolve
> to the *wrong* document later if it resolved at all.

The fix is to cite the **note** instead. `LIT-166` is a real code on `main`;
the practice drawn from it is not yet. Referring to "the four-epoch practice
drawn from [LIT-166](../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md)" says the same thing, resolves today, and stays true after
both branches land under whatever numbers they get.

That generalises: **across branches, refer to the stable thing.** Literature
codes are stable because notes are filed before the practices that cite them;
practice codes filed in the same contribution are not.

## The trade the new workflow bought, stated plainly

Before, parallel branches conflicted on generated views, so the natural move
was to stack — and stacking made every merge a re-resolution. Now branches
are independent and the only thing they can collide on is a temporary code,
which the lint catches at the citing site rather than at merge time.

That is a better failure: it is local, it names the file and the code, and it
is fixed by writing a sentence differently rather than by re-running a
generator and re-staging nineteen files.

## The cluster

Two practices — filter by token horizon, and build synthetic data by editing
human text — and two notes that now say why they keep none. Those two
refusals are worth having beside each other, because the reasons are
different and both are reusable:

- **[LIT-184](../../record/literature.d/LIT-184.md), FineWeb: scope.** A dataset is not a technique. Its
  transferable content is an ablation methodology, and it lands in the
  filtering practice as the position that practice argues against.
- **[LIT-125](../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md), Qwen2.5-Coder: [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md).** A model report describes a recipe in
  full and isolates none of it. It supplies adoption, not evidence about a
  claim.

Neither is "nobody at frontier scale does it", which is the reason the whole
sweep exists to stop giving.

<a id="20260908020135"></a>

## The principles were already written, scattered across a week of journal entries

*2026-09-08 02:01:35 · method · record*

**Nothing in the four new principles is new.** Every one of them was argued
in full, at length, inside a devlog entry or a decision written in the last
few days. What they lacked was the one property that makes a principle
useful: being in the place a person looks *before* making the mistake rather
than after.

That is worth noticing about the shape of this record. A journal entry is
indexed by date. A decision is indexed by the choice it settles. Neither is
indexed by the situation a future reader will be in — and "I have a paper
with weak evidence and a real recommendation, what do I do" is a situation,
not a date or a decision.

## The selection criterion, since four were filed and several were not

The test used: **would stating this in advance have prevented a specific
mistake that was actually made this week?** Not "is it true", which too much
is, and not "is it interesting", which is how a principles page fills up with
observations nobody applies.

Filed on that test:

- *Filing is not endorsement* — would have prevented twelve practices being
  absent for months.
- *Agreement has no author* — would have prevented three trunk practices
  going unfiled while their branches were documented.
- *Adoption is not evidence* — would have prevented a support list of four
  model reports under a practice whose own prose called them adoption.
- *A vocabulary is a scope decision* — would have replaced a bad reason for
  declining a vision paper with the real one.

Held back, and worth saying why, because both are true and neither passed:

- **"A pass finds the defect its query is shaped like."** The strongest
  general lesson of the week — it recurred three times, in the source pass,
  the consensus pass, and the refusal grep. It is a principle about *method*,
  not about what belongs in this record, and the four filed here are
  deliberately one subject. It should probably be filed, and as its own
  thing.
- **"Derived state belongs where writes serialize."** Genuinely earned by
  four merge conflicts, and it is luria's decision to make rather than this
  project's — [ADR-018](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-018.md) adopts it wholesale and cites upstream. A principle
  restating a dependency's principle is a copy that will drift.

## The reflexive bit, which is not a joke

The reason these four principles went unwritten is the reason the practices
they are about went unfiled: **nothing prompts you to record what you already
know.** The trunk of a line of work has no arrival event; neither does the
rule you have been following successfully for a week. Both get written down
only if somebody goes looking on purpose.

Which suggests the same defence in both cases — a deliberate pass, run
against a question rather than against a diff — and suggests running it after
any stretch of work where the same correction was made twice.

<a id="20260908022205"></a>

## Four merges in forty seconds, four failed runs, and a lost concretization

*2026-09-08 02:22:05 · method · mechanism*

**I merged four pull requests in under a minute and every resulting run on
the trunk failed.** Nothing about the changes was wrong. The failure was
entirely in the cadence, and it is worth writing down because the same
mistake is available to anybody with merge rights and a queue of green
branches.

## What actually happened

Each merge starts a push run. Each push run regenerates the views and pushes
them to the branch it ran on. Four of those started within seconds of each
other, so three of them finished a regeneration only to find the branch had
moved — and the recovery, pulling and rebasing their own regeneration commit
onto the winner's, conflicts by construction, because both commits rewrite
the same generated files.

The log is unambiguous, and the ordering in it is the painful part:

    rename record/principles.d/{[DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8).md => [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8).md} (94%)
    ...
    CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in docs/curation/2026-09.md
    error: could not apply 213771b... docs: regenerate views [skip ci]

The run **had already done the concretization correctly**. It numbered five
principles, then lost all of it to a rebase conflict on generated pages it
had also just rewritten. `main` was left carrying temporary codes, which is
precisely the state the trunk guard exists to forbid, reached by the
machinery meant to prevent it.

## Why it was not caught by the fix that preceded it

An hour earlier the views moved to the trunk only, on the argument that a
shared generated file cannot be edited by two branches at once. That
argument was right and incomplete: it removed the conflict between two
*branches* and left the conflict between two *runs on the same branch*
untouched. Serialization by placement is not serialization in time.

That is worth stating generally. **Making a file single-writer by location
does nothing about concurrent writers at that location.** The second half of
the problem is invisible while merges are spaced apart by human reading
speed, and arrives the first time they are not.

## The fix, and the smaller lesson about cadence

`concurrency:` keyed on the workflow and ref, with `cancel-in-progress:
false`, so runs for one branch queue rather than race. A burst of merges
collapses to the run in flight plus one more, and the last one regenerates
from the final source state — which is the only state that has to be right.

[ADR-002](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-002.md) had already made this argument once, for the changelog collector:
a per-merge bot commit races in-flight rebases, so collection runs on a
cadence and never per merge. The reasoning transferred to a different job in
the same workflow and nobody carried it across, which is the ordinary way a
decision fails to generalize — it was filed against the job it was about.

The behavioural half is simpler and I should have known it: **merging a stack
is not a batch operation.** Each merge is a deployment. Spacing four of them
by twenty seconds would have cost nothing and prevented all of this.

## And a second finding, from trying to ship the first one

The pull request carrying this fix started **no CI run at all**. Not a
failure — nothing. The cause was in its own commit message, which quoted the
CI log above, and the log line ends in the bot's skip marker.

The workflow's header comment had warned about exactly this trap and got the
scope wrong: it said the marker suppresses a run "in the first or last line".
The marker here was on line 18 of 56, and the run was suppressed anyway.
Amending the message to spell the marker in prose made the same tree build
immediately.

Two things worth keeping:

- **The comment is now corrected**, because a warning with the wrong
  precondition is worse than none — it invites exactly the reasoning I did,
  which was to check the position, find it mid-message, and conclude this
  could not be the cause.
- **Pasting a CI log into a commit message is the likeliest way to quote the
  marker by accident**, and it is a thing anybody debugging CI will want to
  do. The failure mode is silent: no run, no error, no skipped-run entry.
  Looking for a red check finds nothing wrong, because there is nothing
  there.

That is the same shape as the earlier note about a shell fallback that cannot
tell "absent" from "the lookup failed": a diagnostic that reports nothing is
read as a diagnostic reporting no problem.

<a id="20260908023553"></a>

## The lowest-yield cluster was the one where the earlier work had already been done

*2026-09-08 02:35:53 · method · record*

**Eight candidates, three practices.** Every earlier cluster in this sweep
converted at better than half; this one converted at three-eighths, and the
reason is worth recording because it is the first evidence that the sweep is
approaching its end rather than that it stalled.

Five of the eight are **line members**, and their notes had already said so
in detail. Mamba's selectivity is inherited by everything the record
recommends. The state-space duality is a *premise* of the hybrid practices,
not a rival to them. Gated Linear Attention is parallel invention that the
record's actual line does not run through. Griffin is the origin of the
interleave and takes the other side of a fork the practice already argues.
The gated-convolution paper is the origin of a unit `SOTA-034` recommends a
variant of.

None of those is a recommendation to file. All of them are things a reader
meeting the practice should be told, and in three of five cases the practice
already told them: `SOTA-034` had a "Where the gate came from" section,
`SOTA-132`'s Variations already carried the intra-layer layout and the
parallel-head one.

## What that says about the previous clusters

The four earlier clusters each found a defect. This one mostly found work
already done — and the difference is not that this material is better tended.
It is that **the architecture half of the record has been worked on recently
and repeatedly**, in the reference pass and the two hybrid passes, while the
data and optimizer halves had not been touched since the migration.

So the sweep's yield is a measure of when a section was last read, not of how
important it is. Worth knowing before reading a low-yield cluster as evidence
that a subject is in good shape: it is evidence that somebody was here
recently.

## The one real gap, and it was two steps back

`SOTA-132`'s `Sequence` began at the Gated DeltaNet hybrids of 2024. The
interleave starts at Griffin, and the delta-rule paper says so in as many
words — its sliding-window hybrid "follows Griffin and Samba". The practice
had been describing a line from its middle.

The fork at that first step is the part that matters and was nowhere: Griffin
puts **local** attention in the minority layers, the practice puts **global**
attention there, and only global preserves exact retrieval at arbitrary
distance — which is the entire reason the minority layers exist. A reader
taking "interleave at 3:1" from the earlier work would get the ratio and lose
the reason.

That is a fourth variety of the trunk problem: not a missing trunk, but a
line **entered halfway**, where the steps before the entry point carry the
argument for why the practice is shaped as it is.

## A small one from the lint

A directive in `SOTA-171` vouched for a citation that a file-scope directive
at the top of the same file already covered, and the lint reported it as no
longer applying. That is the guard catching a **redundant** acknowledgement
rather than a stale one — a third thing it can find, after the missing vouch
and the vouch for a document that has since gone `Active`. Cheap to fix and
worth knowing the report means three different things.

<a id="20260908025054"></a>

## What the sweep cost, what it found, and the number that says it worked

*2026-09-08 02:50:54 · method · record*

**The sweep is done.** Every post-migration note carrying a practice-eligible
topic now either sources a practice or says why it does not, in its own
Standing section, in terms a reader can disagree with.

## The count

Twenty-four practices added across six clusters, 157 → 181. But the
distribution is the part worth keeping:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Proposed` | 14 | 28 |
| carrying a `consensus:` value | 28 | 50 |

**The provisional half of the status vocabulary doubled.** That is the direct
consequence of the entry rule this all started from — file the claim, let
`status:` carry the belief — and it is the measurable version of what
[DP-006](../../docs/design-principles.md) argues. A vocabulary whose provisional values were used fourteen
times in a corpus of 157 was barely a vocabulary; at 28 of 181 it is doing
work.

## What the sweep actually found, sorted by kind

Not one kind of defect. Six, and only the first was the one it went looking
for:

1. **Refused for adoption** — the `Active` bar applied to whether a document
   should exist. Three cases, all refused in writing, one of them in an ADR.
2. **Never noticed at all** — deduplication and multi-token prediction, in
   every pipeline the record describes, argued about by nobody, filed by
   nobody.
3. **A trunk with its branches filed** — three times, in three unrelated
   subjects, found by three different methods.
4. **A refinement filed before the thing it refines** — the loss-masking
   footnote four months ahead of the practice of constructing a fill-in-the-
   middle sample at all.
5. **A line entered halfway** — the interleave practice beginning two steps
   after the interleave does, losing the fork that explains its own shape.
6. **Exegesis filed as a note** — four papers read closely, in detail,
   because a frontier report cited them, and filed as explanations of
   somebody else's decision rather than as advice.

The through-line is in [DP-007](../../docs/design-principles.md): the filing habit runs on arrivals, and
none of these six had one.

## What it cost, honestly

Six pull requests of content, plus three of infrastructure that the content
work forced: views moved off branches, runs serialized per ref, and a
skip-marker caution corrected. Two of those three were caused by my own
mistakes — regenerating shared files on branches, and merging four pull
requests in forty seconds — and both were the kind that only appear at a
tempo a person would not have reached.

That is worth naming as a cost of working this way rather than as bad luck.
**Working faster than a human would find the same bugs faster, and it finds
bugs a human would not have hit at all.** Both halves are real, and the
second one is not free: three of the nine contributions here were repairs to
damage the pace caused.

## The one number that says it worked

Not the practice count. **Zero.** That is how many post-migration notes with
a practice-eligible topic now lack either a practice or a written reason —
and it is checkable in about fifteen lines of Python, which is the property
that makes it worth having. The count of practices will drift. The invariant
either holds or it does not, and the next person can find out in a minute.

The invariant is also, per [DP-004](../../docs/design-principles.md), evidence about exactly one query. It says
nothing about the inherited 119 notes, which were never audited under these
rules, and nothing about whether the practices filed are *good*. Those are
different passes and they are filed as such.

<a id="20260908041409"></a>

## The legacy flush: what came out, and what stayed

*2026-09-08 04:14:09 · infrastructure*

Issue [#41](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/41) asked for the pre-record Python to go. It was three tools sharing
one dependency: a README generator that assembled `README.md` and
`README_LLM.md` from Jinja templates, a directory summariser that wrote
per-directory prose into `docs/`, and a package-lock helper for a frontend
that no longer exists. All three imported `llamero`; the workflows that ran
them are gone with them.

Four things were checked before deleting anything, because each one could
have made a deletion lossy:

- **Nothing in the record referenced the modules.** The `[luria.code]` globs
  scanned `src/**/*.py` and `docs/**/*.j2`; with the templates gone the second
  glob names nothing, so it went too.
- **The templates were not templates.** `README.md` and `README_LLM.md` were
  concatenations of *static* fragments — no Jinja expressions in any of them —
  so the rendered files already in the tree are byte-complete, and the
  generator was rendering nothing. Deleting it loses no content.
- **`assets.logo.svg`** (the misnamed one at the repo root, a build artifact of
  an old workflow) is byte-identical to `assets/logo.svg`. Only the copy is
  gone.
- **`src/scripts/migration/`** stays. `CLAUDE.md` and [ADR-008](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-008.md) both promise the
  import stays re-runnable, and `to_record.py` needs only the standard library
  and `pyyaml` — so `pyproject.toml` shrank to that one dependency rather than
  disappearing.

The surprise was the test suite. It looked broken — `conftest.py` imports
`scripts.registry`, a module that has not existed for some time — so the first
read was "the tests are already dead, delete them." They were not: those
imports are inside fixture bodies, and the two tests that run never request
those fixtures. With `PYTHONPATH=src` the suite passed. The tests came out
because the code they covered came out, not because they were broken; the
distinction matters, because "already broken" would have been a reason to skip
checking what else the deletion took with it.

`README_LLM.md` was rewritten rather than trimmed. It had described
optional-dependency groups, a test suite, and a rule that "all workflows
depend on tests passing" — none of which survive, and two of which had not
been true for a while. A generated file that nobody regenerates decays into
a confident description of a repository that no longer exists.

<a id="20260908044455"></a>

## The inherited corpus, counted — and the duplicates it was hiding

*2026-09-08 04:44:55 · curation*

First pass at [#85](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/85). Before auditing 118 notes one at a time, two cheap
mechanical queries: what is actually in there, and does any paper appear
twice.

**The inventory.** The issue estimated "roughly 87 pre-migration" of 115
unsourced notes. The real numbers, taking [LIT-001](../../record/literature.d/LIT-001.md)..118 as the inherited set:

| | notes |
|---|---|
| inherited total | 118 |
| sourced by at least one practice | 45 |
| unsourced | 73 |
| unsourced *and* in a topic the SOTA scheme can hold | **37** |

So the audit's actual surface is 37 notes, not 87. The other 36 unsourced
notes sit in `generative-modeling`, `vision-and-graphics`,
`analysis-and-evaluation`, `adaptation-and-tuning` and
`inference-optimization` — five topics `practices.d/tags.yaml` does not
carry, which is [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8) working as designed rather than a backlog. Confirming
that reasoning applies is one paragraph, not 36 readings.

**The duplicates.** Grouping all 218 notes by `arxiv:` and by normalized
title found three pairs. One ([LIT-090](../../record/literature.d/LIT-090.md) / [LIT-105](../../record/literature.d/LIT-105.md), Lion) was already
deliberately retired in September. The other two were live:

- **[LIT-006](../../record/literature.d/LIT-006.md) / [LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md)**, Loshchilov and Hutter's SGDR. [LIT-006](../../record/literature.d/LIT-006.md) read `Active`
  and [LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md) read `Superseded`, so the record asserted both about one paper.
  Nothing cited [LIT-006](../../record/literature.d/LIT-006.md); everything that mattered pointed at [LIT-042](../../record/literature.d/LIT-042.md), which
  carries the schedule chain. Retired [LIT-006](../../record/literature.d/LIT-006.md).
- **[LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md) / [LIT-114](../../record/literature.d/LIT-114.md)**, Xiong et al. on layer normalization. Both `Active`.
  Retired [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md).

**What the second pair was concealing**, which is the part worth the
contribution. The two notes reached the same paper from opposite directions,
and that is why a year of lints never saw it. [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md) was filed with the
*right identifier and the wrong reading* — a single migration-authored bullet
claiming the paper shows "RMSNorm pre-norm permits stable training at scale".
Xiong et al. never discuss RMSNorm; that is Zhang and Sennrich, [LIT-023](../../record/literature.d/LIT-023.md),
which the record already held. [LIT-114](../../record/literature.d/LIT-114.md) was filed with a *fabricated title
against an unrelated arXiv id* and was repaired in September by re-sourcing
it to Xiong et al. Neither repair could see the other, because no check
compares identifiers across notes (luria#165).

The cost was not the extra document. [SOTA-032](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-032.md) sourced [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md) and inherited
its conflation: "Use pre-norm (RMSNorm) for transformer layers" — two
independently adoptable choices, one citation, and that citation supports
only the placement half. GPT-2 is Pre-LN with centered LayerNorm; nothing
stops a Post-LN model using RMSNorm. Split into the placement practice
([SOTA-032](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-032.md), now sourced to [LIT-114](../../record/literature.d/LIT-114.md)) and the statistic ([SOTA-182](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-182.md), sourced
to [LIT-023](../../record/literature.d/LIT-023.md)).

**What this says about the query, per [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4).** The duplicate scan is exact
and finds exactly duplicates — identical `arxiv:` or identical title. It
cannot see the same paper filed under two different identifiers, which is
what the [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md) / [LIT-114](../../record/literature.d/LIT-114.md) pair *was* until the September repair happened to
converge them. That pair became findable by accident. How many others are
still divergent is not something this query can answer, and a title-similarity
pass is a different contribution.

It also says nothing about correctness. [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md)'s bullet was wrong about its
own paper and no check could have caught it; it was found because the
duplicate scan put two readings of one work side by side. That is the second
argument for luria#165 — a duplicate detector is a cheap correctness check
you get for free.
