<a id="20260908045940"></a>

## The tag is not the scope boundary — and I applied that error twice in one hour

*2026-09-08 04:59:40 · curation*

Second pass at [#85](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/85). The issue proposed that the inherited notes tagged
`generative-modeling`, `vision-and-graphics`, `adaptation-and-tuning`,
`inference-optimization` and `analysis-and-evaluation` are unfiled because
`practices.d/tags.yaml` declines those subjects — [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8), a stated scope
decision rather than a backlog. About 36 notes, expected yield zero, one
paragraph of confirmation.

That premise is wrong, and I got it wrong twice on the way to saying so.

**The issue's error.** The record already holds twelve
post-training and quantization practices — [SOTA-126](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-126.md) on DPO epochs, [SOTA-129](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-129.md)
on the pretrain/SFT/RLVR staging, [SOTA-154](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-154.md) on evolution strategies, [SOTA-160](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-160.md)
and [SOTA-163](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-163.md) on quantization — filed under `training-optimization` and
`systems-optimization`. Every one of them sources a *post-migration* note. So
the anthology has not declined to hold fine-tuning, preference training or
quantization. It holds them, under the seven topics.

The `LIT` scheme has twelve topics and the `SOTA` scheme has seven, and the
extra five are not a scope boundary. **The two vocabularies overlap; they do
not nest.** What happened is that post-migration papers on these subjects were
read and filed, and pre-migration ones got a tag outside the practice seven
and were never looked at again. The tag concealed them rather than excluding
them. LoRA — one of the most widely adopted training practices in the corpus
— sat unfiled for a year behind `adaptation-and-tuning`.

**The second error was mine, and it was the opposite one.** Having written
that paragraph, I asserted that the 24 notes tagged `generative-modeling` and
`vision-and-graphics` were "out of scope by construction" — from their tags,
without opening one. Challenged on it, I accepted the challenge, rewrote the
reasoning to say that domain never decides scope, and pushed that.

Then I read the record. [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8) says, in as many words, that *the
recommendations are scoped to language-model training by construction* — that
a vision paper can be a note and cannot be a recommendation, "not on
judgement, not on evidence, but because there is no category for it to take."
[ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md) made that split deliberately and rejected the single-vocabulary
alternative precisely because it "puts a diffusion sampler paper under
`training-optimization` or `model-architecture` and makes both pages worse."

So the conclusion was right and the reasoning was not, and then I replaced
correct reasoning with wrong reasoning because I did not check. Which is the
generator this whole audit exists to catch: a claim that sounds right,
asserted without opening the source. Three of the migration's errors were
that. So was this.

**What actually survives.** [ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md) justifies all five extra `LIT` topics
with one sentence — "the reading list covers ground the practice registry
does not." That is true of `generative-modeling` and `vision-and-graphics`,
and it is *false* of `adaptation-and-tuning` and `inference-optimization`: the
record holds fine-tuning, preference-training and quantization practices under
the seven, several of each. [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8) names "vision, generative and theory work"
and never claims otherwise. **Five topics were bundled under a reason that
holds for three of them**, and the bundling is what made LoRA look declined
rather than overlooked.

**The corrected surface.** Of 71 inherited notes that source no practice: 18
carry a written reason, 13 are retired, and 53 are bare. Of the 53, 23 are the
generative and vision corpus, which [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8) settles — they need a written
reason each or, better, one statement in the index, not a reading. The other
30 need reading.

**Two errors, opposite directions, one cause.** The issue over-applied a scope
decision to topics it never covered. I then under-applied it to the topics it
does cover. Neither of us read [ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md). A decision that is written down and
not read is, operationally, a decision that was not made — which is [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8)'s
own point about vocabularies, turned on the document that states it.

Filed two practices as the demonstration that the concealment in those two
topics is real rather than theoretical, and left the rest for a pass that
reads them.

<a id="20260908051115"></a>

## Four notes read, and the difference between a gap and a decision

*2026-09-08 05:11:15 · curation*

The four notes deferred from the scope-correction pass, now read. All four
were migration stubs whose bullets named the area rather than the method.
Two attributions were checkable and one was wrong.

**GPTQ ([LIT-081](../../record/literature.d/LIT-081.md)) sources a practice.** Error-compensating one-shot
post-training quantization: round column by column and push each rounding
error into the columns not yet done, using second-order information from a
calibration set. 3–4 bits at 175B in about four GPU-hours, where reaching
that before had meant quantization-aware training. Filed as the *approach*
rather than the artifact — the specific search and ordering have been
improved on many times since, and what converged is the shape.

**Three notes carry no practice, and now say so.** This is the distinction
worth recording, because "no practice" covers two quite different situations
and the record could not previously tell them apart:

- **P-Tuning v2 ([LIT-055](../../record/literature.d/LIT-055.md)) is a decision.** The record recommends low-rank
  adaptation for the same job, and recommending both would be recommending
  neither. But the note stays `Active` because the comparison is the content:
  deep prefix tuning is competitive on *quality* and lost on *deployment
  shape* — a prefix occupies context at every layer forever, where a low-rank
  update folds into the weight and disappears. A corpus holding only the
  winner cannot say that.
- **The lottery-ticket pair ([LIT-019](../../record/literature.d/LIT-019.md), [LIT-039](../../record/literature.d/LIT-039.md)) is a gap, and a different
  gap than it looks.** The record holds no sparsity or pruning practice at
  all, which is not a scope decision — sparsity is expressible in
  `model-architecture` and there is live work on it. But these two notes are
  not what would close it. LTH's procedure costs a full dense training run
  before producing anything, so as an instruction it reads "train the model,
  then train a smaller one." And Evci et al. is the deflation: a rewound
  ticket re-learns the solution the dense run already found rather than
  discovering a good sparse architecture. The record needs both, precisely so
  the hypothesis is not carried unqualified.

**The attribution error is the interesting one.** [LIT-039](../../record/literature.d/LIT-039.md) was filed as
Frankle. It is a lottery-ticket paper, and Frankle wrote the lottery-ticket
paper, so the guess is nearly right and completely wrong — Evci et al. This
is the same generator as [LIT-029](../../record/literature.d/LIT-029.md)'s fabricated RMSNorm bullet and [LIT-082](../../record/literature.d/LIT-082.md)'s
Askell: describing a work from its subject produces text that is plausible in
every respect except being true. Three instances now, all from one migration.

**On verification.** The arXiv API stopped responding partway through this
pass — three of seven lookups returned, then timeouts. Semantic Scholar
answered the rest. Worth writing down because the alternative was to assert
four attributions from memory, which is exactly the failure being repaired,
and because "the check is unavailable" is a reason to stop rather than a
reason to proceed carefully.

<a id="20260908053627"></a>

## Widening the scope, and the axis I built and took back out

*2026-09-08 05:36:27 · ontology*

The scope was drawn around language-model training, and that turned out to be
wrong in both directions at once.

**Too narrow, already.** [SOTA-113](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-113.md) and [SOTA-115](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-115.md) are `Active` recommendations
about serving, filed under `systems-optimization`, and they had been sitting
outside the written scope for a year with nobody noticing. So had the
quantization practices. [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8) asserted "scoped to language-model training by
construction" as a fact about the record; it was a fact about the sentence.

**Too broad, in the sense that mattered.** A scope drawn by domain declines
work whose transferable content is exactly the kind of claim the seven topics
collect. EDM contributes a preconditioning scheme, a noise-level sampling
distribution and a loss weighting. Segment Anything contributes a
model-in-the-loop annotation bootstrap. Those are a `training-optimization`
claim and a `data-pipeline` claim that happen to have been found in image
models.

So: scope by the kind of claim. That is the whole decision, and it needed no
new machinery — which is not where this started.

**The part worth writing down is the axis I built and then removed.** The
first draft added a `domain:` field to the practice scheme: a many-valued
vocabulary saying what a practice applies to, with `domain-general` marking
what transfers. It survived a design review with the user, got sharpened
(many-valued rather than scalar, because where a practice holds is a set that
accumulates), was implemented, backfilled, linted and pushed.

Then the objection that should have come first: **it lets a practice assert
where it applies while naming no evidence for the assertion.** In a record
whose first principle is [DP-001](../design-principles.md#dp-1), and which had just spent a contribution
establishing that `source:` holds the work that produced evidence about the
claim. The draft demonstrated its own failure in the same diff — three of the
eight backfills claimed `domain-general`, meaning "transfers across every
modality", each on the strength of one language-model paper.

Three more, any one sufficient:

- **It would be ~99% default.** One note in 218 is a cross-domain transfer
  result. A field that is overwhelmingly default is not neutral: absence gets
  read as a value. `consensus:` gets away with it because you assess consensus
  while touching the practice; you cannot assess domain without reading papers
  in another field.
- **It aims at the weakest link.** Blindness has a pipeline — never
  encountering a paper, refusing it on scope, filing a note and drawing no
  practice, filing a practice nobody finds. The scope widening fixes the
  second. [#85](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/85) says the third is the binding constraint: 53 bare notes. The
  field addresses only the fourth.
- **[DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8)'s own corollary** — a category added to admit a single document is
  how a scope stops being one — applied to the decision that amends [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8).

**What I got wrong about the alternatives, too.** I pitched "derive the
practice's domain from its sources" as the evidence-respecting option. It is
not available: only two of the twelve `LIT` topics carry domain information at
all, the other ten being kind-of-claim words. Deriving would mean first adding
a domain axis to the notes — so that option is not cheaper than the one it was
meant to replace, it is the same thing plus a second step.

The shape that *would* work is [ADR-016](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-016.md)'s: a value asserting that specific
other work exists must name it. `shown-to-transfer` requiring a
`transfers_shown_by:` reference needs no new machinery. Recorded in the ADR
along with the three-row decomposition, so the next person inherits the
reasoning rather than the field.

**The convergence that settled it.** The one cross-domain transfer result the
corpus already holds is [LIT-090](../../record/literature.d/LIT-090.md) — Lion, reported across vision,
vision-language, diffusion and language modelling. It sits `Rejected`, on an
inherited retirement its own note flags as unreviewed. It is at once the
evidence a transfer axis would need and a question the widened scope makes
live. Read that first; if a second one turns up, build the axis.

**Cost of the detour:** one design, one implementation, one backfill, all
reverted. Cheap in absolute terms and worth naming anyway, because the
objection that killed it — *what evidence backs this field?* — is the
project's own first principle, and I applied it to every other field in the
record before I applied it to the one I was adding.

<a id="20260908071238"></a>

## The cluster the old scope hid, read

*2026-09-08 07:12:38 · curation*

Twenty-three notes in the generative and vision corpus had been set aside as
out of scope by construction — twice, once by the issue and once by me, both
times from the tag rather than the paper. [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md) removed that exit. This is
the first pass over them with the question [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md) actually asks: does the
work contain an instruction one of the seven topics can express?

**Three do, and all three are claims that outgrow their domain.**

EDM ([LIT-075](../../record/literature.d/LIT-075.md)) contributes a preconditioning scheme, a training-noise
distribution and a loss weighting. A denoiser does a different job at every
noise level, so without adjustment the loss is dominated by whichever regime
has the largest raw magnitudes. Wrap the network in level-dependent scalings
so the target has unit variance everywhere, and sample the level from a
log-normal concentrated where there is something to learn rather than
uniformly. The shape generalizes past diffusion: when a network is
conditioned on a variable that changes the difficulty of its task, normalize
the target so the loss means the same thing at every value, and sample that
variable where the signal is.

Segment Anything ([LIT-096](../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md)) contributes a three-stage annotation loop —
assisted-manual, semi-automatic, fully automatic, retraining between stages.
Nothing about segmentation. The claim is that when annotation binds, the
right structure is a staged loop whose escalation is driven by the current
model uncertainty, not a one-shot labelling contract.

Latent Diffusion ([LIT-062](../../record/literature.d/LIT-062.md)) contributes a compute-allocation argument:
likelihood models spend most of their capacity on imperceptible detail, so
strip it with a cheap model first. Two stages — learn a compact
representation, then model that — filed under model-architecture because
that is what it is.

**Eight carry no practice today, and the reasons split in a way worth noticing.** The
radiance-field and task-solution papers — Instant-NGP, K-Planes, 3D Gaussian
Splatting, NeuS2, OnePose, Gaussian Shell Maps, OWL-ViT, MiDaS. Two are worth
the specific reason rather than the generic one. 3D Gaussian Splatting is
consequential and carries no training instruction because there is no network
being trained; it is an optimization over primitives, and it stays as reading
because the radiance-field line is unintelligible without it. MiDaS has a
genuinely transferable half — mix many datasets under an objective invariant
to their differing scale conventions — but the note carries no evidence about
it beyond the released models, which is the [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) case: shipping is not
measuring.

**Four of those eight are the vocabulary's fault, not the paper's.** Where a
claim has no category to take, that is a shortcoming of the topic set rather
than evidence the literature is irrelevant — and Instant-NGP, K-Planes,
OnePose and Gaussian Splatting are all declined on exactly that. The first
three carry representation and encoding claims and the record's encoding
practices are scattered (RoPE in `attention-techniques`, quantization formats
in `systems-optimization`); the fourth optimizes explicit primitives rather
than network weights, with densification and pruning schedules the record has
no comparable entry for. Written up as gaps to close, not as papers turned
away. The first draft of this entry said the seven topics "cannot express"
them, which reads as a verdict on the work and is the wrong way round.

**A workflow note.** The first draft closed each of the eleven notes with the
same paragraph explaining that it had been read under [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md). The lint
reported ten unacknowledged citations of a `Proposed` decision, which was the
correct complaint about the wrong thing: ten identical directives would have
been the fix, and eleven identical paragraphs were the actual defect. Removed
them; the fact belongs here once, which is what a curation entry is for. The
guard caught a repetition problem by way of a reference problem.

**What is left.** The generative half still has ten bare notes, and they are
the harder ones: DDIM and DPM-Solver are sampler algorithms, which is the
inference-shaped gap [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md) explicitly declined to open a topic for;
Progressive Distillation and Consistency Models are training procedures that
buy inference speed and probably do carry practices; Textual Inversion and
DreamBooth are personalization methods that sit beside LoRA; ControlNet and
T2I-Adapter are conditioning architectures; DALL-E 2 and Imagen are model
reports where [ADR-017](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md) applies, though Imagen has a real capacity-allocation
finding underneath it. Each needs a reading, and none of them is settled by a
tag.

<a id="20260908072519"></a>

## Ten topics, and a query that names nothing

*2026-09-08 07:25:19 · ontology*

Prompted by a correction: where a paper carries a claim the topic set cannot
express, that is a shortcoming of the topic set, not evidence the literature
is irrelevant.

I had been doing the opposite. The generative and vision pass filed eight
notes as carrying no practice, and four of those declined the paper because
"the seven topics cannot express" its claim — which reads as a verdict on the
work and is exactly backwards. Corrected in that branch; the principle it
violated is now written down as its own document, because it is more general
than one pass.

**The argument for the principle is that the two readings are not
symmetric.** When a document arrives with a real claim and no category, either
the claim is out of scope or the vocabulary is short a category. The first is
cheaper, requires no work, and is self-confirming: decline the document and
the vocabulary still looks complete, because the evidence that would have
shown otherwise has just been turned away. So the default has to be the
second, and the burden sits on an argument about the kind of claim rather than
on a shrug at the absence of a slot.

**And the evidence was already in the record.** Two counts, neither
speculative:

- Seven practices about serving, filed under four different topics —
  model-stability, model-architecture, attention-techniques and
  systems-optimization. Running statistics at inference, multi-query
  attention, PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefill/decode overlap, and
  two on quantization.
- Six about adaptation, across four more. In-context learning, tiny-model
  pretraining, RoPE rescaling, evolution-strategies fine-tuning, low-rank
  adaptation, and the preference-training pair.

A subject scattered across four ill-fitting categories is a category that
exists in the corpus and not in the list. That is a checkable test, and it is
what the decision rests on rather than my judgement about what deserves a
page.

**The words come from the reading list.** The LIT scheme has had
`inference-optimization` and `adaptation-and-tuning` since [ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md). Where both
vocabularies name the same kind of claim they should use the same word, and
what stays LIT-only is `generative-modeling` and `vision-and-graphics` —
domains rather than kinds of claim, and [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md)'s argument against domain
topics is untouched.

**What was declined, and why that matters here.** `analysis-and-evaluation`
is the third kind-of-claim word in the LIT extras and it is not being added,
because no practice in the record wants it. Adding a category to hold zero
documents is [DP-008](../design-principles.md#dp-8)'s corollary run backwards, and a principle that says
"expand the vocabulary" would be worthless if it could not also say when not
to. The same holds for a representation or encoding topic: [LIT-064](../../record/literature.d/LIT-064.md), [LIT-086](../../record/literature.d/LIT-086.md)
and [LIT-111](../../record/literature.d/LIT-111.md) all want one, and the record's encoding practices are scattered
the way serving was — but nothing has been *filed* on those yet, so the
retagging evidence does not exist. File one and see where it wants to live.

**And then a better query found a third topic.** The first two came out of
searching practice *titles* for `inference`, `serving`, `fine-tune`. That works
and it has [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4)'s defect exactly: it finds the categories you already
suspect, because you have to name one to search for it.

The second query names nothing. Take the declared relation graph — `extends`,
`corrects`, `compared_against` and their converses — find its connected
components, and ask whether each sits inside one topic. A lineage is a set of
practices the record has *asserted* belong together; a topic is a set it has
*declared* belong together. Where they disagree, one of them is wrong.

Twelve components span more than one practice, and three crossed:

- **RoPE, rescaling it for context, and dropping it from global layers** —
  one argument about positional encoding under three different topics. Add
  the low-frequency truncation practice and tokenization and it is five
  practices, which is the same evidence standard the other two topics met.
  Nobody had to think of the word "encoding" to find it, which is the whole
  point.
- **The GRPO baseline, its correction, and the evolution-strategies
  alternative** — a crossing *this decision's own first draft created*, by
  moving one of the three to `adaptation-and-tuning` and leaving the other
  two. Repaired.
- **Flash attention and keeping its output in FP32** — genuinely both an
  attention technique and a stability claim. Left crossing, because not every
  disagreement is an error and a check that cannot say so gets ignored.

After the retagging: one of twelve crosses, and it is the third.

The check wants to exist as a check. `luria.edges.graph()` already builds the
cross-scheme relation graph and `Graph.inbound()` already exists, so it needs
no new machinery — and `luria site` already calls the rendering of that graph
"lineage", which is the name this reframe arrived under. Proposed upstream
rather than built here: every record with both relations and tags has this
question.

**A pattern worth naming.** This is the third decision about this vocabulary
in one day: [ADR-003](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-003.md) set it, [ADR-020](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-020.md) stopped it being read as a domain
boundary, this one widens it. That is not coincidence. Seven categories
transcribed from a 2024 document are now governing 185 practices across a
subject that has widened twice since. Expect a fourth, and treat the next
homeless claim as data rather than as a nuisance.

<a id="20260908161610"></a>

## The invariant check, declared and read once

*2026-09-08 16:16:10*

luria 0.12.0 lets a chain name the field its relations are asserting a
shared value in. Declared `invariant = "tags"` on both chains and read the
report once, cold.

**The practice chain had one finding and it was the one predicted.**
[SOTA-085](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-085.md) (use flash attention) `extended_by` [SOTA-161](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-161.md) (keep the attention
output in FP32, because flash attention's rounding bias compounds). An
attention technique and a stability claim, joined by a relation, with
nothing in either document naming the thing they are both about. Fixed with
a `flash-attention` secondary tag on both — narrow, true of each
independently, and it is what the relation was pointing at all along.

**The trap: the fix cannot be the other primary topic.** `primary_topic` is
`require = "exactly-one"`, so giving [SOTA-161](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-161.md) a second tag from the
vocabulary would trade one violation for another. Any remedy for an unbound
relation is therefore *either* a new vocabulary word *or* a secondary tag
outside the vocabulary — never a second topic. That constraint is what makes
the check's own framing land: it says the vocabulary is short a word, and
the schema will not let you pretend otherwise.

**The reading list had five unbound lines, and they are a worklist, not
noise.** Every LIT note carries exactly one topic and none carries a
secondary, so a lineage crossing a fault line in the twelve topics is
unbound by construction. The five:

- **Positional encoding.** RoFormer and ALiBi under `model-architecture`;
  the six papers extending them — position interpolation, YaRN, length
  generalization, RoPE-to-NoPE, SWAN-GPT, "Round and Round We Go" — under
  `attention-techniques`. This is the same fault line the practice
  vocabulary already answered with `representation-and-encoding`, found by
  hand in [ADR-021](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-021.md) before the check existed. The check found it again, from
  the other scheme, unprompted. That agreement is the reason to trust the
  rest of this list.
- **Linear attention and state space.** Mamba, Mamba-2, Mamba-3 under
  `model-architecture`; Kimi Linear, Gated DeltaNet, parallel DeltaNet under
  `attention-techniques`. Whether a selective SSM is an architecture or an
  attention technique is a real question the vocabulary declines to answer.
- **Mixture of experts.** GShard under `distributed-optimization`; Sparsely-
  Gated MoE, Switch, DeepSeekMoE under `model-architecture`. GShard is
  genuinely both, and the topic it holds is the half its neighbours do not.
- **Activations.** GLU variants and gated convnets under
  `model-architecture`; PowLU under `model-stability`.
- **Fine-tuning objectives.** DeepSeekMath under `adaptation-and-tuning`;
  evolution strategies for LLM fine-tuning under `training-optimization`.

Left as findings. The remedy for each is a vocabulary judgement, and [#85](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/85) is
already the reading that would make it — pre-empting it here would be
retagging twenty-three inherited notes on the strength of a report skimmed
in one sitting.

<a id="20260909083223"></a>

## Verifying every arXiv id's author against the API found five wrong names

*2026-09-09 08:32:23 · provenance · tooling*

`LIT-052` was found by hand: five practices had no bodies, writing them
meant reading the paper, and the paper turned out to be about something
else entirely. That is an expensive way to find a defect, so the obvious
next question was whether the same class could be found mechanically
across all 223 notes.

Partly, yes. The check that works is **`first_author` against the arXiv
API's author list**, and it found five wrong names in 210 resolvable ids.

## What the sweep can and cannot catch

`arxiv:` ids all resolve, and every declared `title:` matches the title
at its id — 0 findings on both. That is the reassuring half and also the
trap: `LIT-052` passed both of those checks. Its title, id, author and
year were all correct and mutually consistent. Only the *content* was
another paper's, and no API call can see that.

So the sweep is worth keeping, and it does not close the `LIT-052` class.
The bullets under a note are checkable only by reading, which is what the
`#107` body backlog turned out to be doing as a side effect.

## The five

| note | declared | actual | how it went wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LIT-030` | `Noam` | Shazeer | given name in a surname field |
| `LIT-086` | `Nerfstudio` | Fridovich-Keil | a software project, not a person |
| `LIT-087` | `Liu` | Xie | a name belonging to nobody on the paper |
| `LIT-107` | `Ranftl` | Birkl | right series, wrong paper's first author |
| `LIT-115` | `Bhardwaj` | Fu | a name belonging to nobody on the paper |

`LIT-107` is the instructive one. Ranftl leads the original MiDaS papers;
`arXiv:2307.14460` is MiDaS v3.1, whose first author is Birkl. A series
where the first author changes between versions defeats the check a human
does, which is "does this name sound right for this work" — it does.

`LIT-115` is the one that cost something. Its wrong name was rendered
into the prose of `SOTA-110`, `SOTA-111` and `SOTA-112`, so "Bhardwaj et
al." appeared six times across the record for a paper with no Bhardwaj
on it.

## The trap in writing the sweep

The arXiv API **does not return entries in `id_list` order**. Pairing
requests to responses positionally produced 166 "id mismatches" and,
because the id check `continue`d past the author and title checks, *zero*
author findings — a result that looks like a catastrophe and a clean bill
of health at the same time. Key results by the `<id>` in the response.

The tell was the shape, not any single row: 166 of 172 wrong is not a
corpus with a problem, it is a script with one. A defect rate near 100%
should always be read as a bug in the detector first. The same mistake in
the other direction had already happened this session, where a body
detector that accepted `## Known implementations` reported zero remaining
work while seven practices were empty.

## What CI caught that I did not

The version bumps that came with these corrections were written by a
script that inserted each new `history:` entry at the *top* of the list.
`luria lint` requires history to **end** at the document's current
version, so four practices failed with "`history:` ends at version 2 but
the document says 3".

That is the guard working. What is worth recording is why it reached CI
at all: I had been reading `luria lint` through `head -8`, and the
violations print *after* the warnings and the pending-decisions line. The
warning count looked unchanged, so the run looked clean.

`luria lint` is warn-first and its hard violations come last. Read the
tail, or read all of it — a truncated lint is not a lint.

## Also checked, no action

Three arXiv ids are each held by two notes: `2302.06675` (`LIT-090`,
`LIT-105`), `2002.04745` (`LIT-029`, `LIT-114`), `1608.03983` (`LIT-006`,
`LIT-042`). All three pairs were already triaged — one of each is
`Rejected` or `Superseded`, and only `LIT-114` is cited. Duplicate ids
are worth a periodic look but are not currently a defect.

Seven notes declare a corporate author (`Kimi Team`, `Olmo Team`,
`Falcon-LLM Team`) that the API returns with the words in the other order
(`Team Kimi`). These are false positives of the surname check, not
findings, and the sweep should special-case them rather than have someone
re-triage them next time.

## Re-running it

    python -m src.scripts.audit.verify_arxiv

The script is committed rather than described, because a sweep worth
running twice is worth not rewriting. It carries the two things that were
expensive to learn — batch the `id_list` at 40 with the API's own
three-second pause, and key results by the returned id — and it
special-cases corporate authors so the seven false positives do not come
back.

Fired once against three deliberately re-introduced defects before being
trusted: `LIT-115`'s wrong author, `LIT-107`'s wrong author, and a title
swapped onto `LIT-096`. All three caught, both check types firing. On the
corrected record it reports zero findings and the three known duplicate
ids.

<a id="20260909164644"></a>

## A version bump is two edits and I got the order wrong three times

*2026-09-09 16:46:44 · tooling · workflow*

Correcting a document in this record means two edits: increment `version:`,
and append an entry to `history:`. I did that by hand about thirty times
working [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114), and three of them were wrong in exactly the same way.

## The failure

The natural edit is to find the `version:` line and replace it with the new
version *plus* a fresh `history:` block. That reads correctly and is wrong
whenever the document already has a history, because the new block lands
**above** the old one. Two outcomes, both caught by `luria lint`:

- a second `history:` key, and YAML keeps the last one — so the new entry
  silently disappears;
- or, where the insert merged, entries in descending order, which trips
  ``history: ends at version N but the document says N+1``.

It happened on `SOTA-034`/`110`/`111`/`112` (as one batch), on `SOTA-086`,
and again on `SOTA-111`/`112`. The first time CI caught it, because I had
been reading `luria lint` through `head -8` and its hard violations print
last. The second and third times I caught it locally, which is better and is
not the same as fixing it.

## The fix is not "be careful"

luria's own working agreement says a guard that keeps catching you is a bug
report about the workflow — one catch is the net working, the same catch
twice means the hazard is upstream. Three times is not a discipline problem.

`src/scripts/audit/bump_version.py`:

    python -m src.scripts.audit.bump_version record/practices.d/[SOTA-042](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-042.md).md \
        --note "What changed and why."

It finds the existing `history:` block and **appends** to it, starts one under
`version:` when there is none, and refuses rather than guessing if it finds
more than one `history:` key. Fired once on both paths before being trusted —
a document with four history entries (appended as the fifth, order preserved)
and one with none (block created, single key).

## The part worth generalising

The bug was invisible in the diff. Adding a correctly-formatted YAML block in
the wrong *place* looks exactly like adding it in the right place unless you
read the surrounding lines, and I was writing these edits with `str.replace`
on a version line whose neighbours I could not see.

Any edit that inserts structure near other structure of the same shape wants
a tool that knows about the structure. That is the whole lesson, and the
`_history_span` regex in the script is the only interesting line in it.

<a id="20260909212842"></a>

## The #114 worklist was the whole at-risk set, and the census that proves it

*2026-09-09 21:28:42 · curation · method*

Before starting on the pending-decisions backlog I wanted to know whether
[#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114) had actually finished the job or only finished its worklist. [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114) read 23
`LIT` notes and found eight of them materially wrong. If the population it
sampled from was much larger, that defect rate is a standing liability rather
than a closed issue.

So: count. The signature [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114) identified is a `## Key takeaways` section whose
bullets are all short noun phrases with no numbers, no code and no
paper-specific terms — the shape a generated summary takes when nobody read
the paper. Across 224 `LIT` documents, **52 still have that signature and no
reading**.

That number looks alarming until you ask the question that matters, which is
not "how many notes are unread" but **"how many recommendations rest on an
unread note"**. Cross-referencing every `source:` edge in the practice
registry: of those 52, **none** is named as the source of any in-force
practice. Zero.

A zero is exactly the shape of result that has burned me in this repository
before — the arXiv audit's 166 false id mismatches were a zero in disguise —
so I ran it again from the other end: start at every `Active`, `Proposed` or
`Deferred` practice, follow its `source:` edges, and ask whether the paper is
unread and generic. Also zero, out of 150 source edges across 78 cited
papers. Two independent traversals agreeing is worth more than one clean
number.

**The conclusion is that [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114)'s worklist was the complete at-risk set, and
not by luck** — it was built by asking which notes source practices, which is
the same question. What remains is 52 papers in the corpus whose summaries
are decorative: nothing cites them, so nothing is wrong because of them.
Reading them would improve the browsing experience and would not correct a
single recommendation.

Worth writing down because the obvious next move after [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114) is "read the
other 52", and the measurement says that is a low-value use of a session.
The high-value population is the one the lint already names every run: the
pending decisions.

The census scripts were throwaway and deliberately so — the finding is a
snapshot, and it will stop being true the moment someone sources a practice
to one of the 52. If that becomes a recurring question it belongs in
`src/scripts/audit/` as a real check, not re-derived by hand.

## The other trap, for whoever promotes a practice next

Promoting `SOTA-120` from `Deferred` to `Active` broke **eight**
`inactive-ok` directives across five files — every place that had cited it
while acknowledging it was not in force. The lint caught all eight and named
them, which is the net working.

But the directives were the easy half. Each one sat above prose that *also*
asserted the status in words — "`SOTA-120` is `Deferred`, which the reading
does not settle" — and no linter can see that. Deleting the directive and
leaving the sentence would have produced a record that passes clean while
saying something false, which is worse than the finding.

So: **when a status changes, grep for the code, not just for the directive.**
The directive tells you which files to open. The prose next to it is what you
actually have to fix.

<a id="20260909231629"></a>

## I measured that reading the 50 was low value, and I was wrong about what would come out of it

*2026-09-09 23:16:29 · curation · method*

Earlier today I ran a census on the generic-bullet `LIT` corpus, verified from
both directions that **none of the 52 sourced an in-force practice**, and
recommended skipping them: reading them "would correct no recommendation".

dmarx said read them. The measurement was correct and the recommendation drawn
from it was wrong, and the gap between those two is the thing worth writing
down.

## What the measurement missed

I measured the right quantity — *does a wrong note make a wrong
recommendation?* — and treated it as the only quantity. It is not. A note also:

- **states things that are false**, which is a defect whether or not anything
  cites it. Nine documents asserted something their paper does not contain, and
  six of those stated its inverse. `LIT-111` said "category-level pose
  estimation" about a paper whose contribution is needing **no** category-level
  training. `LIT-108` said "dynamic scene optimization" about a static-scene
  paper. `LIT-038`'s bullets were about a different paper entirely.
- **is a place where connections between practices become visible.** Reading
  `LIT-067` produced the antecedent of `SOTA-188`; reading `LIT-017` beside
  `LIT-065` produced the reason 3D parallelism exists; reading `LIT-036`
  produced the measurement behind `SOTA-187`'s premise. None of those is a
  correction. All of them are things the record did not contain and now does.

The census answered "is anything broken?" and the answer was no. It could not
answer "is anything missing?", and I read the first answer as though it settled
both.

## The generalisable version

**A measurement of harm is not a measurement of value.** I checked that these
documents were not causing errors, concluded they were inert, and skipped the
question of what reading them would *produce*. The second question has no cheap
proxy — you find out by doing the work — which is exactly why it is easy to let
the first stand in for it.

Where this bites: any time a cheap check comes back clean and the expensive work
is then declined on the strength of it. The clean check is evidence about one
failure mode.

## What I would keep from the census anyway

The census was not wasted and the finding in it is still true: `#114`'s worklist
was the complete at-risk set, and no recommendation in this record rested on an
unread note. That is worth knowing and it is worth having verified from both
directions. What it did not license was the conclusion I drew from it.

## Practical notes for the next pass

- **`ar5iv` renders 48 of 49 arXiv papers here.** One (`arXiv:1908.08681`) has
  no rendering and became `Skimmed`, the same route EDM took. The fetch script
  and text extractor are in the session scratchpad and were disposable by
  design; if this recurs they belong in `src/scripts/`.
- **`Skimmed` earned a second meaning this pass.** It had been "the full text
  was unavailable". `LIT-026` is `Skimmed` because reading 66,000 words of
  federated-learning open problems, to correct four bullets on a document
  nothing cites, is not a good use of a session. That is a judgement about
  **proportion**, and the status carries it fine.
- **`luria link --fix` moves lines, so place `inactive-ok` directives after
  running it, not before.** I placed several against pre-fix line numbers and
  the lint correctly reported them as applying to nothing. The directive covers
  its own line and the one below; anchor it to the paragraph's first line.
- **Body headings must match `title:` exactly.** I shortened five and the lint
  caught all five. Scaffold with the full title and leave the heading alone.

## Auditing the notes that source nothing: the silence was the finding, not the count

*2026-09-10 06:51:32 · curation*

**Audit of the `LIT` documents no practice sources ([#121](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/121)).** 70 of 224 at the
start. The useful number turned out not to be 70.

## The criterion already existed

The audit needed a test for whether a note *should* be a source, and `ADR-017`
had already written one for a different purpose: **if this paper were retracted
tomorrow, would the practice need rewriting?** That decision was filed to settle
whether adopters belong in `source:`. It answers this question too, and using it
meant the audit did not invent a private rule in a commit message — which is the
specific failure `ADR-017` records having cost thirteen practices.

## What 70 decomposed into

- **12 retired or tombstoned.** Four are deduplication tombstones with the
  survivor named in `superseded_by` — `LIT-006`/`LIT-042` (SGDR),
  `LIT-029`/`LIT-114` (Pre-LN), `LIT-105`/`LIT-090` (Lion). For these the status
  *is* the reason and nothing needed writing.
- **10 cited in a practice's body but not in its `source:`.** This looked like
  the richest vein and was almost entirely a false alarm: adoption evidence and
  lineage, which `ADR-017` explicitly routes to `consensus_note` instead. The
  discipline was being followed. **One** was a real miss — see below.
- **~25 already stating why they were unsourced**, several of them well. The
  model was `LIT-110`: "Nothing in the record cites this note", followed by the
  reason.
- **24 with a Standing section that said nothing about linkage at all.** This
  was the working set, and it is where the finding is.

## The finding

A note that sources no practice is not a defect. A note that sources no
practice *and does not say why* is, and for the reason `DP-008` gives: nobody
re-reads a vocabulary, or an absence. The silence is indistinguishable from
nobody having got round to it, so every future audit pays the full cost of
finding out again.

That is what made this issue worth doing at the size it was done. Counting
unsourced notes measures nothing; **asking each one to state its own standing
is what converts a backlog into a record.**

## Two gaps the silence was hiding

**Diffusion sampling.** The record held four diffusion practices — `SOTA-187`,
`SOTA-188`, `SOTA-195`, `SOTA-202` — every one about training or
parametrization, and three unsourced papers — DDIM, DPM-Solver, Consistency
Models — every one about sampling. The record said how to train a diffusion
model and nothing about how to sample from one, while holding the three papers
that decided how everyone samples. Four practices filed.

**A convergence three readings had already noticed.** `vision-and-graphics`
held thirteen notes and zero practices. Under `ADR-026`'s filing rule an empty
domain topic is not by itself a gap — a claim merely discovered in a domain
takes its kind. But `NOTE-037` calls K-Planes "the third explicit-structure
replacement for a large coordinate network", `NOTE-042` names the same pairing
from the other side, and `NOTE-046` records NeuS2 inheriting the line. Four
papers, three mechanically unrelated structures, one conclusion, inside
eighteen months. **The convergence was stated three times in the reading list
and was invisible in the registry.** One practice, four sources.

Both had the same shape: the readings had done the work and the registry had
not been told.

## Why they were unfiled, and it is not what it looks like

Every one of those seven papers was read in the pass that deliberately filed
nothing, and all three sampling readings end with the same sentence — *"Nothing
is sourced to this paper and this reading files no practice."* That is a
**pass policy**, and a year later it reads as a judgement about the paper.

Worth stating as a rule: **a deliberate deferral must say it is one.** "Nothing
is filed" and "nothing should be filed" are different claims and were written
the same way.

## The one real link fix

`SOTA-051` had been arguing from `LIT-089`'s zero convolutions for its sharpest
content — *zero is not "near zero"* — without naming it in `source:`. Under the
retraction test that section does not survive the paper's removal. The link
existed in prose and not in data, which is the inverse of the failure the last
three contributions kept hitting, and equally invisible to the lint.

## What the audit found and did not fix

`LIT-004` — the gradient checkpointing paper — is a **generic-bullet note that
the bullet-signature pass missed**, because that pass selected on a signature
and a document can be equally empty without matching it. It sits on a gap: the
record recommends recomputation only for attention (`SOTA-087`) and has no
general activation-memory practice among its twenty-nine
`distributed-optimization` entries. Nothing was filed from it. Filing a practice
from four bullets naming the category is the failure two passes have been spent
correcting, and the fix is a reading, not a guess.

Seven notes are unsourced because **nobody has read them** — three of them a
coherent joint-embedding cluster. That is a different finding from a paper read
and declined, and the determinations say so rather than implying an assessment
that never happened.

## Afterwards

Every unsourced note now either states its standing or is retired, where the
status is the reason. 62 remain unsourced, down from 70, and the number is no
longer the interesting thing about them.

## A derived field stored by hand: eight practices dated by a source they no longer cite

*2026-09-10 07:54:42 · curation*

**Making `published:` true on every scheme ([#119](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/119)).** The issue asked for a field on
three schemes. The field was the small half, and the answer arrived from
upstream before the work landed.

## The convention was discovered, not chosen

183 practices already carried `published:` and nothing said what it meant. A
practice can have several sources spanning years — `SOTA-205` has four across
nineteen months — so "the publication date" is genuinely ambiguous and I could
have picked earliest, latest, or the practice's own filing date.

Measuring first was the right call: **175 of the 183 used the *primary*
source's date**, the first entry in `source:`. That is not a coincidence of
single-source practices; it holds for the multi-source ones too, and it is the
principled answer, because `ADR-010` makes the list ordered and `ADR-017` makes
the first entry the one that would force a rewrite if it were retracted.

The convention was already in the record. It had just never been written down,
which is the same shape as `#121`'s finding that `ADR-017` already contained
the criterion that audit needed.

## The eight that disagreed were all one accident

Not eight judgements — **eight leftovers.** In every case the `source:` list
was corrected and `published:` stayed behind, still holding the date of the
paper that used to be first.

The clearest is `SOTA-048`. Its date came from `LIT-051`, and `LIT-051` **is
not in its `source:` list**: the source comment says "Re-sourced: Tensor Fusion
is Horovod's… `LIT-051` assumed both." The paper was removed and its date was
not.

Two of the eight (`SOTA-025`, `SOTA-026`) were left by `#114`, and one
(`SOTA-122`) by `#58` — **passes whose entire purpose was correcting
`source:`.** A pass that fixes a field does not think about the fields derived
from it, and nothing made it think.

## Why nothing caught it

`published:` is ground truth in one place: a `LIT` note, where it is the paper's
date and feeds the alias template. Everywhere else it is a **copy**.

- `luria concretize` rewrites *references*, not *values*.
- `luria lint` has no rule relating one document's field to another document's.

So a copy can disagree with its original indefinitely and every mechanical
check stays green. This is the sixth stale-derived-data finding this week, and
the first where the staleness was in a **value** rather than in prose or a
code. The others were legible to a human reading the file; this one was not
legible to anyone, because being wrong looks exactly like being right.

legible to anyone, because being wrong looks exactly like being right.

## The fix was a checker, for about three hours

The tempting fix is to stop storing it and let the field derive from the
reference. **luria could not do that.** `derive` read a document's own fields;
there was no way to say *take this from the document you point at*.

So the first answer was to store it and check it — a `check_published.py`
reporting every stored date that disagreed with its original, wired into CI and
fired once on a real regression before being trusted. It worked. It was also a
per-project reimplementation of something the schema should be able to state,
and that argument was strong enough to take upstream **with a measured failure
behind it rather than a hypothetical**.

luria 0.15.0 gives `derive` a `from`, naming the reference to render the
template against. The checker was superseded before it ever merged. What
shipped instead is three lines per scheme:

    [luria.schemes.SOTA.fields.published]
    derive = "{published}"
    from   = "source[0]"

**281 hand-maintained values became zero**, and the eight above are not
corrected — they are **unrepresentable**, because no second copy remains to
hold a different answer.

The checker was not wasted, and it is worth being precise about why. It
established the convention, proved the eight defects real, and gave the
upstream issue its evidence. What it could not do is be *found*: a rule living
in a script scaffolds nothing, appears on no record page, and is reinvented by
the next project — the argument `#216` made for `derive` existing at all,
arriving again from the other end.

## The rules this leaves

**When you correct a field, ask what was copied from it.** Three re-sourcing
passes changed `source:` and none asked. The general form of a lesson this
record keeps relearning from the other direction — when a status changes, grep
for the code — except here the stale thing was not text a reader could catch.

**A check you had to write yourself is a question for the tool.** The gap
between "I can enforce this" and "the schema can state this" is the gap between
a script and a contract.

## The sliding window had seven downstream notes and no origin

*2026-09-13 18:02:40 · gap · literature*

**The query was one paper, and the finding was the shape of its absence.**
Asked whether the record held `ARXIV-1904.10509`. It did not — no `arxiv:`
match, no `first_author: 'Child'`, no mention of the title anywhere in
`record/` or `docs/`. What made it worth a journal entry is what *was* there.

Seven reading notes stand downstream of a sliding window: `LIT-033`
(Longformer), `LIT-191` (attention sinks), `LIT-204` (Griffin), `LIT-176`
(native hybrid attention), `LIT-208` and `LIT-209` (NoPE global layers
interleaved with windowed local ones), `LIT-143` (natively trainable sparse
attention). Five practices use the term and two of them — `SOTA-153` and
`SOTA-176` — recommend designs whose local half is one. In none of the
seventeen documents that say "sliding window" is the window itself a claim;
it is a term the reader is assumed to already have.

This is `DP-007` exactly — *what everyone agrees on has no author, so nothing
prompts anyone to write it down* — and worth noting that the record found it
the way that principle says it will not be found. Nobody reading the
corpus noticed. It took someone arriving with a specific arXiv id.

## The query that would have found it, and the one that would not

Grepping `record/` for "sliding window" returns seventeen documents and
looks like healthy coverage. That query cannot answer the question, because the
documents it returns are exactly the ones that use the term without defining
it — the density of mentions is the *symptom*, not evidence against.

The query that works runs backwards from the term to its first use: for a
mechanism `n` documents assume, is there a document that introduces it? That
is mechanical, it is cheap, and nothing in the record currently runs it.
`SOTA-132`'s "describing a line from its middle" (`2026-09-08`) was the same
defect at the practice layer, found the same way — by someone following a
citation backwards rather than by reading forwards.

## What was not done, and what changed about that

The first pass filed the note and stopped, on the reasoning that the paper's
recommendations were either superseded or already in the record from later
sources. **Both halves of that were wrong, and wrong in the same direction.**

*Superseded is not a reason not to file.* `DP-003` is explicit — "do this,
and here is the thing everybody did until 2021 and why it stopped being
right" is the content, and it only exists if the abandoned position is
written down. The factorization is now `SOTA-208`, `Superseded` by
`SOTA-138`. Filing it cost a page and bought the strongest argument the
corpus has for its own successor: the enwik8 comparison, where a hand-chosen
escape lost to dense attention outright.

*"Already in the record from later sources" is a description of a defect.* If
a practice is sourced to a paper that did not introduce it, the attribution
is wrong — "we have it already" is the sentence that keeps it wrong. `SOTA-087`
was dating a 2019 recommendation to 2022 and `SOTA-060` was naming the
`1/sqrt(2N)` factor in prose with no citation at all.

## The field that did not exist

Fixing those two by reordering `source:` breaks them. `published:` derives
from `source[0]`, so `SOTA-087` would have become a 2019 practice whose body
argues a 2022 mechanism; and `ADR-017`'s retraction test — the primary source
is the one whose removal forces a rewrite — genuinely selects Dao, because
the body is Dao's argument. The two facts are both true and the field could
only hold one.

`ADR-029` adds `introduced_by:`. It is `DP-005`'s cut made a second time:
that principle sent **adoption** out of `source:` and into `consensus:`, and
this sends **origin** out of `source:` into its own field, leaving `source:`
to mean evidence and nothing else.

Filed `Proposed`, and the condition matters. Three cases found by one person
filing one paper in one afternoon argues that the field is needed; it does not
say how much it carries. The promotion test is the backwards query `DP-004`
asks for — over practices whose primary source postdates the technique they
describe — and the record has no view that surfaces those yet.

## What is still not done

No reading note. The paper was read against its method and experiment
sections, not cover to cover; `ADR-025` makes absence the record's word for
unread, and that is the honest value.

The pre-activation residual block is *not* repointed at this paper, and that
is deliberate. Child et al. adopts it from He et al. (2016) and says so;
`SOTA-032` is sourced to Xiong et al., the paper that **argues** it, which is
`DP-005` working correctly. Using a technique is not introducing it — the same
distinction `introduced_by:` exists to hold, applied in the direction that
says no.

<a id="20260913202008"></a>

## source: is holding at least three relations, and fourteen practices rest on adoption alone

*2026-09-13 20:20:08 · audit · record · method*

Review on `#129` asked whether `source:` is being abused, and guessed it holds
both *the paper that introduced the practice* and *a paper that uses it*.

**It holds at least three relations, and the guess is right about all of them.**

## The query

Classify every `LIT` note whose title reads as a model or system report — a
technical report, a named model family, an "open bilingual pre-trained model"
— then find the practices citing one in `source:`.

    LIT notes that read as model/system reports:        22 of 225
    Practices whose `source:` includes at least one:    26 of 208
      ... of which ALL sources are reports:             14
      ... that also carry `consensus:`:                 12
      ... that also carry `implementations:`:            7

Spot-checked, and the heuristic is not inventing anything: `SOTA-069` rests on
GLM-130B, `SOTA-094` on PaLM, `SOTA-139` on DeepSeek-V4. **Fourteen practices
whose only cited support is that somebody shipped it.**

`DP-005` says exactly what is wrong with that — *adoption is not evidence* — and
says it about this record, which had already fixed one instance. The principle
was filed and the corpus was never swept.

## The three relations

- **evidence about the claim** — the ablation, the controlled comparison. What
  the field is documented as meaning.
- **origin** — the work that first said to do this. `ADR-029` split this
  one out as `introduced_by:` while filing Child et al.
- **adoption** — this system does it. `consensus:` exists for this and 12 of
  the 26 have both, so the practice is citing its adopters twice and its
  evidence never.

## Why nothing caught it

The definition of `source:` lives in a **TOML comment**. A comment cannot
render in a view, cannot appear in the generated configuration reference,
cannot be quoted by the lint, and is never seen by anyone filing a document.
So every one of the fourteen passes every mechanical check there is, and the
only thing that found them was somebody deciding to ask.

That is `DP-004` in its purest form — *a pass finds only the defects its query
is shaped like* — and worth noting that this query did not come from reading
the record either. It came from a reviewer's suspicion about a field.

Filed upstream as `LU-#254`: relations declared with a description that is
data, the way vocabularies already are. It cannot make the distinction
checkable — no schema tells an ablation from a model report — but it moves the
definition somewhere a reader and a scaffold can reach.

## Not done here, deliberately

**The fourteen are not repointed.** Fixing one means deciding, per practice,
whether a controlled result exists at all — and where none does, the honest
outcome may be `Deferred` with a `promote_when:`, not a better citation. That
is a reading pass over fourteen practices, not a find-and-replace, and doing it
badly would convert a visible defect into an invisible one.

**`source:` is not retired.** The review floated it, and the audit supports
splitting it further — but `source:` is required on 208 practices and
`published:` derives from `source[0]`. Retiring it is a migration with a
decision in front of it, and `ADR-029` is still `Proposed`: the record
should find out whether one new relation carries its weight before minting
three more.

**The counts are a heuristic, not a census.** Title-matching finds model
reports that announce themselves. A systems paper that is really an adoption
report — and the reverse, a model report carrying a genuine ablation — is
invisible to it in both directions. The number is a floor.

## Two notes that said, in their own words, that they had nowhere to go

*2026-09-15 07:09:36 · record*

**The `THEORY` scheme came out of a survey that was looking for something
else.** The question on the table was whether the practice registry
accommodates knowledge that is strictly theoretical, or whether that needs a
scheme of its own. The way to answer it was to look at what the record was
already doing with such knowledge, and the answer turned out to be written
down in two places, by earlier contributions, in plain language.

The first pass was a regex over practice titles for verb phrases that
describe rather than instruct. It returned seventeen, which was too many:
"Employ mixed precision to reduce memory usage" matched on *reduce* and is an
instruction by any reading. Reading the seventeen by hand left eight that
genuinely state a behaviour — `SOTA-010`, `SOTA-012`, `SOTA-037`, `SOTA-038`,
`SOTA-040`, `SOTA-064`, `SOTA-092`, `SOTA-097`. The wrong theory worth
recording is that the regex count was ever the evidence. Eight of 208 is not
a large number, and on its own it would have argued for leaving things alone.

The evidence that mattered came from the other side. Scanning for `LIT`
notes that no practice cites returns 48 of 225 — and in
`analysis-and-evaluation`, which is the topic whose blurb explicitly says
"theory, interpretability and debugging belong here too", it is 6 of 12.
Half the topic is papers the registry cannot reach.

Then two of those notes turned out to have anticipated the whole question.
`LIT-019` and `LIT-039` each carry a section headed **"Carries no practice,
deliberately"**, and `LIT-019`'s says exactly what the problem is: the
lottery-ticket procedure "costs a full dense training run before it produces
anything, so as an instruction it reads *train the model, then train a
smaller one* — which is a finding about neural networks rather than advice
about how to train one." Someone had already worked out that the document
was not a practice, had had nowhere else to file it, and had written the
reasoning into the note as a defence of an anomaly.

`LIT-223` is the third instance and the sharpest. It was filed to correct a
conflation, it says in its own body that "the practices that turn on the
*mechanism* — why BN permits what it permits — belong here", and nothing in
the record cites it. Nothing could. What that paper establishes is that batch
normalization does not work for the reason its title gives, and there is no
instruction in that: nobody's behaviour changes. Three statuses are needed to
say it — the practice `Active`, the paper `Active`, the explanation
`Rejected` — and there were two schemes to put them in.

That is the finding: the record was not silent about theory, it was
**annotating the workaround**. The notes that had nowhere to go said so, at
length, in prose that a scheme would have made unnecessary.

The scheme was built around the batch-normalization pair rather than around
the eight practices, and deliberately so. Re-filing an existing practice
leaves a `SOTA` code that is neither `Rejected` nor `Superseded` but simply
moved, and this record's rule is to retire by changing status and never by
deleting — a rule that has nothing to say about a document that was filed in
the wrong drawer. That needs its own decision, and bundling it into the one
that creates the drawer would have hidden the question.

One thing checked and worth not re-checking: `luria` does support a crossing
converse, so `THEORY.explains` → `SOTA.explained_by` is a declared pair and
`luria link --fix` writes both ends. `luria.yaml` claimed otherwise in a
comment on `contested_by:`, which had been true when it was written and
stopped being true at `LU-ADR-097`. The field still has no converse; the
comment now says that is a choice about what a reading note should hold,
rather than a limit.

## The second gradient-free post-training paper, and the first account of why the paradigm works

*2026-09-15 17:40:22 · record*

**One paper arrived and three documents came out of it, which is worth
explaining rather than assuming.** Gan and Isola's *Neural Thickets* is two
things bound together: a measurement of the multi-task loss landscape around
a pretrained checkpoint, and a post-training method built to demonstrate it.
The paper is explicit about the ordering — "our goal is not to promote
RandOpt as superior to alternative methods. Rather, we use it as a probe" —
and the record has had exactly the vocabulary for that distinction since
`ADR-031`. The measurement is a claim about what is true, so it is
`THEORY-006`. The method is a claim about what to do, so it is
`SOTA-212`. Filing them as one document would have meant asserting the
method at whatever confidence the measurement earned, or the reverse.

**The most useful thing the paper did for this record it did as a
bystander.** `SOTA-154` — fine-tune with evolution strategies instead of
policy-gradient RL — has rested since September on `LIT-211` alone, whose
`promote_when` asks for an independent group running ES against a
policy-gradient baseline. This paper runs ES as *its own baseline*, on
different models and a different task suite, and finds it strong enough to
beat the paper's own method in about half the table.

That is not the replication the condition asks for and the status is
unchanged, but the difference is worth being precise about, because it is the
kind of thing that gets rounded off later. A baseline result is run by people
who want it to lose. It is evidence about the method's robustness in
somebody else's hands and it is *not* a second group choosing to test the
claim, which is what `promote_when` is asking for. Both facts are now on
`SOTA-154`'s neighbours rather than in anyone's memory.

**A trap that nearly got written into the practice.** The paper's headline
figure compares RandOpt with a 50-way ensemble against PPO and GRPO answering
with a single sample. It says so — "this setting disadvantages the baseline
but reflects current standard usage" — and it runs the matched arm in §5.4
and Table 4, where ES plus the same 50-way vote takes the best or runner-up
cell about half the time and beats RandOpt outright on GSM8K, MATH-500 and
OlyBench at several scales. A first pass at `SOTA-212` had it beating
`SOTA-154`. **It does not.** What it has over `SOTA-154` is one training step
instead of 167 and no inter-worker communication, and that is what the
practice now claims.

The general form of that trap — an ensembled method compared against a
one-sample baseline is a comparison about ensembling — is filed in
`NOTE-078` as candidate recommendation R2 and **deliberately not as a
practice**. The paper demonstrates it and does not recommend it, and the
distance between those is where a record starts attributing its own opinions
to its sources. Whoever files the practice that does recommend it will find
this paper's table waiting as evidence.

**One tagging decision, made against the reflex.** `LIT-233` wants to be
`adaptation-and-tuning`, because post-training is what a reader would look
for it under, and the first draft gave it both that and
`analysis-and-evaluation`. The `primary_topic` group rejected it, correctly:
`ADR-026`'s rule is that a claim merely *discovered* in a domain still takes
its kind, and the paper's kind is a measurement. The practice drawn from it
carries `adaptation-and-tuning`, which is where the instruction lives and
where a practitioner browsing for one will meet it. The reflex to tag the
paper by where its readers are is how a topic stops meaning anything.

**What this pass did not look at.** The candidate list was one paper, so the
complement is everything. Two specific gaps are worth naming because they are
cheap to run and nobody will be prompted to. PPO has no `LIT` note at all,
despite being a baseline in both papers in this line and the thing `SOTA-129`
and `SOTA-145` are about — an instance of `DP-007` exactly, the trunk nobody
filed because nobody published an argument about it. And the record's
evaluation practices were checked for a test-time-budget rule and found not
to have one; they were not checked for anything else this paper bears on.

## A replication that arrived as a baseline, and a dissent measured below the threshold

*2026-09-15 18:06:38 · record*

**The first pass filed the evidence and then argued it away.** `SOTA-154` had
a promotion condition: an independent group running evolution strategies
against a policy-gradient baseline that got the same tuning budget, on a task
outside Countdown and the conciseness objective. `LIT-233` did exactly
that — six tasks, three model families, matched training FLOPs, and the RL arm
grid-searched over learning rate and batch or group size while ES ran one
fixed configuration. The curation entry filed an hour earlier looked straight
at it and wrote that "a baseline result is run by people who want it to lose…
it is *not* a second group choosing to test the claim".

That reasoning is backwards and it is worth keeping the wrong version
written down, because the error has a shape that will recur. **A baseline is
a replication run by people with an incentive to make it fail.** The
condition's own "what would not move this" clause names the failure mode it
feared — "a comparison in which the RL arm was left at defaults" — and this
comparison is the opposite of that: the RL arm was tuned *harder* than the ES
arm. Everything the condition asked for was present, and the pass invented a
category ("baseline, not replication") that the condition never contained, to
avoid acting on it.

The general form: **a promotion condition is a promise, and re-reading it
strictly enough to avoid keeping it is how a provisional status becomes
permanent.** [DP-006](../design-principles.md#dp-6) says a provisional status with no condition attached is a
refusal wearing a document's clothes; this is the next failure along, where
the condition exists and the bar quietly rises to stay above the evidence.

**Then the opposite problem arrived in the same session.** Following the line
forward turned up Hyper-ES (`LIT-231`), which says in its own second
sentence that "directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly
ineffective". Having just promoted the practice, the tempting move was to
find that dissent unpersuasive. Two facts are worth separating, and the
practice now separates them:

- **Hyper-ES never runs the method it says does not work.** Its ES baseline is
  CMA-ES over LoRA. The case against direct ES is two lemmas about
  near-orthogonal perturbations in high dimensions, plus a figure, plus a
  citation. That is a real argument and it is not a failed reproduction.
- **Every model it tests is at 1.5B or below**, while its abstract says
  "billion-parameter LLMs".

The second is what makes this interesting rather than merely awkward.
`THEORY-006`, filed the same day from a different paper, holds that the
density of task-improving perturbations rises with model scale, with gains
appearing sharply from about 1.5B and absent beneath it. **Hyper-ES's negative
result sits exactly where that account predicts a negative result**, and its
lemma is the needle-in-a-haystack regime under another name. The two papers
were posted five months apart and neither cites the other.

That reconciliation is labelled, in both documents, as *this record's reading
and not either paper's*. It is the kind of claim a record like this should be
able to make and the kind it can most easily make badly: it resolves a
tension, it is unfalsified, and nobody involved would have to agree with it.
What would settle it is the experiment neither ran — full-parameter ES
against a well-tuned GRPO at 7B and above — and that is what the practice now
says.

**On `introduced_by:` and where a recommendation comes from.** `SOTA-212`
was filed with `introduced_by:` pointing at its own source, which was
tidy and wrong. The source paper says in plain words that it is not making
the recommendation. Qiu et al. are; RandOpt is their instruction with the
iteration count set to one and an ensemble on the end. This is the case
[ADR-030](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-030.md) exists for, arriving about four hours after the field became
required, and the first pass still filled it in by reflex — which is a small
piece of evidence that a required field with a sensible default answer gets
the default answer.

**What this pass did not cover, stated so nobody has to guess.** The search
for the ES line returned five papers and this pass filed two, the two named
in the request. The three left out, in case they are wanted:

- `ARXIV-2609.10980` — *EGGROLL, Unrolled*, which introduces LOO-ROLL, a
  leave-one-out estimator replacing EGGROLL's two antithetic evaluations per
  direction with one.
- `ARXIV-2608.27351` — *Understanding Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning*,
  which reports ES ahead on pass@k and GRPO ahead on pass@1 and proposes
  running them in sequence. This one bears directly on `SOTA-154`'s
  `contested` reading and would likely sharpen it.
- `ARXIV-2608.12679` — *Beyond the Best Guess*, on ES and solution coverage.

And the reading depth, since the record's convention is that a `LIT` with no
`NOTE` is an unread paper: EGGROLL and Hyper-ES were read through their
abstracts, introductions, related work, results and hyperparameter
appendices, and **not** through their theory sections — EGGROLL's convergence
analysis and Hyper-ES's two lemmas are taken at their stated results. Neither
carries a reading note, and neither is in any practice's `source:`, which is
the constraint that makes that acceptable.
