## Reading the ES line properly, and what the full readings moved

*2026-09-15 18:40:28 · record*

Six papers now, read end to end rather than by abstract. Four things the
readings changed that the earlier passes had wrong, missing, or filed on
trust.

**The scale evidence was understated and the independence was overstated —
in the same paper.** `LIT-234` runs evolution strategies at 14B and 32B
against OatZero and SimpleRL-Zoo, which is four times the ceiling `SOTA-154`'s
conditions section claimed. It is also Cognizant AI Lab with Qiu among the
authors, running `LIT-211`'s own method — the case that practice's promotion
condition explicitly excluded. **Both facts are load-bearing and they point
opposite ways**, and the temptation on finding either is to let it settle the
question alone. The practice now carries the 32B number *and* the sentence
"the independent evidence stops at 8B", because a reader needs both to know
what they are looking at.

That is the same error as the last pass in a new costume. Then it was refusing
evidence for a category the condition never named; here it would have been
accepting evidence the condition named and excluded, because the number was
impressive. **A condition is only worth writing if it binds in the direction
you did not want.**

**The dissent and the characterization are arguing about one measurement.**
`LIT-231` proves that random perturbations concentrate near orthogonality
to a useful direction, and that the leftover components accumulate as a random
walk — so ES cannot work at LLM scale. `LIT-230`, four months later,
measures that exact drift, agrees it is 40× GRPO's, and finds it harmless:
the gains survive zeroing every update below a single-step magnitude
threshold, so they live in a sparse coordinate subset — and in a *specific*
one, LayerNorm weights and attention projections, where GRPO's largest updates
land in token embeddings and the language-model head instead.

The gap between them is a line and a subspace. Lemma 1 bounds the angle
between a random vector and a single direction; if the useful set is a
`k`-dimensional subspace, the projection behaves differently and the argument
weakens by an amount nobody has computed. That is written into both readings
as an open question. **It is not written in as a refutation, because working
out which of two papers is right from a third document is how a record starts
believing its own summaries.**

There is a second, sharper tension neither paper notices: Hyper-ES's lemmas
are dimension-asymptotic, so read naively they predict ES gets *worse* with
scale, while every empirical paper in the line reports the opposite and
`THEORY-006` says why it should. Something in that argument does not
track the observation. Saying so is the useful contribution here; saying which
is not available yet.

**A prediction was confirmed and the promotion condition still was not met.**
`THEORY-006` asked for the density measurement repeated by an unconnected
group on a family other than Qwen2.5, or a mechanism predicting where the
transition sits. `LIT-230` cites the account by name, reasons that denser
solutions should mean fewer directions suffice, and measures exactly that at
0.5B, 1.5B and 3B. That is an independent group confirming a *consequence* —
arguably better evidence than a repeat, and **not the evidence the condition
asked for**: different measurement, same family, no prediction of the
threshold. The document now states all of that and stays `Proposed`.

Writing this down is the point. A condition met is a promotion; a condition
approached from an unexpected angle is a judgement call, and the judgement
call is where the bar moves without anyone deciding to move it.

**Two practices came out of readings rather than out of the papers' headlines.**
`SOTA-210` exists because two groups, independently, measured the same
thing the post-training literature does not report — that RLVR raises pass@1
and lowers pass@k, often below the base model. `SOTA-211` exists because
two groups reached one instruction from unrelated arguments: an empirical
variance diagnostic showing the antithetic second evaluation buys nothing when
responses are regenerated, and a derivation showing a leave-one-out baseline
preserves the expected field at half the cost. Neither paper's abstract leads
with the thing that became the practice.

**What this pass did not cover.** The line has at least two more members,
both cited by papers filed here and neither read: **Hoy et al. (2026)** and
**Abdi et al. (2026), *Evolutionary strategies at scale lead to catastrophic
forgetting***. The second is the paper `LIT-230`'s entire RQ2 is a reply
to, and the record currently holds the reply without the claim — which is the
shape `DP-004` warns about, arrived at by following citations forward and
never backward. `LIT-231` also cites **Sun et al. (2026)** for a 10×
space-efficiency result, and `LIT-229` cites **Korotyshova et al. (2025)**
for SFT-then-CMA-ES over SVD bases. Four candidates, named here so the next
pass does not have to rediscover them.

On reading depth: all five notes filed today are `Read` and mean it — full
text including appendices, with two exceptions stated in the notes themselves.
`NOTE-080` takes EGGROLL's Theorem 2 at its stated result and rate
without checking the Edgeworth expansion behind it, and `NOTE-079` takes
`LIT-232`'s resolvent derivation at its stated result without verifying
the conservativity theorem's proof. Both are recorded in the `Limitations`
sections where a reader will meet them.

## Following the citations backward, and the boundary that fell out of it

*2026-09-15 19:10:53 · record*

Ten papers now. The four added here were all named in the previous pass's
"what this did not cover" section, which is the first time this record has
closed a gap it had written down rather than rediscovering one — and the
readings changed more than the previous three passes combined.

**The record had filed an answer before the question.** `LIT-230`'s second
research question is, in its entirety, a reply to Abdi et al.: does ES's large
parameter drift cause catastrophic forgetting? The record acquired that reply
two passes ago and acquired the paper it replies to today. `LIT-239`
(ESSA) is the same failure at the other end — the earliest paper in the whole
line, July 2025, filed last, after everything that came after it.

Both have one cause. Every pass so far started from a paper and followed its
citations *forward*, to what cited it or what it responded to among things
already filed. Nothing ever asked **what does this paper cite that we do not
have**, which is a different query with a different answer, and the two gaps
it left were a paper the record was already arguing with and the paper the
line begins at. [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) is about exactly this and did not prevent it, because
knowing that a query has a complement does not tell you to run the complement.
**The cheap fix, written here so the next pass inherits it: after filing a
paper, list its references that the record lacks.** It takes one grep of the
bibliography.

**The most valuable thing in this pass is a table nobody set out to build.**
Sorting all eight ES-versus-RL comparisons by model size:

- GRPO ahead, 1B and 1.5B — Abdi et al.
- Direct ES "highly ineffective", 0.5B and 1.5B — Hyper-ES
- ES ahead in most cells, 1.5B–8B — Neural Thickets
- ES highest on 4 of 4 tasks, 4B — Hoy et al.
- ES ahead on pass@k, ≤7B — Ba et al.
- ES ahead on pass@k, 7B–32B — Hayes et al.

**Every negative is at or below 1.5B. Every positive is at or above it.** Six
groups, mostly not citing each other and none testing `THEORY-006`, recovered
the threshold that account names. That is a real finding and it arrived as a
*side effect of filing*, not from reading any single paper — which is the
argument for a record like this one existing at all.

It is also the most dangerous kind of finding, and both documents say so: it
is read across papers differing in task, tuning and implementation; it is
post-hoc; and it is exactly what an account's author would want to see.
Nobody has run one protocol on both sides of the line, and until someone does
this is suggestive.

**`THEORY-006` has now come close three times and been promoted none.** A
confirmed prediction (population size falling with scale), a mechanism
(functional sparsity), and now the boundary. The condition asks for the
density measurement repeated by an unconnected group on a different family, or
a mechanism predicting where the transition sits, and none of the three is
that. Holding the line a third time is uncomfortable enough that it is worth
naming the discomfort: **either the account is genuinely unconfirmed, or the
condition is asking for an experiment nobody has reason to run while its
consequences keep turning up on their own.** The document takes the first
reading and flags the second, and deliberately does not decide — a condition
rewritten by whoever wants it met is not a condition, and that principle has
been tested twice in this line now.

**Hoy et al. retired an argument rather than winning it.** Three papers here
had measured ES's parameter drift and drawn three conclusions: it causes
forgetting, it is functionally sparse and harmless, it proves the search finds
nothing. The decomposition — an on-manifold component that changes the loss
and an off-manifold random walk that cannot, scaling as `σ²dT/N` — says all
three are describing the same object. The disagreement was never about the
measurement; it was about what each group happened to have measured alongside
it, and over what horizon.

That is the second time in this line that an apparent contradiction turned out
to be two groups measuring different things. The first was Hyper-ES's lemma
about a *direction* against Ba et al.'s sparse *subspace*. **A record that
holds both sides is what makes these visible; a summary of either one alone
would have read as settled.**

**One filing decision worth recording.** ESSA is ES over a few hundred
SFT-initialized singular values. `SOTA-154` recommends ES over the *full*
parameter space in place of policy-gradient RL. Filing ESSA as support for
that practice would have been easy and wrong, and the note says so explicitly
— same method family, different recommendation. What ESSA does instead is turn
the subspace approach into a line: it and Hyper-ES arrived independently,
eighteen months apart, at *seed a low-dimensional subspace with gradients,
then search it gradient-free*. Two independent arrivals is a better argument
for the approach than either paper's numbers, and it means `SOTA-154`'s
`contested` reading is a live methodological disagreement rather than one
group's objection.

**What this pass did not cover.** The line is now filed to the edges this
record can see, but three things are open and cheap. The bibliography sweep
described above has not been run on any of the ten papers. `ARXIV-2605.30148`
(*Overcoming Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning with Evolution Strategies*) turned
up in the search for Abdi et al. and is, by title, the remedy paper for the
problem `SOTA-213` addresses from theory — it was not read, and it is the
obvious next thing. And `LIT-235`'s linear-mode-connectivity result, if it
generalizes, is a claim about post-training reaching one basin regardless of
optimizer, which is worth far more than the use this line makes of it and has
no document of its own.

<a id="20260915192755"></a>

## A practice corrected before it shipped, and a condition finally met

*2026-09-15 19:27:55 · record*

Eleven papers. This one was named in the previous pass's uncovered list and
read for that reason, and it moved two documents that were still sitting
unmerged in the same pull request.

**A practice was wrong and got corrected before anyone could act on it.**
`SOTA-213` was filed an hour earlier as a stopping rule: stop ES
post-training when the target task converges, because drift keeps accumulating
and the gains do not. The reasoning was sound given what the record held.
`LIT-237` ran Countdown to 500 iterations, the task converged near 200,
and *averaged* prior-task accuracy fell across the whole run. Drift is linear
in steps. Therefore stop.

`LIT-238` tracks the prior tasks **individually rather than averaged** and
the picture inverts: HellaSwag drops about 8% over the first 300 iterations and
**returns to its original level by the final iteration**. MMLU-Pro and
ARC-Challenge do the same. ProofWriter runs it upside down, improving and then
settling back. A stopping rule fitted to the average would stop at the bottom
of the dip — the single worst point on the curve.

The lesson is not about evolution strategies. **An average over a set of
measurements can invert the sign of the effect you are inferring from it**, and
a practice derived from one is only as good as the disaggregation nobody ran.
The durable half of the original claim — spend budget on population rather
than steps — survived and is now confirmed directly, which is why this was a
rewrite rather than a retirement.

It was also caught by luck. The paper was in the uncovered list because a
search for something else returned it, and it was read because the previous
pass wrote down what it had not covered. **Writing down the gap is what made
the correction possible**, which is the one process claim these entries can
actually support.

**On correcting in place rather than retiring.** The record's rule is to
retire by changing status and never by deleting, and this practice was
rewritten with its title changed rather than marked `Rejected` with a
successor. The distinction is that it had not landed: it exists only in an
open pull request, and the claim was never one the record made. Filing a
`Rejected` document for a recommendation that was never published would put
something in the attic that nobody ever took out of it. The wrong version is
in this entry and in the changelog instead, which is where a reader looking
for the reasoning will find it.

That reasoning does not extend to anything already on `main`. Once a document
has merged, the rule applies without exception.

**`THEORY-008` is `Active`, and it is the first promotion in this line
that was clean.** Its condition asked for the `σ²dT/N` scaling measured by an
independent group, on a transformer at a different scale, with the
population-size dependence tested directly rather than inferred. That is
Table 1 and Figure 6 of this paper: no shared authors, Qwen2.5-3B rather than
Qwen3-4B, population 30 → 128 halving the update norm — which is what an
inverse dependence of the squared norm on `N` predicts for a 4.3× increase —
and prior-task degradation falling monotonically across three population
sizes.

Worth contrasting with `THEORY-006`, which has now been approached three times
and promoted none. The difference is not that one account is better supported
in some vague sense; it is that **`THEORY-008`'s condition named a
quantity and an operation** — raise `N`, watch drift fall — and `THEORY-006`'s
named a measurement that nobody has reason to repeat. A condition that
specifies an experiment someone would run anyway gets met; one that specifies
an experiment only a partisan would run does not. That is a claim about how to
write `promote_when`, and it is the most transferable thing in this entry.

**One refinement that improves the account it confirms.** Even at population
256 or with an anchor penalty, ES update norms stay an order of magnitude
above GRPO's — while the prior-task KL divergence becomes comparable. So the
harm is not carried by the size of the walk: "it is the randomness of the
drift unconstrained by the target task that leads to prior task forgetting for
ES, rather than the magnitude of updates alone." Three papers in this record
had reached for update norm or update sparsity as the explanatory variable.
None of them was the right one.

**What this pass did not cover.** One new name: **Liang et al. (2026)**, cited
here for low-dimensional curvature of fine-tuning landscapes as the reason
very small populations suffice at billion scale. That is `THEORY-006`'s
subject approached from a third direction and it is not in the record. It is
the only outstanding reference from this paper.

Also still unrun: the bibliography sweep the previous entry prescribed —
after filing a paper, list its references the record lacks. It was prescribed
and then not performed on any of the eleven papers, which is its own small
demonstration that a process note in a journal entry is not a process.

<a id="20260915194321"></a>

## An independence claim that was never checked, and the paper that exposed it

*2026-09-15 19:43:21 · record*

Twelve papers. This one was named in the previous pass's uncovered list, read
for that reason, and the first useful thing it produced was not in its own
abstract — it was in its bibliography.

**The record spent four passes calling a paper independent without opening its
author list.** `SOTA-154` was promoted on `LIT-233`, and the promotion turned
entirely on that paper being an outside check: "an independent group", "a
group with no stake in the result", "nobody here wanted ES to win". The
practice's own condition had excluded "further results from the same group",
so the classification was load-bearing.

**Yulu Gan, `LIT-233`'s first author, is the second author of `LIT-211`.**
It is in `LIT-211`'s author list, in `LIT-233`'s bibliography, and in the
related-work section where that paper cites its own prior work. Nothing was
hidden. Four passes read around it.

The reason is worth naming because it is general. **Independence was inferred
from affiliation and framing** — a different institution, a different senior
author, a paper about something else, the ES comparison arriving as a baseline
rather than as a claim. Every one of those is a proxy, and all of them pointed
the same way, which is exactly when a proxy stops being questioned. The actual
test is one line: *is any author of the new paper an author of the old one?*
It costs a glance at two author lists and it was never run.

**The correction that matters is not to the status.** `SOTA-154` stays
`Active`, because Hoy et al. at 4B with both arms swept and ES highest on all
four tasks is a clean independent positive, and Ba et al., EGGROLL and ESSAM
share no author with `LIT-211` either. The practice would have reached the
same place. **But it would not have got there when it did, on what it did**,
and a record whose promotions rest on misread provenance is failing at the one
thing it exists to do. The consensus note is now tallied by authorship rather
than by institution, and doing that moved four of eight positive results
inside the line they had been counted as independent of.

The corollary, and it belongs beside `DP-005`: **counting is only as good as
the equivalence class you count over.** That principle separates adoption from
evidence; this is the same failure a level down, where several "independent"
results turn out to be one group's line with different mastheads.

**A second thing this paper corrected, in the opposite direction.**
`SOTA-213` has now been rewritten twice in this branch. It began as a
stopping rule, was rewritten when the prior-task dip turned out to recover,
and is rewritten again here — because rise-then-decay means the *target*
reward really does peak and then degrade, so early stopping is right after
all, for a different curve. Prior-task accuracy dips and recovers; target
reward rises and falls. Two curves, two answers, and the first two drafts each
had one of them.

That is three versions of one practice in one afternoon, and it is not a sign
the practice was badly conceived. It is a sign of what filing a line **in
citation order rather than publication order** does: each paper arrived
already answered by one the record had not read yet. Liang et al. is January,
Hoy is April, Schweighofer is May; the record met them backwards.

**On `THEORY-006` and `THEORY-007`, which are not rivals.** They look
like competing explanations of the same phenomenon and they are not, because
`LIT-233` says so itself: the thicket is a broad pretrained basin intersected
with a low-dimensional, degenerate set of task directions, and it cites Liang
for the second half. **The record filed the later paper first and would have
filed them as rivals had the citation not been checked** — the same failure as
the authorship one, caught this time because reading the related-work section
is part of a full reading.

Their one real disagreement is about scale, and it is methodological rather
than substantive: `LIT-233` fixes `σ = 1e-3` at every model size and finds
density rising 0% to 64% across 0.5B–32B; `LIT-236` picks a viable `σ`
per model and finds accessibility flat across 0.5B–7B. A perturbation scale
that suits a 32B model need not suit a 0.5B one, which would produce exactly
this pattern with no disagreement about the geometry. **That also weakens the
scale-boundary table this record built two passes ago**, whose low end may be
a tuning artifact rather than a threshold. The table stays, with the competing
reading beside it.

**What this pass did not cover.** No new names came out of this paper's
references that the record lacks — the first time that has been true in this
line. What remains outstanding is the same two items as last time, both now
overdue: the bibliography sweep prescribed two entries ago and still not run
on any of the twelve papers, and `LIT-235`'s linear-mode-connectivity
result, which if it generalizes is a claim about post-training reaching one
basin regardless of optimizer and still has no document of its own.

And one new one, cheap and specific: **check authorship overlap when filing a
paper into an existing line**, and record the answer rather than the
impression. It would have caught this in the pass that introduced it.

## The bibliography sweep, run at last: what twelve papers cite that the record does not hold

*2026-09-15 19:49:38 · record*

Two entries ago this record prescribed a fix for the gap that let it file a
reply before the claim it answers: **after filing a paper, list its references
that the record lacks.** The next entry observed that the prescription had not
been carried out and called that "its own small demonstration that a process
note in a journal entry is not a process." Here it is, run.

## The query, stated so the next person can run it again

For each of the twelve papers in the evolution-strategies line, parse the
bibliography out of the arXiv HTML (`<li id="bib.bibNN">` list items),
extract every arXiv identifier appearing in each entry, and difference the
union against every `arxiv:` field in `record/literature.d/`.

- **532 bibliography entries** across the twelve.
- **144 distinct arXiv identifiers** extracted.
- **227 arXiv identifiers** currently in the record.
- **117 of the 144 are not in the record.**

No script is committed for this. The project removed its helper scripts
deliberately ([#41](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/41)) and `pyproject.toml` says what remains is the frozen
migration; a sweep that runs four times a year does not earn a maintained
artifact. The paragraph above is the artifact.

## What the query cannot see, which is most of it

**Only 45% of the bibliography entries carry an arXiv identifier at all** —
245 of 532 did; the rest are journal and conference references. Everything
classical in this line is therefore invisible to this sweep: Rechenberg (1973),
Schwefel (1977), Hansen and Ostermeier (2001) on CMA-ES, McCloskey and Cohen
(1989) on catastrophic forgetting, Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) on elastic weight
consolidation. Several are cited by four or more of the twelve.

This is [DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4) operating on the pass that was written to fix an instance of
[DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4). The complement of "references carrying an arXiv id" is not empty,
and running the filter harder does not sample it. **The honest statement is
that this sweep found what an arXiv-shaped query can find**, and a second pass
keyed to author-year strings would return a different and older set.

## The headline, and it is worse than the gap that prompted the sweep

**`ARXIV-1703.03864` — Salimans, Ho, Chen, Sidor and Sutskever, *Evolution
Strategies as a Scalable Alternative to Reinforcement Learning* — is cited by
ten of the twelve papers and is not in this record.**

The record holds nine papers descending from it, a practice recommending the
technique it introduced ([SOTA-154](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-154.md)), two theory documents explaining why
that technique works, and not the paper. This is exactly [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s "trunk with
no document": every fork in the line has an entry because every fork was
somebody's contribution, and the thing all ten take for granted has none.

**`ARXIV-1707.06347` — PPO — is cited by six of the twelve and is also
absent.** That gap was noticed by hand two passes ago and written into a
curation entry as a suspected instance. The sweep confirms it and puts a
number on it.

## The shortlist

Ranked within groups by how many of the twelve cite each. Everything here is
missing from the record.

**The trunk of the method.** Filing these is what [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7) asks for.

dimensionality), `ARXIV-1804.08838` (Li et al., intrinsic dimension of
objective landscapes), `ARXIV-1706.04454` (Sagun et al., Hessian of

`ARXIV-2602.04118` (Morris et al., *Learning to reason in 13 parameters*).

`ARXIV-2010.01412` (Foret et al., SAM — what [LIT-240](../../record/literature.d/LIT-240.md) transposes into zeroth

**Benchmarks, model reports and infrastructure**, which this record has never
systematically filed and which the sweep surfaces in volume: GSM8K
(`ARXIV-2110.14168`, 9 of 12), MBPP, the Qwen2.5 technical report,
HellaSwag, ARC, GPQA, MATH, HumanEval, ROCStories, and verl
(`ARXIV-2409.19256`). **Whether these belong here is a scope question the
record has never answered in writing**, and the sweep is the first time the
cost of not answering it has been visible: they are 9 of the 27 most-cited
missing references, and every pass has silently declined them.

## What this changes about how passes should run

The sweep took minutes and the gap it found is the largest single omission in
this line. Two things follow.

**Run it at filing time, not as a separate pass.** The reason it kept not
happening is that it was written down as a future task rather than as part of
what filing a paper means. A note in a journal entry is a reminder; a step in
the filing procedure is a process. This entry is still only the former.

**Count the citations rather than reading them.** The useful output was not
the 117-item list, which nobody will act on, but the ranking. *Cited by ten of
twelve and absent* is a finding; *cited once and absent* is a reading list.
The ranking is what turned a dump into the Salimans result.

## What this pass did not do

It filed nothing. Every entry above is a candidate, and the top two —
Salimans et al. and PPO — are the ones the record should not go another pass
without, on [DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7)'s argument rather than on any judgement about their
quality.

## Filing the trunk, and what it turned out to have already said

*2026-09-15 20:03:25 · record*

The sweep prescribed two papers and the record filed them. Both readings
found something the record did not know, and in both cases what they found was
that a document already here was newer than its idea.

**Salimans et al. §3.2 is `THEORY-007`.** That account — filed two hours ago
from a 2026 paper — holds that ES scales because what matters is not the
ambient parameter count but a low-dimensional effective structure. The 2017
paper:

> However, it is important to note that this does not mean that larger neural
> networks will perform worse than smaller networks when optimized using ES:
> what matters is the difficulty, or intrinsic dimension, of the optimization
> problem.

It gives the argument (concatenate a regression's features with themselves:
parameters double, difficulty does not, ES behaves identically given `σ` and
the learning rate halved) and the observation (larger Atari networks did
slightly better). `LIT-236` adds a mechanism, a measurement across scales, and
the connection to rise-then-decay, all of which are real contributions. **But
the record filed that account without knowing its central claim was nine years
old**, and would have gone on presenting it as new.

The same shape for PPO. Three practices here modify it — `SOTA-145` removes
its critic, `SOTA-146` corrects an objective descended from its clipped ratio,
`SOTA-129` makes the family a recipe stage — and none could cite it. Reading
it turns up a detail no descendant mentions: the ES line grid-searches PPO's
KL coefficient `β`, and PPO's own §4 reports the KL-penalized variant as the
**worse** of the two its authors tested.

**The general form, and it is what `DP-007` is about from a new angle.** That
principle says the agreed trunk goes unfiled because agreement has no arrival.
The corollary this pass adds: **while the trunk is missing, its claims get
re-filed as though they were new by whoever restates them.** A record that
holds only the branches cannot tell a contribution from a restatement, and the
error runs in the flattering direction — every paper looks more original than
it is, because the thing it is building on is not here to compare against.

That is a sharper reason to file trunks than pedagogy. It is not that a reader
wants the foundational paper; it is that **without it the record cannot
grade the ones it has.**

## On what counts as evidence for a practice, revisited

Filing Salimans also settles something the record had been asserting on
[LIT-211](../../record/literature.d/LIT-211.md)'s authority. That ES "tolerates long-horizon and delayed rewards"
has been in this record since `SOTA-154` was filed, as a claim about a claim.
The argument is in §3.1 here: the policy-gradient score term is a sum of `T`
uncorrelated pieces so its variance grows nearly linearly with episode length,
while the ES term is independent of `T`. Four of the five arguments `SOTA-154`
makes for itself originate in this paper, and the practice has been making
them second-hand.

`introduced_by:` stays on [LIT-211](../../record/literature.d/LIT-211.md) and the reasoning is worth keeping: this
paper recommends ES over policy gradients for **control tasks trained from
scratch**, and the practice recommends it for **LLM fine-tuning**, which this
paper does not attempt and whose feasibility the field doubted for eight
years. The doubt is the evidence that they are different claims. Filing the
ancestor makes that distinction visible rather than dissolving it.

## The scope question, answered

`ADR-032` records what the sweep forced: benchmarks, model reports and
infrastructure are admissible `LIT` documents. Three things about how that
decision was reached are worth keeping.

**The record was already half-doing it.** [LIT-119](../../record/literature.d/LIT-119.md), [LIT-130](../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) and [LIT-222](../../record/literature.d/LIT-222.md) are
model reports and a whitepaper, already `Active`. The practice registry counts
model reports as adoption evidence in `consensus:`. So the boundary would have
had to be drawn between things the record already treats identically — which
is [DP-008](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-8)'s warning realized: the scope existed in what the corpus happened
to contain, not in anything anyone decided.

**Nothing in the vocabulary changes**, and that is the test. A benchmark paper
is `analysis-and-evaluation` by that topic's own blurb; a model report takes
the topic of what it reports on; infrastructure is `systems-optimization`.
[DP-008](../../docs/design-principles.md#dp-8) says a category added to admit a single document is how a scope
stops being one — the converse also holds, and a scope change needing no new
category is one the vocabulary was already sized for.

**The trigger stays narrow.** Something in the record has to cite it. A
benchmark nothing here is argued on has no standing to record, and the ADR
says so, because the failure mode of this decision is a reading list that is
mostly instruments.

## What this pass did not do

The backlog the ADR creates is named and unfiled: GSM8K (cited by 9 of 12),
the Qwen2.5 technical report (4), MBPP (3), verl (3). The sweep's ranking is
the queue.

And the sweep itself still has the hole its own entry described: **only 45% of
bibliography entries carry an arXiv identifier**, so the classical ES
literature — Rechenberg 1973, Schwefel 1977, Hansen and Ostermeier 2001 — is
invisible to it. Salimans et al. cites all three in its first paragraph on ES.
Filing the trunk has not reached the roots, and the query that would is a
different one.

<a id="20260915214538"></a>

## The schema was the tell, and I read it as evidence of a stranger

*2026-09-15 21:45:38 · record · migration*

Seventy-four paper notes arrived from another project. I checked every
identifier against arXiv and CrossRef before filing anything, found three
notes bound to the wrong paper and one citation invented outright, and
concluded that the batch was a secondary source whose claims could not be
trusted. So I filed all sixty-eight papers at `Deferred`, filed no readings,
and sent all 187 recommendations to an issue on the grounds that a practice
may not be sourced to a paper nobody here has read.

The rule is right. The premise was wrong: **they were my own readings, made in
a different session under a different agenda.** Nobody had to tell me the
rule; I had to be told the readings were mine.

## What I had in front of me

The incoming schema, from the batch's own `SCHEMA.md`:

    contribution, key_insight, assumptions, key_results, claims, method,
    concepts, connections, recommendations, research_implications,
    limitations, open_questions

The section headings of every NOTE document in this record:

    Contribution, Key insight, Assumptions, Key results, Claims, Method,
    Concepts, Connections, Recommendations, Bearing on the record,
    Limitations, Open questions

Twelve fields, twelve sections, same order, eleven of them the same name. I
read that table, wrote it into a comparison, and did not draw the conclusion.
The thing I did instead was notice that the batch's schema described
`recommendations` as "project-agnostic" and treat that as a *claim by a
stranger to be checked* rather than as a note I had left myself.

## The reasoning error, stated plainly

I had four pieces of evidence and they pointed two ways.

Pointing at "stranger": a different project, a different agenda, an
identifier bound to the wrong paper three times, and a citation that resolves
to nothing.

Pointing at "mine": a schema that is this record's schema, down to field
order.

I weighted the first four and never priced the fifth, because I had a query
shaped like *how much can I trust this?* and a query finds only defects it is
shaped like ([DP-004](../design-principles.md#dp-4)). "Whose work is this?" was never asked, so the
one piece of evidence that answered it went past as an interesting
coincidence.

The nearest precedent in this record is a week old and is the inverse.
Filing `LIT-233` I inferred a paper's *independence* from affiliation, senior
authorship and framing, three proxies agreeing, and never ran the author-list
check that would have contradicted them. Here I inferred a batch's
*foreignness* from provenance, agenda and error rate, three proxies agreeing,
and never asked who wrote the schema. Same failure, opposite sign: proxies
that agree with each other feel like corroboration and are one observation.

## What the findings turned out to mean

The identifier errors are real and none of them survived as a reason to
withhold a reading.

- **`1805.01361`** is not a bad note about a stranger's paper. It is a second
  reading of `1804.06561`, filed against a stranger's identifier. Both
  readings are genuine and they differ — one is precise about the theorem
  statements, the other reaches for the McKean-Vlasov framing. They are merged
  into one note.
- **`1906.08632`**'s reading is of the paper its identifier names. Only the
  title field was taken from a different Goldt paper.
- **`2102.11742`** is the one that does not rebind: the reading names no paper
  its content matches, and its own first paragraph says so. Filed `Deferred`,
  no note. This is the single case where the first decision was right, and it
  is right for one paper rather than sixty-eight.
- **Wolfowitz (1963)** was given a journal, a volume, a page range and a DOI
  that returns 404. That one is not a labelling slip, and it is why metadata
  in the port comes from resolvers in every case and from the reading in none.

## What actually did not port, and why

Not trust — **scope**.

The field that does not survive is `research_implications`, which answers five
questions from that project's `synthesis/research_agenda.md`. Seventy of those
were replaced by a `## Bearing on the record` section written fresh, answering
this record's question instead: what could a practice here rest on, and is
there one.

Twenty-three of the 187 recommendations are marked in place as not filed.
Seventeen name that project's own system and experiments despite the schema
calling the field project-agnostic — which is worth noticing, because it means
a field I labelled "preserved for reuse beyond this project" was not, and the
label did not stop me writing project-specific advice into it. Six are advice
to a theorist about proof technique. They are struck, not deleted.

## What this pass still has not covered

**The readings themselves were not re-verified against the papers.** The
identifier check was on titles and authors. Nothing compared a single entry
under `key_results` or `claims` against the paper it is about. That was the
honest limit of the first pass and it is unchanged by learning whose work it
is — being my own reading makes it portable, not correct.

**Two papers now have two readings and only one is filed.** `LIT-017`
(McCandlish) and `LIT-028` (Kaplan) already had notes. The incoming readings
of both are mostly about curve-fitting for another project's experiments, so
little was lost, but nothing compared them.

**Four of the seventy-four files arrived truncated mid-scalar**, at the end of
`limitations` or `research_implications`. Two lost a partial limitation; two
lost only dropped material. Recovered by discarding the incomplete line.

**The practices filed are seven of a hundred and sixty-four candidates.** They
are the ones where the claim is crisp, the paper is the right place to source
it, and nothing here already says it. The rest is still a backlog, and it is
now a backlog of *reading already done* rather than of reading still owed —
which is a much cheaper thing to owe.

<a id="20260915224717"></a>

## Sixty-seven documents I filed twice, and the report that was never read

*2026-09-15 22:47:17 · record*

Two findings, and the first was found by accident while collecting data for
the second.

## The duplicates

PR [#138](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/138) went in as two commits. The first filed 68 papers as `Deferred`
literature on the argument that their readings could not be trusted. The
second replaced that decision, filed 70 readings and promoted the papers.

**It did not delete the first commit's files.** The regeneration between the
two ran `git clean -fd record/`, which removes *untracked* files — and the
first commit's 68 were tracked, because they had been committed. So the port
minted a second, separate set of codes for the same 68 papers, and both sets
merged.

Result on `main`: **67 duplicate literature notes**, each a `Deferred` stub
for a paper that also has an `Active` note with a reading attached. The
sixty-eighth is not a duplicate — `2102.11742` is `Deferred` in both passes
and the second one survives.

Nothing cited them. None carried a `NOTE`. They inflated the literature count
from 310 to 376 and the undecided-document count from 54 to 121, and they are
removed rather than retired: *retire by changing status, never by deleting*
protects a decision the record made and later reversed, and these are not a
decision. They are one filing, run twice, by a tool error. Retiring them would
put 67 identical stubs in the attic and make the attic mean less.

**The check that would have caught it costs one line** — group the literature
by `arxiv:`/`doi:`/`url:` and look for a bucket with more than one member —
and it is the same shape as the check that found three misbound identifiers in
the import itself, two commits earlier. I ran that check on the incoming
notes and not on what I had written.

The narrower lesson is about `git clean`: it is not "reset the working tree",
and using it as one between two generations of the same generated corpus is
how the first generation survives. `git rm` was the operation needed, and
nothing in the sequence made its absence visible, because the second
generation's files were all new names.

## The report

`docs/reports/unbound-lineage.md` lists relations whose two documents share no
primary topic. It had 38 relations and 16 lines, generated on every `luria
index` since the chains got their invariant, and had never been read through.

Reading all 38, the prior in its own preamble — *"usually a sign the
vocabulary is short a word"* — turns out to be wrong here. **Not one of the 38
wanted a fourteenth topic.** They were four things:

**Fifteen documents plainly mis-filed (retagged).** Eight positional-encoding
papers split between `model-architecture` and `attention-techniques` because
`representation-and-encoding` did not exist when they were filed and nobody
went back after [#114](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/114) added it — its blurb names positional encoding and the
frequency choices that go with it, which is RoPE, ALiBi, YaRN and the rest
verbatim. [LIT-211](../../record/literature.d/LIT-211.md), a paper with *LLM Fine-Tuning* in its title, under
`training-optimization`. Three batch-size claims under `model-architecture`.
An initialization rule under `distributed-optimization`. Two
instability-detection practices under `training-optimization` while the
practices they are compared against — one from the same paper — sat under
`model-stability`.

**Eleven of those fifteen shared one cause**, which is the finding worth more
than the fifteen fixes: a claim extracted from a model report, a Megatron
paper or a systems paper inherits *that document's* topic instead of its own.
[ADR-026](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-026.md)'s filing rule already says not to. This is the first count of how
often it happens.

**Two relations that were analogies, not comparisons (removed).** [ADR-011](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-011.md)
defines `compared_against:` as the work evaluating itself against the other.
Profiling the input pipeline and profiling memory access were never compared;
neither were overlapping communication and pre-fetching batches. The report
calls this case unusual, and it is — two of 38 — but it exists.

**Seven that cross because `analysis-and-evaluation` is a kind, not a
subject.** Every one joins a paper that does something to a paper that
measures it. Twelve topics name a subject; that one names a kind of work, and
it will unbind a lineage every time a line grows an analysis paper. Not one of
those six documents is mis-tagged — [LIT-230](../../record/literature.d/LIT-230.md)'s body argues its own filing and
the argument holds.

**Fifteen genuine fault lines.** A general practice and its domain-specific
instance; rival fixes made at different layers; trunk papers whose
contribution spans two topics. The first shape wants a relation the record
does not have — `specializes:` — which is a scheme change rather than a retag.

One of the fifteen is none of those and was nearly mis-read as the first:
[SOTA-089](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-089.md) against [SOTA-107](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-107.md), where [SOTA-107](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-107.md) is `Rejected` because the 128 in it
was traced to a head dimension rather than a sequence length. The lint caught
it, by refusing an unacknowledged citation of a retired document — which is
the check this project adopted the record to get, firing on a draft of the
decision that was reading the report. An unbound relation with a retired end
is not a filing question at all.

## What this pass did not do

**It did not touch the SSM line.** Mamba, Mamba-2, Mamba-3 and RWKV-7 are
`model-architecture` while Kimi Linear, Gated DeltaNet, GLA, DeltaNet, Griffin
and Monarch Mixer are `attention-techniques`, and there is a rule under the
inconsistency — a model *family* against a *mechanism* — that Mamba satisfies
both halves of. Retagging four papers to bind one line would be the [#101](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/101) move
that `luria.yaml` records as wrong, so it is written down rather than done.

**It did not re-read the bodies of the fifteen retagged documents.** The
retags were argued from title, blurb and the company each document keeps. For
eleven of them the document is a two-line migrated stub with nothing else to
read, but for [LIT-192](../../record/literature.d/LIT-192.md), [LIT-193](../../record/literature.d/LIT-193.md), [LIT-207](../../record/literature.d/LIT-207.md), [LIT-208](../../record/literature.d/LIT-208.md), [LIT-209](../../record/literature.d/LIT-209.md) and [LIT-210](../../record/literature.d/LIT-210.md) there is
a full note and this pass read the summary, not the body.

**It did not check the other generated reports.** `unbound-lineage.md` was
read because it was asked for. `reference-status.md` gets read before every
lint. The rest of `docs/reports/` has had the same amount of attention this
one had, which was none.

<a id="20260915230432"></a>

## The move ADR-031 asked for, and the field I said did not exist

*2026-09-15 23:04:32 · record*

`SOTA-010` — *skip connections promote training stability by smoothing out the
loss landscape* — is a statement about what is true, filed in the scheme for
statements about what to do. [ADR-031](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-031.md) spotted that, listed it first among eight
practices in the same shape, called it and [SOTA-012](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-012.md) the two clearest
candidates to move, and then did not move it:

> Moving one is not a status change, and "retire by changing status, never by
> deleting" does not cover it: a practice re-filed as a theory leaves a SOTA
> code that is neither `Rejected` nor `Superseded` but simply somewhere else.
> That needs its own decision about what the old code says and what happens to
> links into it.

So the work here was the decision, not the move. The move took ten minutes
once the decision existed.

## What made it non-obvious

`Rejected` means different things in the two schemes, and CLAUDE.md says so
plainly: on a practice it means **do not do this**. The `sota-statuses` attic
blurb even offers *"too theoretical"* as a reason, which reads like an
invitation. It is not — that phrasing belongs to the paper scheme, where a
paper can be too theoretical to carry. A practice whose problem is that it was
never a practice is a different animal, and filing this one `Rejected` would
have published the sentence *do not use skip connections*, which is about the
worst thing this record could say by accident.

`Superseded` carries "replaced, and the record says what" with no instruction
attached to the subject matter. That is the decision.

## The correction worth keeping

I drafted the decision asserting that **no typed field could name a successor
in another scheme**, and that the successor would have to live in prose with a
resolvable code. I wrote a whole numbered point about it.

The lint rejected the first save:

> `record/practices.d/SOTA-010.md`: no `superseded_by:` in frontmatter —
> `superseded_by` names a document in **any** scheme, because
> `status: Superseded`

It already crosses schemes, by an explicit luria decision. The claim in my
draft was invented rather than checked, and it was invented about a field I
could have read in `luria.yaml` in ten seconds. The decision now says so in
place rather than quietly using the field, because this is the second time in
one contribution that a check knew something about the record that I did not —
the first was the same lint refusing an unacknowledged citation of `SOTA-107`
while I was writing a decision *about reading a report*, which is how I
learned that practice was in the attic.

Two for two, in one sitting, on facts I asserted from memory about a record I
was actively reading. The pattern is not "the lint is useful"; it is that I
reach for a confident sentence about the record's own machinery at exactly the
moments I am busy with something else.

## What was not done

**[SOTA-012](../../record/practices.d/SOTA-012.md) stays a practice.** It is the other one [ADR-031](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-031.md) called clearest,
from the same paper and the same figure, and the rule now exists to move it
under. It is left because a rule that has moved one document has one data
point, and the next pass should get to test the rule rather than invent it.
Six of the eight remain besides.

**No practice was filed alongside the theory.** The obvious split — a
`use skip connections` practice plus the explanation — produces an instruction
with no reader, because every model in this record already has them and
[DP-007](../design-principles.md#dp-7) keeps the agreed trunk unfiled. Worth recording that the split was
considered and is the natural first move, because the next person to reach one
of the eight will consider it too.

**The five practices the account `explains:` were not re-read.** They were
taken from what the old body already claimed it underwrote. That list is
plausible and unverified, and a wrong `explains:` edge is a claim about why a
practice works.

<a id="20260916003229"></a>

## A rule I stated, measured, and withdrew

*2026-09-16 00:32:29 · record · mechanism*

Closing the unbound-lineage pass I wrote that eleven of its fifteen findings
had one cause: **a claim inherits the topic of the document it was extracted
from.** It is a good sentence. It reads like a rule, and the obvious next
question was whether luria could enforce it from config, without an upstream
feature.

It cannot, and it should not, and the most useful part of finding that out was
discovering the sentence is mostly wrong.

## What the measurements said

**76%.** Of 220 practices naming a source, 167 already share their source's
topic. That is not a defect signal; it is what a correctly filed practice
looks like. An Adam practice sourced to the Adam paper is `training-optimization`
at both ends, and should be.

**Four of six.** Of the practices that pass retagged, four had inherited their
source's topic — `SOTA-060`, `SOTA-092`, `SOTA-093`, `SOTA-094`. The other two
had not: `SOTA-098` and `SOTA-099` were `training-optimization` against
sources in `model-architecture` and `model-stability`, and were wrong in the
opposite direction from the rule I had just written. I generalised from the
majority of a set of six and did not look at the other two.

**Already answered — and that is where I stopped thinking.** The check is
declarable in config, and `luria/invariants.py` had measured it on this record
before the mechanism shipped: 48 of 235 edges, "every one a cross-domain
citation the record was changed to permit", concluding that "a check that
fires on a project for doing the thing it decided to do is worse than no
check". I re-measured — 73 edges, 64 practices — grouped them by topic pair,
saw the biggest bucket was the evolution-strategies line, and wrote the whole
thing off.

**A histogram is not a reading.** Told so in review, I went back and read the
73 one at a time. They are four kinds and only one is settled:

| kind | n | |
|---|--:|---|
| multi-topic source | 16 | a model report sourcing practices across three or more topics — [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md) admitted these deliberately |
| analysis paper as evidence | 14 | the kind-not-subject fact the lineage pass already documents |
| [ADR-026](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-026.md)'s rule working | ~10 | the practice takes its kind, the paper takes the domain it was discovered in |
| everything else | ~33 | cross-layer fault lines, and candidates worth a reading |

Two from the last row: `LIT-112` — *Efficient Memory Management for Large
Language Model **Serving*** — is filed `attention-techniques` while all four
practices under it are `inference-optimization`, whose blurb names cache
layout and serving-time decisions. `LIT-059` (CheckFreq) is
`systems-optimization` while its four checkpointing practices are
`distributed-optimization`, the topic whose blurb names checkpointing. Neither
is confirmed — that needs a reading — but both are the shape of finding the
lineage pass acted on, arriving through a second channel.

So the principle stands and I had argued against it on bad evidence: **a
relation asserts its documents have something in common, and the invariant is
the record saying what.** That is as true of a practice and its evidence as of
two practices.

**And it cannot be declared anyway.** Three lines of config, and
`luria index` raises `KeyError: 'LIT-001'` from `chains.lines_of` — the chain
walker indexes only documents in the declared scheme, and `source:` crosses
`SOTA` to `LIT`. The invariant machinery is fine; the walker under it has
never been asked to cross. That is an upstream fix, not a judgement, and it is
the answer I would have reached on day one by *trying it* instead of by
reasoning about whether it was a good idea.


## What I did instead

`lint.fail_on` had been `[]` since the record was built, so every check the
lint runs is advice. One of them — `source-mismatch` — answers the question
*is this document about the paper it names*, which is the question [DP-001](../design-principles.md#dp-1)
rests on, and it is at zero today. It is now a failure.

The reason it is the right one is not general principle. It is that
**`source-mismatch` is the check that would have failed [#138](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/138)**, whose three

Verified rather than assumed, on this branch: retitling `LIT-045` to another
paper's title produces *"`arxiv: 2104.09864` resolves to 'RoFormer…', not 'A
Mean Field View…'"* and exit 1. A freshly minted note carrying an identifier
that does not match its title fails the same way, with the identifier resolved
live and pinned in the same run.

## What I proposed and had rejected

The first version of this went further: `source-unchecked` in `fail_on` too,
so a green run would mean every reference was *verified* rather than merely
*remembered*. I wrote the cost into the decision honestly — "a network outage
can now fail a contribution that adds a new paper" — and argued it was narrow
and the remedy was in the author's hands.

Rejected, and the reason is better than my argument. The failure
`source-unchecked` adds is an upstream outage. A contributor who did nothing
wrong cannot act on it, and the only move available to them is to learn that
the dial lies — which takes down the class that does work along with it.

The general form is worth keeping. **A check earns enforcement by failing only
on things that are in the diff.** `source-mismatch` reads the committed
lockfile and fails on a disagreement the author introduced: something somebody
can fix. `source-unchecked` fails on something somebody can only wait out.

Writing the cost down honestly is not the same as pricing it correctly. I did
the first and skipped the second, and "narrow, and the remedy is in the
author's hands" was doing the work of an argument without being one.

## The one it does not cover, and where it already lives

Sixty-seven duplicate notes — the defect [#138](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/138) actually shipped — have correct
titles and correct identifiers. Two documents claiming one identifier is not
in luria's finding vocabulary at all, and no config setting produces it.

It is already filed upstream as `LU-#165`, reached from a two-document
collision rather than a sixty-seven-document one, and it goes further than the
issue I opened here: besides a `duplicate-source` finding it asks for a
`luria merge` that resolves one by rewriting references, appending the loser's
code to `formerly:`, and retiring rather than deleting it — which is exactly
the work I did by hand in [#140](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/140) and would have done by hand again. I filed a
duplicate because I searched the finding *vocabulary* for the check and never
searched the *issues* for somebody having already noticed it was missing.

## The pattern this makes four of

Four times in two days I have asserted something about this record's own
machinery and been corrected — three times by the machinery, once by a reader:

- `SOTA-107` described as a live practice while writing a decision about
  reading a report. It is in the attic, and the lint said so.
- `superseded_by` declared unable to cross schemes, in a decision whose whole
  subject was crossing schemes. It crosses schemes; the lint said so on the
  first save.
- *A claim inherits the topic of its source*, offered as a finding worth
  eleven corrections. 76% base rate; the measurement said so.
- The `source:` invariant argued down on a count. Reading the count's
  contents says otherwise, and the actual blocker — a `KeyError` in the chain
  walker — was one config edit away the whole time.

The first three share a shape: I reach for a confident sentence about the
**tooling** at exactly the moment I am concentrating on the **content**, and
the tooling is what I am least likely to check because it is not what I am
thinking about.

The fourth is different and worse. Nothing about it was inattention — I
measured, I quoted the upstream docstring, I built a table. What I did was
**stop at the number**. 73 was large, the largest bucket had an explanation I
already believed, and that was enough to close the question. Reading the 73
takes about ten minutes and reverses the conclusion.

The rule that would have caught all four is the same one: **when the claim is
about the tooling, run the tooling.** Declaring the chain takes three lines
and fails in four seconds, which is less effort than the paragraph I wrote
arguing it was a bad idea.

<a id="20260916020333"></a>

## Replace where I should have added, and the constraint that made it look like a choice

*2026-09-16 02:03:33 · taxonomy · record*

The retagging pass in [#140](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/140) moved fifteen documents. Review:

> you've replaced a bunch of tags where you just needed to add an additional
> tag. the old tags still seem applicable in the cases I reviewed.

Re-reading them, that is right about eleven of the fifteen. `LIT-192`
(Positional Interpolation) and `LIT-193` (YaRN) went from
`attention-techniques` to `representation-and-encoding` — and
`attention-techniques` names *context length* in its own blurb, which is
exactly what a context-extension paper is about. `LIT-208` proposes a hybrid
**attention** strategy; the title says so. In each case the new topic is
better and the old one was not wrong.

## The part I did not notice I was choosing

`fields.tags.groups.primary_topic` required `exactly-one` of the thirteen, so
a second topic was a hard lint violation. **There was no additive option.**

That is the uncomfortable part. I did not weigh "replace" against "add" and
pick replace — the schema offered one move and I took it without registering
that it was a constraint rather than a decision. A constraint you do not
notice reads exactly like a judgement you made, and the artefact it leaves
behind is indistinguishable: fifteen documents that assert their old topic was
wrong, when eleven of them assert no such thing.

`luria.yaml` already records this corner from the other side, at [#101](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/101):
*"the only move available under `exactly-one` — it satisfied the check rather
than answering it."* There the constraint forced an incidental secondary tag
*in*. Here it forced a true topic *out*. Same constraint, opposite damage, and
the note about it was three screens above the rule while I was editing the
file.

## What changed

`require: any`, on all four schemes. `primary_topic` still derives
`{tags[0]}`, so the primary is still one value and the chain invariants still
compare one against one — verified, because it was the thing most likely to
break: `docs/reports/unbound-lineage.md` is byte-identical at 24 relations and
10 lines with the group relaxed and a second topic added.

The four that stay replacements are the ones where the old tag named **where
the claim was found** rather than what it is about — `SOTA-060` filed
`distributed-optimization` because its source is a Megatron paper,
`SOTA-092`/`093`/`094` filed `model-architecture` because theirs is a model
report. Restoring those would preserve a mistake rather than information.

## What this costs, and what it does not

**Tag order is now load-bearing.** Reordering `tags:` silently retags a
document, and nothing checks it. Measured before changing anything: all 596
documents currently list a topic first, so nothing is broken today — but the
convention was already unguarded and the ways to trip it just got more
plausible. `LU-#229` is the upstream ask.

**The invariant moved too, on the same review.** *"the primary topic doesn't
need to be invariant, just the presence of a common tag across the edge"* —
which is what a relation asserts. The objection that kept it on
`primary_topic` — *"any shared tag is too weak to carry it"* — was correct
only while `exactly-one` made every secondary a free-form label. Relaxing the
group is what made moving the invariant safe, and I had written the opposite
into the decision an hour earlier.

Measured rather than argued: three edges bind, two rightly, and the third on
the `flash-attention` label [#101](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/101) added to bind it. Removing those two tags
re-opens the edge — the finding `luria.yaml` says should stay open — and the
count settles at 22.

**What the move does not license.** Letting a shared *secondary* bind a
relation is still the failure `luria.yaml` rejects by name, and it is now
possible rather than impossible — giving two documents a common word is a
cheap way to close a finding. The two `flash-attention` tags were exactly
that, and removing them is the price of the change rather than a bonus.
Widening what a document may **say** is not widening what a relation may
**assert**, and the vocabulary being closed is what keeps the cheap move
from being a silent one.

**And closing it has its own cost**, raised in the same review: a guard
mainly teaches people not to trip it. The lint says *"is not in the `topics`
vocabulary — the values are …"*, which sets up "pick the nearest of these
fourteen" — the failure this entire pass repaired, eight papers filed under
the nearest available word because the right one did not exist yet. So
`CLAUDE.md` now says in as many words that the closure is an invitation and
adding a word is the intended move, and `LU-#273` asks luria to let the rule
carry that note itself, where the failure is. If that is refused the honest
answer is to re-open the vocabulary: a guard that teaches the wrong lesson is
worse than the typo it catches.

## The pattern, updated

This is the fifth correction in three days, and the first that is not about
asserting something unverified. The previous four were claims about the
tooling made from memory. This one is the opposite: I read the tooling
correctly, did what it allowed, and never asked whether what it allowed was
what I wanted. The check that would have caught it is not "run the tool" but
"when the tool permits exactly one move, say out loud that it is the tool
choosing" — because that sentence, written down, is obviously a question for
the person who owns the schema.

<a id="20260916051556"></a>

## I argued they were the same object and then built a check for whether they agreed

*2026-09-16 05:15:56 · taxonomy · record*

luria 0.23.0 made it possible to assert a shared field across a scheme
boundary. This record has six relations that cross one, so I measured all six
and declared `invariant: tags` on the one that earned it — `NOTE.paper`, 4
findings in 158 edges against 20-47% for the other five. The argument for
picking it was that a note and its paper are **the same object**, where the
others join two things this record files on different axes on purpose.

Review:

> given that a note and its paper are the same object, rather than specifying
> an invariant (an "at least one" similarity), I feel like it would be more
> appropriate to use a derived field.

That is my own premise, carried one step further than I carried it. If the
two are the same object, the note has no subject of its own to agree or
disagree about — it should *derive* the paper's, the way `NOTE.published`
already derived the paper's date for exactly this reason. I had the argument
and stopped at the weaker mechanism: reporting a disagreement that should not
have been representable.

The tell was available and I did not read it. `NOTE.published` was sitting
four lines above `NOTE.tags` in the config, doing the thing, with a comment
saying why.

## What it cost to find out, and what it bought

Building it turned up a luria bug worth more than the change: `derive` refused
`many` on any field, and dropping `many` to satisfy the refusal made the
derived list read as *no values at all*, which deleted all fourteen
`docs/notes/tags/*.md` pages with nothing failing. [LU-#276](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/276), fixed in 0.24.0 —
found because this record was the first to want a derived list.

## The part the redesign forced

Four notes disagreed with their papers, and I had deliberately left them
standing: retagging a paper inside the commit that turns a check on is [#101](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/101)'s
mistake with better manners.

Deriving changes that. The note now adopts the paper's tag, so the
disagreement does not become a finding to work through later — it becomes
invisible. And two of the four were the only reason anyone noticed the
*paper* was wrong: `LIT-024` filing multi-query attention under
`model-architecture`, `LIT-112` filing vLLM under `attention-techniques`.
Under the invariant they could wait. Under the derivation they could not, so
they went in the same contribution.

Worth keeping: **a decision about mechanism can change what counts as scope.**
"Leave the findings standing" was right for the check and wrong for the
derivation, and nothing about the four documents changed in between.

## What the record gives up

A note can no longer say its paper is filed wrong. It was never the note's
job, it was doing it by accident, and it was the only mechanism the record had
for noticing — four in 158, all four real. What comes back is that retagging a
paper now moves its reading for free, so fixing one costs less than noticing
one used to.

<a id="20260916151302"></a>

## The file with the most reasons in it was the one nothing checked

*2026-09-16 15:13:02 · record · ci*

A question — does concretization fire here after a merge? — turned into this.
It does: the decision written earlier today was numbered [ADR-038](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-038.md) on the
merge an hour before this. But
answering it meant checking which files the rename actually touches, and the
answer was *the record*, not `luria.yaml`.

`code.globs` was `src/**/*.py`. The config was scanned by nothing, and it
holds **87 code citations across 38 documents** — more than any other file
here, and all of them the same kind of claim: this is why the schema is shaped
this way. Sixteen were dead. Ten were the temporary code that became [ADR-035](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-035.md)
back in [#140](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/140), which had been pointing at nothing for days.

The check's own justification, in luria's configuration reference, is that *"a
decision number in a code comment is the strongest form of the claim being
checked"*. By that argument `luria.yaml` should have been the first entry in
the globs. It was not in them at all, and nobody noticed because an unscanned
file produces no findings, which looks exactly like a clean one.

## Three things the check caught in the act of being added

**A directive that half-worked.** The first `inactive-ok-file:` named nine
codes across two wrapped lines. It suppressed the four on the first line and
silently ignored the five on the second — so the warning count dropped, which
is the signal an author reads as "it worked". Wrapping is the ordinary thing
to do at nine codes. Filed as [LU-#278](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/278); noted in the directive itself so the
next person does not spend the same ten minutes.

**My own ADR, twice.** Writing the decision, I cited two luria ADRs without
the `LU-` prefix — the exact bug the contribution exists to fix, committed
while fixing it. Then the dead temp codes I had quoted *as examples of dead
temp codes* were read as citations, and one of them voided the annotation
meant to cover them. Backticks do not make a code a mention here, whatever I
remembered.

**A stale directive is itself a finding.** Naming one unknown code in an
`inactive-ok-file:` voids the whole annotation — and luria says so, naming
what was left unacknowledged as a result. That is the behaviour to want: the
failure was loud instead of quiet, which is the entire difference between this
and the sixteen citations that rotted in silence.

## The general shape

Every finding in this contribution has the same structure. Something was
true, then stopped being true, and the mechanism that would have said so did
not cover the place it happened. Concretization rewrites the record;
`luria link --fix` rewrites record prose; neither touches a code-glob file,
and the config was in no category at all.

Left open, and it has no mechanism anywhere: a *remote's* temporary code.
[LU-ADR-084](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/blob/main/record/decisions.d/ADR-084.md) was cited here as a temp code from luria's repo. No local merge can
fix that, because the concretization that resolved it happened in a different
repository. The lint now reports it as unresolved, which is how this one
surfaced — but reporting is all there is.

<a id="20260916173108"></a>

## The fix for a directive with too many codes is not a longer line

*2026-09-16 17:31:08 · record*

I filed [LU-#278](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/278) because a wrapped `inactive-ok-file:` had suppressed the codes
on its first line and silently ignored the rest. That much was true and is
worth having found. What I proposed was that luria read the continuation.

Closed, and the reasoning is better than mine:

> a file-wide acknowledgement isn't even position sensitive, so there's zero
> risk breaking this up into multiple acknowledgements if the author doesn't
> like having it all on a single line. If this emerges as a more pervasive
> issue, I think the question should be why certain acknowledgements are
> accumulating so many codes and what we can do about that.

Two things I had not thought about.

**The constraint was not binding.** I had treated "every code on one line" as
a cost to be paid and written a warning into the config telling the next
person to pay it. A file-scoped directive applies to the whole file, so
`n` directives and one directive naming `n` codes are the same statement.
There was never a reason to crowd the line — I only ever considered one
directive because that is the shape the first one happened to have.

**Splitting made the prose better, which is the tell.** The eight codes fell
into two groups without any effort: three Superseded and named *as* history,
five Proposed and merely unmoved. The one-line version had to explain both in
a single trailing paragraph. Two directives each carry their own reason and
the paragraph disappears. When a workaround's removal improves the thing it
was working around, the workaround was hiding a design smell rather than a
tool limitation.

**And the question to hold onto.** Not "how do I fit more codes on a line"
but "why is one place citing this many retired documents". Here the answer is
benign — the config implements the decisions, so of course it cites them —
but it is the right question and I would not have asked it.

## What I wrote into the file, and shouldn't have

The config carried a paragraph beginning *"Every code on ONE line,
deliberately"*, pointing at an open issue. That is a note about a tool
defect, sitting in a record whose whole subject is this project's own
choices. It is gone. The replacement says why there are two directives, which
is a fact about the acknowledgement rather than about luria's parser.

<a id="20260916180822"></a>

## The contradiction was in the reading, not between the papers

*2026-09-16 18:08:22 · record*

Issue [#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) lists four unreconciled contradictions and calls them the valuable
part of the backlog. The first is LAMB against Shallue: *"Whichever is right,
they cannot both be applied."* I took that one first.

It dissolved on contact with the papers, and the way it dissolved is the
finding.

**LAMB cites Shallue. Approvingly. As motivation.** Its related-work section
summarises `LIT-058` as showing that "learning rate scaling heuristics with the
batch size do not hold across all problems or across all batch sizes", and then
proposes a different optimizer rather than a better heuristic. The two papers
have never disagreed about anything.

**LAMB labels its own headline tables *untuned*.** Tables 4 and 5 say so in the
title. The body says three separate times that manual tuning does better — at a
batch of 16K, changing one learning rate moves SQuAD F1 from the reported 91.345
to 91.688. The claim was never that the square-root rule is *correct*. It is
that the rule is *sufficient to reach a fixed target without a sweep* under an
optimizer that normalizes per layer and per coordinate.

**And Shallue never swept an optimizer of that kind.** Three optimizers, all
SGD-family, all with one global step size. LAMB is outside its sample, not a
counterexample to it.

So the record had constructed a conflict out of two compatible claims by
collapsing *sufficient for one target* into *the heuristic is right*, and by
reading a result about three optimizers as a result about heuristics in general.
`SOTA-218` closed with a paragraph announcing the standoff; `NOTE-132` refused a
practice on its strength. Both are now the other thing.

The reconciliation needed a third document to hold it, and `THEORY-012` is
it: a scaling rule is a guess about how the usable step grows with the batch,
that step is bounded by the worst-conditioned direction the optimizer does not
normalize away, and an optimizer that normalizes more directions carries the
same rule further. Shallue's own discussion says this — momentum extends perfect
scaling past plain SGD, and "optimizers that estimate local curvature
information might be able to benefit more from large batches". That sentence is
in the paper most often cited against the position.

## The part that should worry someone

I went to the papers to settle an argument and came back with four wrong
numbers, none of which had anything to do with the argument.

`SOTA-218` was filed yesterday, well written, and said the study ran **71
million training runs across seven workloads and four optimizers**. The paper
ran **168,160 models across 35 workloads with three optimizers**; 71,638,836 is
its count of *loss measurements*, the published database of training curves.
The run count was off by a factor of 426. The practice also merged the two
ranges the paper reports separately — where perfect scaling ends (2^4 to 2^13)
and where the plateau begins (2^9 to 2^16) — into a single span running from the
bottom of the first to the top of the second, which is not a quantity the paper
names. `LIT-058` had the model-family and data-set counts transposed.

Every one of those figures is in the abstract or the conclusion. Nothing in the
record could have caught them: the lint checks that citations resolve and that
cited documents are live, and all of these citations resolved to a live document
that simply says something else.

This is exactly the loose end [#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) names — *"No reading in the port was
re-verified against its paper. The check that ran was on identifiers... nothing
says the error rate is lower in the fields nothing can check."* It is now one
observed instance rather than a worry, and it was found the only way it could
be: by needing a number badly enough to go and look.

`DP-004` is the principle, arriving from a direction it did not list. The
identifier check was a pass whose query was *does this code resolve*, and a
clean run of it is evidence about codes. The complement — *does this sentence
describe the paper* — has no mechanical query at all, which makes it the shape
of defect this record is least equipped to find and most likely to accumulate.

## What I did not do

Three contradictions remain on [#139](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/issues/139) (DiLoCo's `H=500` against post-local SGD,
the duplicated noise-scale statistic, SlowMo against `SOTA-155`), five practice
candidates, and two class-closing ADRs. I took one, and took it all the way
down, on the theory that a contradiction half-reconciled is worse than one left
open — the second reader cannot tell which half was checked.
